title: Throwing a Forward Pass
snippet: Throwing a Forward Pass: A quarterback is standing on the football field preparing to throw a pass. His receiver is standing 20 yd down the field and 15 yd to the quarterback’s left. The quarterback throws the ball at a velocity of 60 mph...
body_xml:
<example number="2.20" title="Throwing a Forward Pass">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A quarterback is standing on the football field preparing to throw a pass. His receiver is standing 20 yd down the field and 15 yd to the quarterback’s left. The quarterback throws the ball at a velocity of 60 mph toward the receiver at an upward angle of $$30^\circ$$ (see the following figure). Write the initial velocity vector of the ball, $$\mathbf{ \text{v} },$$ in component form.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The first thing we want to do is find a vector in the same direction as the velocity vector of the ball. We then scale the vector appropriately so that it has the right magnitude. Consider the vector $$\mathbf{ \text{w} }$$ extending from the quarterback’s arm to a point directly above the receiver’s head at an angle of $$30^\circ$$ (see the following figure). This vector would have the same direction as $$\mathbf{ \text{v} },$$ but it may not have the right magnitude.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The receiver is 20 yd down the field and 15 yd to the quarterback’s left. Therefore, the straight-line distance from the quarterback to the receiver is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Dist from QB to receiver} = \sqrt{15^{2} + 20^{2}} = \sqrt{225 + 400} = \sqrt{625} = 25 \text{yd} .$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We have $$\frac{25}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{w} } \right\|} = \cos 30^\circ.$$ Then the magnitude of $$\mathbf{ \text{w} }$$ is given by</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\| \mathbf{ \text{w} } \right\| = \frac{25}{\cos 30^\circ} = \frac{25 \cdot 2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{50}{\sqrt{3}} \text{yd}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and the vertical distance from the receiver to the terminal point of $$\mathbf{ \text{w} }$$ is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Vert dist from receiver to terminal point of} \mathbf{ \text{w} } = \left\| \mathbf{ \text{w} } \right\|\sin 30^\circ = \frac{50}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{25}{\sqrt{3}} \text{yd} .$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then $$\mathbf{ \text{w} } = \left\langle {20,15,\frac{25}{\sqrt{3}}} \right\rangle,$$ and has the same direction as $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Recall, though, that we calculated the magnitude of $$\mathbf{ \text{w} }$$ to be $$\left\| \mathbf{ \text{w} } \right\| = \frac{50}{\sqrt{3}},$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }$$ has magnitude $$60$$ mph. So, we need to multiply vector $$\mathbf{ \text{w} }$$ by an appropriate constant, $$k.$$ We want to find a value of $$k$$ so that $$\left\| {k\mathbf{ \text{w} }} \right\| = 60$$ mph. We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\| {k\mathbf{ \text{w} }} \right\| = k\left\| \mathbf{ \text{w} } \right\| = k\frac{50}{\sqrt{3}} \text{mph,}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>so we want</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} & & \\ & & \\ {k\frac{50}{\sqrt{3}}} & = & 60 \\ k & = & \frac{60\sqrt{3}}{50} \\ k & = & {\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{5}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = k\mathbf{ \text{w} } = k\left\langle {20,15,\frac{25}{\sqrt{3}}} \right\rangle = \frac{6\sqrt{3}}{5}\left\langle {20,15,\frac{25}{\sqrt{3}}} \right\rangle = \left\langle {24\sqrt{3},18\sqrt{3},30} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let’s double-check that $$\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\| = 60.$$ We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\| = \sqrt{\left( {24\sqrt{3}} \right)^{2} + \left( {18\sqrt{3}} \right)^{2} + (30)^{2}} = \sqrt{1728 + 972 + 900} = \sqrt{3600} = 60 \text{mph} .$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, we have found the correct components for $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

        <item>Find the dot product of $$\mathbf{ \text{u} } = \left\langle {3,5,2} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {-1,3,0} \right\rangle.$$</item>

We still have three components for each vector to substitute into the formula for the dot product: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{p} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{q} }} & {= u_{1}v_{1} + u_{2}v_{2} + u_{3}v_{3}} \\ & {= 10(-2) + (-4)(1) + (7)(6) = -20 - 4 + 42 = 18.} \end{array}$$</item>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="2.3" title="Properties of the Dot Product">
    <heading level="4">Properties of the Dot Product</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{u} },$$ $$\mathbf{ \text{v} },$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{w} }$$ be vectors, and let c be a scalar.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lccrllccl} \text{i.} & & & {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} }} & = & {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{u} }} & & & \text{Commutative property} \\ \text{ii.} & & & {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{v} } + \mathbf{ \text{w} }} \right)} & = & {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} } + \mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{w} }} & & & \text{Distributive property} \\ \text{iii.} & & & {c\left( {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} }} \right)} & = & {\left( {c\mathbf{ \text{u} }} \right) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} } = \mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \left( {c\mathbf{ \text{v} }} \right)} & & & \text{Associative property} \\ \text{iv.} & & & {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} }} & = & \left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\|^{2} & & & \text{Property of magnitude} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Using Properties of the Dot Product
snippet: Using Properties of the Dot Product: Let \mathbf{ \text{a} } = \left\langle {1,2,-3} \right\rangle, \mathbf{ \text{b} } = \left\langle {0,2,4} \right\rangle, and \mathbf{ \text{c} } = \left\langle {5,-1,3} \right\rangle. Find each of the...

<example number="2.22" title="Using Properties of the Dot Product">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{a} } = \left\langle {1,2,-3} \right\rangle,$$ $$\mathbf{ \text{b} } = \left\langle {0,2,4} \right\rangle,$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{c} } = \left\langle {5,-1,3} \right\rangle.$$ Find each of the following products.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left( {\mathbf{ \text{a} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{b} }} \right)\mathbf{ \text{c} }$$</item>
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{a} } \cdot \left( {2\mathbf{ \text{c} }} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\left\| \mathbf{ \text{b} } \right\|^{2}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Note that this expression asks for the scalar multiple of c by $$\mathbf{ \text{a} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{b} }:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\left( {\mathbf{ \text{a} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{b} }} \right)\mathbf{ \text{c} }} & {= \left( {\left\langle {1,2,-3} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {0,2,4} \right\rangle} \right)\left\langle {5,-1,3} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \left( {1(0) + 2(2) + (-3)(4)} \right)\left\langle {5,-1,3} \right\rangle} \\ & {= -8\left\langle {5,-1,3} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \left\langle {-40,8,-24} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>This expression is a dot product of vector a and scalar multiple 2c: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{a} } \cdot \left( {2\mathbf{ \text{c} }} \right)} & {= 2\left( {\mathbf{ \text{a} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{c} }} \right)} \\ & {= 2\left( {\left\langle {1,2,-3} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {5,-1,3} \right\rangle} \right)} \\ & {= 2\left( {1(5) + 2(-1) + (-3)(3)} \right)} \\ & {= 2(-6) = -12.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>Simplifying this expression is a straightforward application of the dot product: $$\left\| \mathbf{ \text{b} } \right\|^{2} = \mathbf{ \text{b} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{b} } = \left\langle {0,2,4} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {0,2,4} \right\rangle = 0^{2} + 2^{2} + 4^{2} = 0 + 4 + 16 = 20.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Finding the Angle between Two Vectors: Find the measure of the angle between each pair of vectors. i + j + k and 2i – j – 3k \left\langle {2,5,6} \right\rangle and \left\langle {-2,-4,4} \right\rangle To find the cosine of the angle formed...
body_xml:
<example number="2.23" title="Finding the Angle between Two Vectors">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the measure of the angle between each pair of vectors.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>i + j + k and 2i – j – 3k</item>
        <item>$$\left\langle {2,5,6} \right\rangle$$ and $$\left\langle {-2,-4,4} \right\rangle$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To find the cosine of the angle formed by the two vectors, substitute the components of the vectors into Equation 2.5: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\cos \theta} & {= \frac{(\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \mathbf{ \text{j} } + \mathbf{ \text{k} }) \cdot \left( {2\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \mathbf{ \text{j} } - 3\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right)}{\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \mathbf{ \text{j} } + \mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\| \cdot \left\| {2\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \mathbf{ \text{j} } - 3\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{1(2) + (1)(-1) + (1)(-3)}{\sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2} + 1^{2}} \sqrt{2^{2} + {(-1)}^{2} + {(-3)}^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{-2}{\sqrt{3} \sqrt{14}} = \frac{-2}{\sqrt{42}}.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, $$\theta = \arccos \frac{-2}{\sqrt{42}}$$ rad.</item>
        <item>Start by finding the value of the cosine of the angle between the vectors: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\cos \theta} & {= \frac{\left\langle {2,5,6} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {-2,-4,4} \right\rangle}{\left\| \left\langle {2,5,6} \right\rangle \right\| \cdot \left\| \left\langle {-2,-4,4} \right\rangle \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{2(-2) + (5)(-4) + (6)(4)}{\sqrt{2^{2} + 5^{2} + 6^{2}} \sqrt{{(-2)}^{2} + {(-4)}^{2} + 4^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{0}{\sqrt{65} \sqrt{36}} = 0.} \end{array}$$ Now, $$\cos \theta = 0$$ and $$0 \leq \theta \leq \pi,$$ so $$\theta = {\pi/2.}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="2.25" title="Measuring the Angle Formed by Two Vectors">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {2,3,3} \right\rangle.$$ Find the measures of the angles formed by the following vectors.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\textbf{v}$$ and i</item>
        <item>$$\textbf{v}$$ and j</item>
        <item>$$\textbf{v}$$ and k</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Let α be the angle formed by $$\textbf{v}$$ and i: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\cos \alpha} & {= \frac{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{i} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\| \cdot \left\| \mathbf{ \text{i} } \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{\left\langle {2,3,3} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {1,0,0} \right\rangle}{\sqrt{2^{2} + 3^{2} + 3^{2}} \sqrt{1}}} \\ & {= \frac{2}{\sqrt{22}}.} \end{array}$$ $$\alpha = \arccos \frac{2}{\sqrt{22}} \approx 1.130 \text{rad} .$$</item>
        <item>Let β represent the angle formed by $$\textbf{v}$$ and j: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\cos \beta} & {= \frac{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{j} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\| \cdot \left\| \mathbf{ \text{j} } \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{\left\langle {2,3,3} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {0,1,0} \right\rangle}{\sqrt{2^{2} + 3^{2} + 3^{2}} \sqrt{1}}} \\ & {= \frac{3}{\sqrt{22}}.} \end{array}$$ $$\beta = \arccos \frac{3}{\sqrt{22}} \approx 0.877 \text{rad.}$$</item>
        <item>Let γ represent the angle formed by $$\textbf{v}$$ and k: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\cos \gamma} & {= \frac{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{k} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\| \cdot \left\| \mathbf{ \text{k} } \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{\left\langle {2,3,3} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {0,0,1} \right\rangle}{\sqrt{2^{2} + 3^{2} + 3^{2}} \sqrt{1}}} \\ & {= \frac{3}{\sqrt{22}}.} \end{array}$$ $$\gamma = \arccos \frac{3}{\sqrt{22}} \approx 0.877 \text{rad.}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Vectors in an Economic Context
snippet: Using Vectors in an Economic Context: AAA Party Supply Store sells invitations, party favors, decorations, and food service items such as paper plates and napkins. When AAA buys its inventory, it pays 25¢ per package for invitations and...
body_xml:
<example number="2.26" title="Using Vectors in an Economic Context">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>AAA Party Supply Store sells invitations, party favors, decorations, and food service items such as paper plates and napkins. When AAA buys its inventory, it pays 25¢ per package for invitations and party favors. Decorations cost AAA 50¢ each, and food service items cost 20¢ per package. AAA sells invitations for \$2.50 per package and party favors for \$1.50 per package. Decorations sell for \$4.50 each and food service items for \$1.25 per package.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>During the month of May, AAA Party Supply Store sells 1258 invitations, 342 party favors, 2426 decorations, and 1354 food service items. Use vectors and dot products to calculate how much money AAA made in sales during the month of May. How much did the store make in profit?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The cost, price, and quantity vectors are</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{ \text{c} } = \left\langle {0.25,0.25,0.50,0.20} \right\rangle} \\ {\mathbf{ \text{p} } = \left\langle {2.50,1.50,4.50,1.25} \right\rangle} \\ {\mathbf{ \text{q} } = \left\langle {1258,342,2426,1354} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>AAA sales for the month of May can be calculated using the dot product $$\mathbf{ \text{p} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{q} }.$$ We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{p} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{q} }} & {= \left\langle {2.50,1.50,4.50,1.25} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {1258,342,2426,1354} \right\rangle} \\ & {= 3145 + 513 + 10917 + 1692.5} \\ & {= 16267.5.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, AAA took in \$16,267.50 during the month of May.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To calculate the profit, we must first calculate how much AAA paid for the items sold. We use the dot product $$\mathbf{ \text{c} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{q} }$$ to get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{c} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{q} }} & {= \left\langle {0.25,0.25,0.50,0.20} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {1258,342,2426,1354} \right\rangle} \\ & {= 314.5 + 85.5 + 1213 + 270.8} \\ & {= 1883.8.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, AAA paid \$1,883.80 for the items they sold. Their profit, then, is given by</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{p} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{q} } - \mathbf{ \text{c} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{q} }} & {= 16267.5 - 1883.8} \\ & {= 14383.7.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, AAA Party Supply Store made \$14,383.70 in May.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: The vector projection of \textbf{v} onto \textbf{u} is the vector labeled projuv in Figure 2.50. It has the same initial point as \textbf{u} and \textbf{v} and the same direction as \textbf{u} , and represents the component of...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>The vector projection of $$\textbf{v}$$ onto $$\textbf{u}$$ is the vector labeled projuv in Figure 2.50. It has the same initial point as $$\textbf{u}$$ and $$\textbf{v}$$ and the same direction as $$\textbf{u}$$ , and represents the component of $$\textbf{v}$$ that acts in the direction of $$\textbf{u}$$ . If $$\theta$$ represents the angle between $$\textbf{u}$$ and $$\textbf{v}$$ , then, by properties of triangles, we know the length of $$\text{proj} _{\mathbf{ \text{u} }}\mathbf{ \text{v} }$$ is $$\left\| \text{proj} _{\mathbf{ \text{u} }}\textbf{v} \right\| = {\left\| \textbf{v} \right\| \cdot}\left| \cos \right| \theta.$$ Note that when the angle $$\theta$$ between $$\mathbf{ \text{u} }$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }$$ is an obtuse angle, the projection will be in the opposite direction of $$\mathbf{ \text{u} }$$ . When expressing $$\cos \theta$$ in terms of the dot product, this becomes</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} \left\| \text{proj} _{\mathbf{ \text{u} }}\textbf{v} \right\| & {= {\left\| \textbf{v} \right\| \cdot}\left| \cos \right| \theta} \\ & {= \left\| \textbf{v} \right\|\left( \frac{\left| \textbf{u} \cdot \textbf{v} \right|}{\left\| \textbf{u} \right\|\left\| \textbf{v} \right\|} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{\left| \textbf{u} \cdot \textbf{v} \right|}{\left\| \textbf{u} \right\|}.} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We now multiply by a unit vector in the direction of $$\textbf{u}$$ to get $$\text{proj} _{\mathbf{ \text{u} }}\mathbf{ \text{v} }:$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{proj} _{\mathbf{ \text{u} }}\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \frac{\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{u} } \right\|}\left( {\frac{1}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{u} } \right\|}\mathbf{ \text{u} }} \right) = \frac{\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{u} } \right\|^{2}}\mathbf{ \text{u} }.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The length of this vector is also known as the scalar projection of $$\textbf{v}$$ onto $$\textbf{u}$$ and is denoted by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{comp} _{\mathbf{ \text{u} }}\textbf{v} = \frac{\textbf{u} \cdot \textbf{v}}{\left\| \textbf{u} \right\|}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding Projections
snippet: Finding Projections: Find the projection of \textbf{v} onto u. \mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {3,5,1} \right\rangle and \mathbf{ \text{u} } = \left\langle {-1,4,3} \right\rangle \mathbf{ \text{v} } = 3\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 2\mathbf{...
body_xml:
<example number="2.27" title="Finding Projections">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the projection of $$\textbf{v}$$ onto u.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {3,5,1} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{u} } = \left\langle {-1,4,3} \right\rangle$$</item>
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = 3\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 2\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{u} } = \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Substitute the components of $$\textbf{v}$$ and $$\textbf{u}$$ into the formula for the projection: $$\begin{array}{cl} { \text{proj} _{\mathbf{ \text{u} }}\mathbf{ \text{v} }} & {= \frac{\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{u} } \right\|^{2}}\mathbf{ \text{u} }} \\ & {= \frac{\left\langle {-1,4,3} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {3,5,1} \right\rangle}{\left\| \left\langle {-1,4,3} \right\rangle \right\|^{2}}\left\langle {-1,4,3} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \frac{-3 + 20 + 3}{(-1)^{2} + 4^{2} + 3^{2}}\left\langle {-1,4,3} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \frac{20}{26}\left\langle {-1,4,3} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \left\langle {- \frac{10}{13},\frac{40}{13},\frac{30}{13}} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>To find the two-dimensional projection, simply adapt the formula to the two-dimensional case: $$\begin{array}{cl} { \text{proj} _{\mathbf{ \text{u} }}\mathbf{ \text{v} }} & {= \frac{\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{u} } \right\|^{2}}\mathbf{ \text{u} }} \\ & {= \frac{\left( {\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right) \cdot \left( {3\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 2\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right)}{\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right\|^{2}}\left( {\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{1(3) + 6(-2)}{1^{2} + 6^{2}}\left( {\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right)} \\ & {= - \frac{9}{37}\left( {\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right)} \\ & {= - \frac{9}{37}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{54}{37}\mathbf{ \text{j} }.} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>

snippet: Resolving Vectors into Components: Express \mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {8,-3,-3} \right\rangle as a sum of orthogonal vectors such that one of the vectors has the same direction as \mathbf{ \text{u} } = \left\langle {2,3,2}...
body_xml:
<example number="2.28" title="Resolving Vectors into Components">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Express $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {8,-3,-3} \right\rangle$$ as a sum of orthogonal vectors such that one of the vectors has the same direction as $$\mathbf{ \text{u} } = \left\langle {2,3,2} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let p represent the projection of $$\textbf{v}$$ onto $$\textbf{u}$$ :</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \mathbf{ \text{p} } & {= \text{proj} _{\mathbf{ \text{u} }}\mathbf{ \text{v} }} \\ & {= \frac{\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{v} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{u} } \right\|^{2}}\mathbf{ \text{u} }} \\ & {= \frac{\left\langle {2,3,2} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {8,-3,-3} \right\rangle}{\left\| \left\langle {2,3,2} \right\rangle \right\|^{2}}\left\langle {2,3,2} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \frac{16 - 9 - 6}{2^{2} + 3^{2} + 2^{2}}\left\langle {2,3,2} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \frac{1}{17}\left\langle {2,3,2} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \left\langle {\frac{2}{17},\frac{3}{17},\frac{2}{17}} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{q} } = \mathbf{ \text{v} } - \mathbf{ \text{p} } = \left\langle {8,-3,-3} \right\rangle - \left\langle {\frac{2}{17},\frac{3}{17},\frac{2}{17}} \right\rangle = \left\langle {\frac{134}{17}, - \frac{54}{17}, - \frac{53}{17}} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To check our work, we can use the dot product to verify that p and $$\textbf{q}$$ are orthogonal vectors:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{p} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{q} } = \left\langle {\frac{2}{17},\frac{3}{17},\frac{2}{17}} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {\frac{134}{17}, - \frac{54}{17}, - \frac{53}{17}} \right\rangle = \frac{268}{289} - \frac{162}{289} - \frac{106}{289} = 0.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \mathbf{ \text{p} } + \mathbf{ \text{q} } = \left\langle {\frac{2}{17},\frac{3}{17},\frac{2}{17}} \right\rangle + \left\langle {\frac{134}{17}, - \frac{54}{17}, - \frac{53}{17}} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Scalar Projection of Velocity
snippet: Scalar Projection of Velocity: A container ship leaves port traveling 15^\circ north of east. Its engine generates a speed of 20 knots along that path (see the following figure). In addition, the ocean current moves the ship northeast at a...
body_xml:
<example number="2.29" title="Scalar Projection of Velocity">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A container ship leaves port traveling $$15^\circ$$ north of east. Its engine generates a speed of 20 knots along that path (see the following figure). In addition, the ocean current moves the ship northeast at a speed of 2 knots. Considering both the engine and the current, how fast is the ship moving in the direction $$15^\circ$$ north of east? Round the answer to two decimal places.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$\textbf{v}$$ be the velocity vector generated by the engine, and let $$\textbf{w}$$ be the velocity vector of the current. We already know $$\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\| = 20$$ along the desired route. We just need to add in the scalar projection of $$\textbf{w}$$ onto $$\textbf{v}$$ . We get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} { \text{comp} _{\mathbf{ \text{v} }}\mathbf{ \text{w} }} & {= \frac{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{w} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\|\left\| \mathbf{ \text{w} } \right\|\cos \left( {30^\circ} \right)}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\|}} \\ & {= \left\| \mathbf{ \text{w} } \right\|\cos \left( {30^\circ} \right)} \\ & {= 2\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73 \text{knots} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The ship is moving at 21.73 knots in the direction $$15^\circ$$ north of east.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Calculating Work
snippet: Calculating Work: A conveyor belt generates a force \mathbf{ \text{F} } = 5\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 3\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \mathbf{ \text{k} } that moves a suitcase from point \left( {1,1,1} \right) to point \left( {9,4,7} \right) along a...
body_xml:
<example number="2.30" title="Calculating Work">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A conveyor belt generates a force $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = 5\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 3\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ that moves a suitcase from point $$\left( {1,1,1} \right)$$ to point $$\left( {9,4,7} \right)$$ along a straight line. Find the work done by the conveyor belt. The distance is measured in meters and the force is measured in newtons.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The displacement vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ}$$ has initial point $$\left( {1,1,1} \right)$$ and terminal point $$\left( {9,4,7} \right):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} = \left\langle {9 - 1,4 - 1,7 - 1} \right\rangle = \left\langle {8,3,6} \right\rangle = 8\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{k} }.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Work is the dot product of force and displacement:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} W & {= \mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{PQ}} \\ & {= \left( {5\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 3\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right) \cdot \left( {8\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right)} \\ & {= 5(8) + (-3)(3) + 1(6)} \\ & {= 37 \text{N} \cdot \text{m} } \\ & {= 37 \text{J} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="2.6" title="Properties of the Cross Product">
    <heading level="4">Properties of the Cross Product</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{u} },\mathbf{ \text{v} },$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{w} }$$ be vectors in space, and let $$c$$ be a scalar.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lccrllcl} \text{i.} & & & {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \mathbf{ \text{v} }} & = & {-\left( {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \times \mathbf{ \text{u} }} \right)} & & \text{Anticommutative property} \\ \text{ii.} & & & {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \left( {\mathbf{ \text{v} } + \mathbf{ \text{w} }} \right)} & = & {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \mathbf{ \text{v} } + \mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \mathbf{ \text{w} }} & & \text{Distributive property} \\ \text{iii.} & & & {c\left( {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \mathbf{ \text{v} }} \right)} & = & {\left( {c\mathbf{ \text{u} }} \right) \times \mathbf{ \text{v} } = \mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \left( {c\mathbf{ \text{v} }} \right)} & & \text{Multiplication by a constant} \\ \text{iv.} & & & {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \mathbf{0}} & = & {\mathbf{0} \times \mathbf{ \text{u} } = \mathbf{0}} & & \text{Cross product of the zero vector} \\ \text{v.} & & & {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \times \mathbf{ \text{v} }} & = & \mathbf{0} & & \text{Cross product of a vector with itself} \\ \text{vi.} & & & {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \times \mathbf{ \text{w} }} \right)} & = & {\left( {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \mathbf{ \text{v} }} \right) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{w} }} & & \text{Scalar triple product} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

<note type="rule" source_type="Rule: Cross Product Calculated by a Determinant" title="Rule: Cross Product Calculated by a Determinant">
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{u} } = \left\langle {u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}} \right\rangle$$ be vectors. Then the cross product $$\mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \mathbf{ \text{v} }$$ is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{u} } \times \mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left| \begin{array}{lll} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ u_{1} & u_{2} & u_{3} \\ v_{1} & v_{2} & v_{3} \end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{ll} u_{2} & u_{3} \\ v_{2} & v_{3} \end{array} \right|\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left| \begin{array}{ll} u_{1} & u_{3} \\ v_{1} & v_{3} \end{array} \right|\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left| \begin{array}{ll} u_{1} & u_{2} \\ v_{1} & v_{2} \end{array} \right|\mathbf{ \text{k} }.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Using Determinant Notation to find p×qp×q
snippet: Using Determinant Notation to find p×qp×q: Let \mathbf{ \text{p} } = \left\langle {-1,2,5} \right\rangle and \mathbf{ \text{q} } = \left\langle {4,0,-3} \right\rangle. Find \mathbf{ \text{p} } \times \mathbf{ \text{q} }. We set up our...
body_xml:
<example number="2.37" title="Using Determinant Notation to find p×qp×q">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{p} } = \left\langle {-1,2,5} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{q} } = \left\langle {4,0,-3} \right\rangle.$$ Find $$\mathbf{ \text{p} } \times \mathbf{ \text{q} }.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We set up our determinant by putting the standard unit vectors across the first row, the components of $$\mathbf{ \text{u} }$$ in the second row, and the components of $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }$$ in the third row. Then, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{p} } \times \mathbf{ \text{q} }} & {= \left| \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ -1 & 2 & 5 \\ 4 & 0 & -3 \end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{rr} 2 & 5 \\ 0 & -3 \end{array} \right|\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left| \begin{array}{rr} -1 & 5 \\ 4 & -3 \end{array} \right|\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left| \begin{array}{rr} -1 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 \end{array} \right|\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= \left( {-6 - 0} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {3 - 20} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {0 - 8} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= -6\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 17\mathbf{ \text{j} } - 8\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that this answer confirms the calculation of the cross product in Example 2.31.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding a Unit Vector Orthogonal to Two Given Vectors
snippet: Finding a Unit Vector Orthogonal to Two Given Vectors: Let \mathbf{ \text{a} } = \left\langle {5,2,-1} \right\rangle and \mathbf{ \text{b} } = \left\langle {0,-1,4} \right\rangle. Find a unit vector orthogonal to both \mathbf{ \text{a} }...
body_xml:
<example number="2.38" title="Finding a Unit Vector Orthogonal to Two Given Vectors">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{a} } = \left\langle {5,2,-1} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{b} } = \left\langle {0,-1,4} \right\rangle.$$ Find a unit vector orthogonal to both $$\mathbf{ \text{a} }$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{b} }.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The cross product $$\mathbf{ \text{a} } \times \mathbf{ \text{b} }$$ is orthogonal to both vectors $$\mathbf{ \text{a} }$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{b} }.$$ We can calculate it with a determinant:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{a} } \times \mathbf{ \text{b} }} & {= \left| \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ 5 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 \end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{rr} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 4 \end{array} \right|\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left| \begin{array}{rr} 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 4 \end{array} \right|\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left| \begin{array}{rr} 5 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \end{array} \right|\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= \left( {8 - 1} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {20 - 0} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {-5 - 0} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= 7\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 20\mathbf{ \text{j} } - 5\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Normalize this vector to find a unit vector in the same direction:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{a} } \times \mathbf{ \text{b} }} \right\| = \sqrt{(7)^{2} + (-20)^{2} + (-5)^{2}} = \sqrt{474}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, $$\left\langle {\frac{7}{\sqrt{474}},\frac{-20}{\sqrt{474}},\frac{-5}{\sqrt{474}}} \right\rangle$$ is a unit vector orthogonal to $$\mathbf{ \text{a} }$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{b} }.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Area of a Triangle
snippet: Finding the Area of a Triangle: Let P = \left( {1,0,0} \right),Q = \left( {0,1,0} \right), \text{and} R = \left( {0,0,1} \right) be the vertices of a triangle (Figure 2.58). Find its area. We have \overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} = \left\langle...
body_xml: Let $$P = \left( {1,0,0} \right),Q = \left( {0,1,0} \right), \text{and} R = \left( {0,0,1} \right)$$ be the vertices of a triangle (Figure 2.58). Find its area. We have $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} = \left\langle {0 - 1,1 - 0,0 - 0} \right\rangle = \left\langle {-1,1,0} \right\rangle$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PR} = \left\langle {0 - 1,0 - 0,1 - 0} \right\rangle = \left\langle {-1,0,1} \right\rangle.$$ The area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PR}$$ is given by $$\left\| {\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{PR}} \right\|:$$ $$\begin{array}{rll} {\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{PR}} & = & {\left| \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right| = \left( {1 - 0} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {-1 - 0} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {0 - (-1)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} } = \mathbf{ \text{i} } + \mathbf{ \text{j} } + \mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ \left\| {\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{PR}} \right\| & = & {\left\| \left\langle {1,1,1} \right\rangle \right\| = \sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2} + 1^{2}} = \sqrt{3}.} \end{array}$$ The area of $$\text{Δ} PQR$$ is half the area of the parallelogram, or $$\sqrt{3}/2.$$

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="2.9" title="Calculating a Triple Scalar Product">
    <heading level="4">Calculating a Triple Scalar Product</heading>
    <paragraph>The triple scalar product of vectors $$\mathbf{ \text{u} } = u_{1}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + u_{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + u_{3}\mathbf{ \text{k} },$$ $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = v_{1}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + v_{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + v_{3}\mathbf{ \text{k} },$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{w} } = w_{1}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + w_{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + w_{3}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ is the determinant of the $$3 \times 3$$ matrix formed by the components of the vectors:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \times \mathbf{ \text{w} }} \right) = \left| \begin{array}{lll} u_{1} & u_{2} & u_{3} \\ v_{1} & v_{2} & v_{3} \\ w_{1} & w_{2} & w_{3} \end{array} \right|.$$</paragraph>

    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Apply Calculating a Triple Scalar Product directly:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \times \mathbf{ \text{w} }} \right)} & {= \left| \begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & -1 \end{array} \right|} \\ & {= 1\left| \begin{array}{rr} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{array} \right| - 3\left| \begin{array}{rr} 2 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 \end{array} \right| + 5\left| \begin{array}{rr} 2 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 \end{array} \right|} \\ & {= \left( {1 - 0} \right) - 3\left( {-2 - 0} \right) + 5\left( {0 - 3} \right)} \\ & {= 1 + 6 - 15 = -8.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

body_xml: Let $$\mathbf{ \text{u} } = \left\langle {-1,-2,1} \right\rangle,\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {4,3,2} \right\rangle, \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{w} } = \left\langle {0,-5,-2} \right\rangle.$$ Find the volume of the parallelepiped with adjacent edges $$\mathbf{ \text{u} },\mathbf{ \text{v} }, \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{w} }$$ (Figure 2.60). We have $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \times \mathbf{ \text{w} }} \right)} & {= \left| \begin{array}{rrr} -1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -5 & -2 \end{array} \right| = (-1)\left| \begin{array}{rr} 3 & 2 \\ -5 & -2 \end{array} \right| + 2\left| \begin{array}{rr} 4 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{array} \right| + \left| \begin{array}{rr} 4 & 3 \\ 0 & -5 \end{array} \right|} \\ & {= (-1)\left( {-6 + 10} \right) + 2\left( {-8 - 0} \right) + \left( {-20 - 0} \right)} \\ & {= -4 - 16 - 20} \\ & {= -40.} \end{array}$$ Thus, the volume of the parallelepiped is $$|-40| = 40$$ units3.

<example number="2.42" title="Using the Triple Scalar Product">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the triple scalar product to show that vectors $$\mathbf{ \text{u} } = \left\langle {2,0,5} \right\rangle,\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {2,2,4} \right\rangle, \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{w} } = \left\langle {1,-1,3} \right\rangle$$ are coplanar—that is, show that these vectors lie in the same plane.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Start by calculating the triple scalar product to find the volume of the parallelepiped defined by $$\mathbf{ \text{u} },\mathbf{ \text{v} }, \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{w} }:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{u} } \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \times \mathbf{ \text{w} }} \right)} & {= \left| \begin{array}{rrr} 2 & 0 & 5 \\ 2 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & 3 \end{array} \right|} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {2(2)(3) + (0)(4)(1) + 5(2)(-1)} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {5(2)(1) + (2)(4)(-1) + (0)(2)(3)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= 2 - 2} \\ & {= 0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The volume of the parallelepiped is $$0$$ units3, so one of the dimensions must be zero. Therefore, the three vectors all lie in the same plane.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="2.43" title="Finding an Orthogonal Vector">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Only a single plane can pass through any set of three noncolinear points. Find a vector orthogonal to the plane containing points $$P = \left( {9,-3,-2} \right),Q = \left( {1,3,0} \right),$$ and $$R = \left( {-2,5,0} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The plane must contain vectors $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{QR}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} = \left\langle {1 - 9,3 - (-3),0 - (-2)} \right\rangle = \left\langle {-8,6,2} \right\rangle} \\ {\overset{\rightarrow}{QR} = \left\langle {-2 - 1,5 - 3,0 - 0} \right\rangle = \left\langle {-3,2,0} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The cross product $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{QR}$$ produces a vector orthogonal to both $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{QR}.$$ Therefore, the cross product is orthogonal to the plane that contains these two vectors:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{QR}} & {= \left| \left. \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ {- 8} & 6 & 2 \\ {- 3} & 2 & 0 \end{array} \right| \right.} \\ & {= 0\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 6\mathbf{ \text{j} } - 16\mathbf{ \text{k} } - \left( {-18\mathbf{ \text{k} } + 4\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 0\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right)} \\ & {= -4\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 6\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 2\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Torque, $$\tau$$ (the Greek letter tau), measures the tendency of a force to produce rotation about an axis of rotation. Let $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }$$ be a vector with an initial point located on the axis of rotation and with a terminal point located at the point where the force is applied, and let vector $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }$$ represent the force. Then torque is equal to the cross product of $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }:$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\tau = \mathbf{ \text{r} } \times \mathbf{ \text{F} }.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>See Figure 2.61.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Evaluating Torque
snippet: Evaluating Torque: A bolt is tightened by applying a force of 6 N to a 0.15-m wrench (Figure 2.62). The angle between the wrench and the force vector is 40^\circ. Find the magnitude of the torque about the center of the bolt. Round the...
body_xml: A bolt is tightened by applying a force of $$6$$ N to a 0.15-m wrench (Figure 2.62). The angle between the wrench and the force vector is $$40^\circ.$$ Find the magnitude of the torque about the center of the bolt. Round the answer to two decimal places. Substitute the given information into the equation defining torque: $$\left\| \tau \right\| = \left\| {\mathbf{ \text{r} } \times \mathbf{ \text{F} }} \right\| = \left\| \mathbf{ \text{r} } \right\|\left\| \mathbf{ \text{F} } \right\|\sin \theta = (0.15 \text{m} )(6 \text{N} )\sin 40^\circ \approx 0.58 \text{N} \cdot \text{m} .$$

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="2.11" title="Parametric and Symmetric Equations of a Line">
    <heading level="4">Parametric and Symmetric Equations of a Line</heading>
    <paragraph>A line $$L$$ parallel to vector $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {a,b,c} \right\rangle$$ and passing through point $$P\left( {x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}} \right)$$ can be described by the following parametric equations:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x = x_{0} + ta,y = y_{0} + tb, \text{and} z = z_{0} + tc.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If the constants $$a,b, \text{and} c$$ are all nonzero, then $$L$$ can be described by the symmetric equation of the line:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{x - x_{0}}{a} = \frac{y - y_{0}}{b} = \frac{z - z_{0}}{c}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Parametric Equations of a Line Segment: Find parametric equations of the line segment between the points P(2,1,4) and Q\left( {3,-1,3} \right). By Equation 2.16, we have x = x_{0} + t\left( {x_{1} - x_{0}} \right),y = y_{0} + t\left(...
body_xml:
<example number="2.46" title="Parametric Equations of a Line Segment">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find parametric equations of the line segment between the points $$P(2,1,4)$$ and $$Q\left( {3,-1,3} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>By Equation 2.16, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x = x_{0} + t\left( {x_{1} - x_{0}} \right),y = y_{0} + t\left( {y_{1} - y_{0}} \right),z = z_{0} + t\left( {z_{1} - z_{0}} \right),0 \leq t \leq 1.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Working with each component separately, we get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} x & {= x_{0} + t\left( {x_{1} - x_{0}} \right)} \\ & {= 2 + t\left( {3 - 2} \right)} \\ & {= 2 + t,} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} y & {= y_{0} + t\left( {y_{1} - y_{0}} \right)} \\ & {= 1 + t\left( {-1 - 1} \right)} \\ & {= 1 - 2t,} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} z & {= z_{0} + t\left( {z_{1} - z_{0}} \right)} \\ & {= 4 + t\left( {3 - 4} \right)} \\ & {= 4 - t.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the parametric equations for the line segment are</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x = 2 + t,y = 1 - 2t,z = 4 - t,0 \leq t \leq 1.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <heading level="4">Distance from a Point to a Line</heading>

snippet: Calculating the Distance from a Point to a Line: Find the distance between the point M = \left( {1,1,3} \right) and line \frac{x - 3}{4} = \frac{y + 1}{2} = z - 3. From the symmetric equations of the line, we know that vector \mathbf{...
body_xml: Find the distance between the point $$M = \left( {1,1,3} \right)$$ and line $$\frac{x - 3}{4} = \frac{y + 1}{2} = z - 3.$$ From the symmetric equations of the line, we know that vector $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {4,2,1} \right\rangle$$ is a direction vector for the line. Setting the symmetric equations of the line equal to zero, we see that point $$P\left( {3,-1,3} \right)$$ lies on the line. Then, $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PM} = \left\langle {1 - 3,1 - (-1),3 - 3} \right\rangle = \left\langle {-2,2,0} \right\rangle.$$ To calculate the distance, we need to find $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PM} \times \mathbf{ \text{v} }:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\overset{\rightarrow}{PM} \times \mathbf{ \text{v} }} & {= \left| \begin{array}{rcc} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & 2 & 1 \end{array} \right|} \\ & {= \left( {2 - 0} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {-2 - 0} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {-4 - 8} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= 2\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\mathbf{ \text{j} } - 12\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the distance between the point and the line is (Figure 2.66) $$\begin{array}{cl} d & {= \frac{\left\| {\overset{\rightarrow}{PM} \times \mathbf{ \text{v} }} \right\|}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{\sqrt{2^{2} + 2^{2} + 12^{2}}}{\sqrt{4^{2} + 2^{2} + 1^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{2\sqrt{38}}{\sqrt{21}}.} \end{array}$$

body_xml:
<example number="2.48" title="Classifying Lines in Space">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each pair of lines, determine whether the lines are equal, parallel but not equal, skew, or intersecting.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$L_{1}:x = 2s - 1,y = s - 1,z = s - 4$$ $$L_{2}:x = t - 3,y = 3t + 8,z = 5 - 2t$$</item>
        <item>$$L_{1}:$$ $$x = -y = z$$ $$L_{2}:\frac{x - 3}{2} = y = z - 2$$</item>
        <item>$$L_{1}:x = 6s - 1,y = -2s,z = 3s + 1;s \neq 0$$ $$L_{2}:\frac{x - 4}{6} = \frac{y + 3}{-2} = \frac{z - 1}{3}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Line $$L_{1}$$ has direction vector $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }_{\mathbf{1}} = \left\langle {2,1,1} \right\rangle;$$ line $$L_{2}$$ has direction vector $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }_{\mathbf{2}} = \left\langle {1,3,-2} \right\rangle.$$ Because the direction vectors are not parallel vectors, the lines are either intersecting or skew. To determine whether the lines intersect, we see if there is a point, $$\left( {x,y,z} \right),$$ that lies on both lines. To find this point, we use the parametric equations to create a system of equalities: $$2s - 1 = t - 3; s - 1 = 3t + 8; s - 4 = 5 - 2t.$$ By the first equation, $$t = 2s + 2.$$ Substituting into the second equation yields $$\begin{array}{rll} {s - 1} & = & {3\left( {2s + 2} \right) + 8} \\ {s - 1} & = & {6s + 6 + 8} \\ {5s} & = & -15 \\ s & = & -3. \end{array}$$ Substitution into the third equation, however, yields a contradiction: $$\begin{array}{rll} {s - 4} & = & {5 - 2\left( {2s + 2} \right)} \\ {s - 4} & = & {5 - 4s - 4} \\ {5s} & = & 5 \\ s & = & 1. \end{array}$$ There is no single point that satisfies the parametric equations for $$L_{1} \text{and} L_{2}$$ simultaneously. These lines do not intersect, so they are skew (see the following figure).</item>
        <item>Line L1 has direction vector $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }_{\mathbf{1}} = \left\langle {1,-1,1} \right\rangle$$ and passes through the origin, $$\left( {0,0,0} \right).$$ Line $$L_{2}$$ has a different direction vector, $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }_{\mathbf{2}} = \left\langle {2,1,1} \right\rangle,$$ so these lines are not parallel or equal. Let $$r$$ represent the parameter for line $$L_{1}$$ and let $$s$$ represent the parameter for $$L_{2}:$$ $$\begin{array}{lccl} \begin{array}{ll} x & {= r} \\ y & {= -r} \\ z & {= r} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{ll} x & {= 2s + 3} \\ y & {= s} \\ z & {= s + 2.} \end{array} \end{array}$$ Solve the system of equations to find $$r = 1$$ and $$s = - 1.$$ If we need to find the point of intersection, we can substitute these parameters into the original equations to get $$\left( {1,-1,1} \right)$$ (see the following figure).</item>
        <item>Lines $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ have equivalent direction vectors: $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {6,-2,3} \right\rangle.$$ These two lines are parallel (see the following figure).</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Definition: Given a point P and vector \mathbf{ \text{n} }, the set of all points Q satisfying the equation \mathbf{ \text{n} } \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} = 0 forms a plane. The equation \mathbf{ \text{n} } \cdot...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Given a point $$P$$ and vector $$\mathbf{ \text{n} },$$ the set of all points $$Q$$ satisfying the equation $$\mathbf{ \text{n} } \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} = 0$$ forms a plane. The equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{n} } \cdot \overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is known as the vector equation of a plane.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The scalar equation of a plane containing point $$P = \left( {x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}} \right)$$ with normal vector $$\mathbf{ \text{n} } = \left\langle {a,b,c} \right\rangle$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a\left( {x - x_{0}} \right) + b\left( {y - y_{0}} \right) + c\left( {z - z_{0}} \right) = 0.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This equation can be expressed as $$ax + by + cz + d = 0,$$ where $$d = -ax_{0} - by_{0} - cz_{0}.$$ This form of the equation is sometimes called the general form of the equation of a plane.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Writing an Equation of a Plane Given Three Points in the Plane
snippet: Writing an Equation of a Plane Given Three Points in the Plane: Write an equation for the plane containing points P = \left( {1,1,-2} \right), Q = \left( {0,2,1} \right), and R = \left( {-1,-1,0} \right) in both standard and general forms....
body_xml:
<example number="2.49" title="Writing an Equation of a Plane Given Three Points in the Plane">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write an equation for the plane containing points $$P = \left( {1,1,-2} \right),$$ $$Q = \left( {0,2,1} \right),$$ and $$R = \left( {-1,-1,0} \right)$$ in both standard and general forms.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To write an equation for a plane, we must find a normal vector for the plane. We start by identifying two vectors in the plane:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} \overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} & = & {\left\langle {0 - 1,2 - 1,1 - (-2)} \right\rangle = \left\langle {-1,1,3} \right\rangle} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{QR} & = & {\left\langle {-1 - 0,-1 - 2,0 - 1} \right\rangle = \left\langle {-1,-3,-1} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The cross product $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{QR}$$ is orthogonal to both $$\overset{\rightarrow}{PQ}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{QR},$$ so it is normal to the plane that contains these two vectors:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \mathbf{ \text{n} } & {= \overset{\rightarrow}{PQ} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{QR}} \\ & {= \left| \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ -1 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -3 & -1 \end{array} \right|} \\ & {= \left( {-1 + 9} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {1 + 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {3 + 1} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= 8\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 4\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 4\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, $$\mathbf{ \text{n} } = \left\langle {8,-4,4} \right\rangle,$$ and we can choose any of the three given points to write an equation of the plane:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {8(x - 1) - 4(y - 1) + 4(z + 2)} & = & 0 \\ {8x - 4y + 4z + 4} & = & 0. \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Writing an Equation for a Plane Given a Point and a Line: Find an equation of the plane that passes through point \left( {1,4,3} \right) and contains the line given by x = \frac{y - 1}{2} = z + 1. Symmetric equations describe the line that...
body_xml:
<example number="2.50" title="Writing an Equation for a Plane Given a Point and a Line">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find an equation of the plane that passes through point $$\left( {1,4,3} \right)$$ and contains the line given by $$x = \frac{y - 1}{2} = z + 1.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Symmetric equations describe the line that passes through point $$\left( {0,1,-1} \right)$$ parallel to vector $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }_{1} = \left\langle {1,2,1} \right\rangle$$ (see the following figure). Use this point and the given point, $$\left( {1,4,3} \right),$$ to identify a second vector parallel to the plane:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{v} }_{2} = \left\langle {1 - 0,4 - 1,3 - (-1)} \right\rangle = \left\langle {1,3,4} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Use the cross product of these vectors to identify a normal vector for the plane:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \mathbf{ \text{n} } & {= \mathbf{ \text{v} }_{1} \times \mathbf{ \text{v} }_{2}} \\ & {= \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \end{matrix} \right|} \\ & {= \left( {8 - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {4 - 1} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {3 - 2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= 5\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 3\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The scalar equations for the plane are $$5x - 3\left( {y - 1} \right) + \left( {z + 1} \right) = 0$$ and $$5x - 3y + z + 4 = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Distance between a Point and a Plane: Find the distance between point P = \left( {3,1,2} \right) and the plane given by x - 2y + z = 5 (see the following figure). The coefficients of the plane’s equation provide a normal vector for the...
body_xml:
<example number="2.51" title="Distance between a Point and a Plane">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the distance between point $$P = \left( {3,1,2} \right)$$ and the plane given by $$x - 2y + z = 5$$ (see the following figure).</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The coefficients of the plane’s equation provide a normal vector for the plane: $$\mathbf{ \text{n} } = \left\langle {1,-2,1} \right\rangle.$$ To find vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{QP},$$ we need a point in the plane. Any point will work, so set $$y = z = 0$$ to see that point $$Q = \left( {5,0,0} \right)$$ lies in the plane. Find the component form of the vector from $$Q \text{to} P:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\overset{\rightarrow}{QP} = \left\langle {3 - 5,1 - 0,2 - 0} \right\rangle = \left\langle {-2,1,2} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Apply the distance formula from Equation 2.19:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} d & {= \frac{\left| {\overset{\rightarrow}{QP} \cdot \mathbf{ \text{n} }} \right|}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{n} } \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{\left| {\left\langle {-2,1,2} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {1,-2,1} \right\rangle} \right|}{\sqrt{1^{2} + (-2)^{2} + 1^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{\left| {-2 - 2 + 2} \right|}{\sqrt{6}}} \\ & {= \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Line of Intersection for Two Planes
snippet: Finding the Line of Intersection for Two Planes: Find parametric and symmetric equations for the line formed by the intersection of the planes given by x + y + z = 0 and 2x - y + z = 0 (see the following figure). Note that the two planes...
body_xml:
<example number="2.52" title="Finding the Line of Intersection for Two Planes">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find parametric and symmetric equations for the line formed by the intersection of the planes given by $$x + y + z = 0$$ and $$2x - y + z = 0$$ (see the following figure).</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Note that the two planes have nonparallel normals, so the planes intersect. Further, the origin satisfies each equation, so we know the line of intersection passes through the origin. Add the plane equations so we can eliminate the one of the variables, in this case, $$y:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} \underset{ \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_} }{\begin{array}{rcccccc} x & + & y & + & z & = & 0 \\ {2x} & - & y & + & z & = & 0 \end{array}} \\ \\ { 3x + 2z = 0.} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This gives us $$x = - \frac{2}{3}z.$$ We substitute this value into the first equation to express $$y$$ in terms of $$z:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {x + y + z} & = & 0 \\ {- \frac{2}{3}z + y + z} & = & 0 \\ {y + \frac{1}{3}z} & = & 0 \\ y & = & {- \frac{1}{3}z.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We now have the first two variables, $$x$$ and $$y,$$ in terms of the third variable, $$z.$$ Now we define $$z$$ in terms of $$t.$$ To eliminate the need for fractions, we choose to define the parameter $$t$$ as $$t = - \frac{1}{3}z.$$ Then, $$z = -3t.$$ Substituting the parametric representation of $$z$$ back into the other two equations, we see that the parametric equations for the line of intersection are $$x = 2t,y = t,z = -3t.$$ The symmetric equations for the line are $$\frac{x}{2} = y = \frac{z}{-3}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Angle between Two Planes
snippet: Finding the Angle between Two Planes: Determine whether each pair of planes is parallel, orthogonal, or neither. If the planes are intersecting, but not orthogonal, find the measure of the angle between them. Give the answer in radians and...
body_xml:
<example number="2.53" title="Finding the Angle between Two Planes">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether each pair of planes is parallel, orthogonal, or neither. If the planes are intersecting, but not orthogonal, find the measure of the angle between them. Give the answer in radians and round to two decimal places.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$x + 2y - z = 8 \text{and} 2x + 4y - 2z = 10$$</item>
        <item>$$2x - 3y + 2z = 3 \text{and} 6x + 2y - 3z = 1$$</item>
        <item>$$x + y + z = 4 \text{and} x - 3y + 5z = 1$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The normal vectors for these planes are $$\mathbf{ \text{n} }_{1} = \left\langle {1,2,-1} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{n} }_{2} = \left\langle {2,4,-2} \right\rangle.$$ These two vectors are scalar multiples of each other. The normal vectors are parallel, so the planes are parallel.</item>
        <item>The normal vectors for these planes are $$\mathbf{ \text{n} }_{1} = \left\langle {2,-3,2} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{n} }_{2} = \left\langle {6,2,-3} \right\rangle.$$ Taking the dot product of these vectors, we have $$\mathbf{ \text{n} }_{1} \cdot \mathbf{ \text{n} }_{2} = \left\langle {2,-3,2} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {6,2,-3} \right\rangle = 2(6) - 3(2) + 2(-3) = 0.$$ The normal vectors are orthogonal, so the corresponding planes are orthogonal as well.</item>
        <item>The normal vectors for these planes are $$\mathbf{ \text{n} }_{1} = \left\langle {1,1,1} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{n} }_{2} = \left\langle {1,-3,5} \right\rangle:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\cos \theta} & {= \frac{\left| {\mathbf{ \text{n} }_{1} \cdot \mathbf{ \text{n} }_{2}} \right|}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{n} }_{1} \right\|\left\| \mathbf{ \text{n} }_{2} \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{\left| {\left\langle {1,1,1} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {1,-3,5} \right\rangle} \right|}{\sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2} + 1^{2}} \sqrt{1^{2} + {(-3)}^{2} + 5^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{3}{\sqrt{105}}.} \end{array}$$ The angle between the two planes is $$1.27$$ rad, or approximately $$73^\circ.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

Since a single point does not tell us what the shape is, we can move up the z-axis to an arbitrary plane to find the shape of other traces of the figure. The trace in plane $$z = 5$$ is the graph of equation $$x^{2} + \frac{y^{2}}{2^{2}} = 1,$$ which is an ellipse. In the xz-plane, the equation becomes $$z = 5x^{2}.$$ The trace is a parabola in this plane and in any plane with the equation $$y = b.$$ In planes parallel to the yz-plane, the traces are also parabolas, as we can see in the following figure.

title: Chapter Opener: Finding the Focus of a Parabolic Reflector
snippet: Chapter Opener: Finding the Focus of a Parabolic Reflector: Energy hitting the surface of a parabolic reflector is concentrated at the focal point of the reflector (Figure 2.86). If the surface of a parabolic reflector is described by...
body_xml: Energy hitting the surface of a parabolic reflector is concentrated at the focal point of the reflector (Figure 2.86). If the surface of a parabolic reflector is described by equation $$\frac{x^{2}}{100} + \frac{y^{2}}{100} = \frac{z}{4},$$ where is the focal point of the reflector? Since z is the first-power variable, the axis of the reflector corresponds to the z-axis. The coefficients of $$x^{2}$$ and $$y^{2}$$ are equal, so the cross-section of the paraboloid perpendicular to the z-axis is a circle. We can consider a trace in the xz-plane or the yz-plane; the result is the same. Setting $$y = 0,$$ the trace is a parabola opening up along the z-axis, with standard equation $$x^{2} = 4pz,$$ where $$p$$ is the focal length of the parabola. In this case, this equation becomes $$x^{2} = 100 \cdot \frac{z}{4} = 4pz$$ or $$25 = 4p.$$ So p is $$6.25$$ m, which tells us that the focus of the paraboloid is $$6.25$$ m up the axis from the vertex. Because the vertex of this surface is the origin, the focal point is $$\left( {0,0,6.25} \right).$$

title: Identifying Equations of Quadric Surfaces
snippet: Identifying Equations of Quadric Surfaces: Identify the surfaces represented by the given equations. 16x^{2} + 9y^{2} + 16z^{2} = 144 9x^{2} - 18x + 4y^{2} + 16y - 36z + 25 = 0 The x,y, and z terms are all squared, and are all positive, so...
body_xml:
<example number="2.59" title="Identifying Equations of Quadric Surfaces">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Identify the surfaces represented by the given equations.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$16x^{2} + 9y^{2} + 16z^{2} = 144$$</item>
        <item>$$9x^{2} - 18x + 4y^{2} + 16y - 36z + 25 = 0$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The $$x,y,$$ and $$z$$ terms are all squared, and are all positive, so this is probably an ellipsoid. However, let’s put the equation into the standard form for an ellipsoid just to be sure. We have $$16x^{2} + 9y^{2} + 16z^{2} = 144.$$ Dividing through by 144 gives $$\frac{x^{2}}{9} + \frac{y^{2}}{16} + \frac{z^{2}}{9} = 1.$$ So, this is, in fact, an ellipsoid, centered at the origin.</item>
        <item>We first notice that the $$z$$ term is raised only to the first power, so this is either an elliptic paraboloid or a hyperbolic paraboloid. We also note there are $$x$$ terms and $$y$$ terms that are not squared, so this quadric surface is not centered at the origin. We need to complete the square to put this equation in one of the standard forms. We have $$\begin{array}{rll} & & \\ {9x^{2} - 18x + 4y^{2} + 16y - 36z + 25} & = & 0 \\ {9x^{2} - 18x + 4y^{2} + 16y + 25} & = & {36z} \\ {9\left( {x^{2} - 2x} \right) + 4\left( {y^{2} + 4y} \right) + 25} & = & {36z} \\ {9\left( {x^{2} - 2x + 1 - 1} \right) + 4\left( {y^{2} + 4y + 4 - 4} \right) + 25} & = & {36z} \\ {9\left( {x - 1} \right)^{2} - 9 + 4\left( {y + 2} \right)^{2} - 16 + 25} & = & {36z} \\ {9\left( {x - 1} \right)^{2} + 4\left( {y + 2} \right)^{2}} & = & {36z} \\ {\frac{\left( {x - 1} \right)^{2}}{4} + \frac{\left( {y + 2} \right)^{2}}{9}} & = & {z.} \end{array}$$ This is an elliptic paraboloid centered at $$\left( {1,2,0} \right).$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <heading level="4">Conversion between Cylindrical and Cartesian Coordinates</heading>

  </note>

title: Converting from Rectangular to Cylindrical Coordinates
snippet: Converting from Rectangular to Cylindrical Coordinates: Convert the rectangular coordinates (1,-3,5) to cylindrical coordinates. Use the second set of equations from Conversion between Cylindrical and Cartesian Coordinates to translate...
body_xml:
<example number="2.61" title="Converting from Rectangular to Cylindrical Coordinates">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Convert the rectangular coordinates $$(1,-3,5)$$ to cylindrical coordinates.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use the second set of equations from Conversion between Cylindrical and Cartesian Coordinates to translate from rectangular to cylindrical coordinates:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} r^{2} & = & {x^{2} + y^{2}} \\ r & = & { \text{±} \sqrt{1^{2} + (-3)^{2}} = \text{±} \sqrt{10}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We choose the positive square root, so $$r = \sqrt{10}.$$ Now, we apply the formula to find $$\theta.$$ In this case, $$y$$ is negative and $$x$$ is positive, which means we must select the value of $$\theta$$ between $$\frac{3\pi}{2}$$ and $$2\pi:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {\tan \theta} & = & {\frac{y}{x} = \frac{-3}{1}} \\ \theta & = & {\arctan {(-3) + 2\pi} \approx 5.03 \text{rad} .} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In this case, the z-coordinates are the same in both rectangular and cylindrical coordinates:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$z = 5.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The point with rectangular coordinates $$(1,-3,5)$$ has cylindrical coordinates approximately equal to $$\left( {\sqrt{10},5.03,5} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <problem>
      <paragraph>Describe the surfaces with the given cylindrical equations.</paragraph>

        <item>$$r^{2} + z^{2} = 9$$</item>
        <item>$$z = r$$</item>

    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>When the angle $$\theta$$ is held constant while $$r$$ and $$z$$ are allowed to vary, the result is a half-plane (see the following figure). Figure 2.94 In polar coordinates, the equation $$\theta = \pi/4$$ describes the ray extending diagonally through the first quadrant. In three dimensions, this same equation describes a half-plane.</item>
        <item>Substitute $$r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ into equation $$r^{2} + z^{2} = 9$$ to express the rectangular form of the equation: $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 9.$$ This equation describes a sphere centered at the origin with radius $$3$$ (see the following figure). Figure 2.95 The sphere centered at the origin with radius $$3$$ can be described by the cylindrical equation $$r^{2} + z^{2} = 9.$$</item>
        <item>To describe the surface defined by equation $$z = r,$$ is it useful to examine traces parallel to the xy-plane. For example, the trace in plane $$z = 1$$ is circle $$r = 1,$$ the trace in plane $$z = 3$$ is circle $$r = 3,$$ and so on. Each trace is a circle. As the value of $$z$$ increases, the radius of the circle also increases. The resulting surface is a cone (see the following figure). Figure 2.96 The traces in planes parallel to the xy-plane are circles. The radius of the circles increases as $$z$$ increases.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>In the spherical coordinate system, a point $$P$$ in space (Figure 2.97) is represented by the ordered triple $$(\rho,\theta,\varphi)$$ where</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>$$\rho$$ (the Greek letter rho) is the distance between $$P$$ and the origin $$\left( {\rho \neq 0} \right);$$</item>
      <item>$$\theta$$ is the same angle used to describe the location in cylindrical coordinates;</item>
      <item>$$\varphi$$ (the Greek letter phi) is the angle formed by the positive z-axis and line segment $$\overset{-}{OP},$$ where $$O$$ is the origin and $$0 \leq \varphi \leq \pi.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Converting among Spherical, Cylindrical, and Rectangular Coordinates
snippet: Converting among Spherical, Cylindrical, and Rectangular Coordinates: Converting among Spherical, Cylindrical, and Rectangular Coordinates Rectangular coordinates \left( {x,y,z} \right) and spherical coordinates \left(...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="2.16" title="Converting among Spherical, Cylindrical, and Rectangular Coordinates">
    <heading level="4">Converting among Spherical, Cylindrical, and Rectangular Coordinates</heading>
    <paragraph>Rectangular coordinates $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ and spherical coordinates $$\left( {\rho,\theta,\varphi} \right)$$ of a point are related as follows:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} x & = & {\rho \sin \varphi \cos \theta} & & & \text{These equations are used to convert from} \\ y & = & {\rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta} & & & \text{spherical coordinates to rectangular} \\ z & = & {\rho \cos \varphi} & & & \text{coordinates.} \\ & \text{and} & & & & \\ \rho^{2} & = & {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} & & & \text{These equations are used to convert from} \\ {\tan \theta} & = & \frac{y}{x} & & & \text{rectangular coordinates to spherical} \\ \varphi & = & {\arccos {\left( \frac{z}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}} \right).}} & & & \text{coordinates.} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If a point has cylindrical coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta,z} \right),$$ then these equations define the relationship between cylindrical and spherical coordinates.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} r & = & {\rho \sin \varphi} & & & \text{These equations are used to convert from} \\ \theta & = & \theta & & & \text{spherical coordinates to cylindrical} \\ z & = & {\rho \cos \varphi} & & & \text{coordinates.} \\ & \text{and} & & & & \\ \rho & = & \sqrt{r^{2} + z^{2}} & & & \text{These equations are used to convert from} \\ \theta & = & \theta & & & \text{cylindrical coordinates to spherical} \\ \varphi & = & {\arccos \left( \frac{z}{\sqrt{r^{2} + z^{2}}} \right)} & & & \text{coordinates.} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Converting from Spherical Coordinates
snippet: Converting from Spherical Coordinates: Plot the point with spherical coordinates \left( {8,\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{6}} \right) and express its location in both rectangular and cylindrical coordinates. Use the equations in Converting among...
body_xml: Plot the point with spherical coordinates $$\left( {8,\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{6}} \right)$$ and express its location in both rectangular and cylindrical coordinates. Use the equations in Converting among Spherical, Cylindrical, and Rectangular Coordinates to translate between spherical and cylindrical coordinates (Figure 2.100): $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ {x = \rho \sin \varphi \cos \theta = 8 \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right)\cos \left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) = 8\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)\frac{1}{2} = 2} \\ {y = \rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta = 8 \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right)\sin \left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right) = 8\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 2\sqrt{3}} \\ {z = \rho \cos \varphi = 8 \cos \left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) = 8\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) = 4\sqrt{3}.} \end{array}$$ The point with spherical coordinates $$\left( {8,\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{6}} \right)$$ has rectangular coordinates $$\left( {2,2\sqrt{3},4\sqrt{3}} \right).$$ Finding the values in cylindrical coordinates is equally straightforward: $$\begin{array}{rll} & & \\ r & = & {\rho \sin \varphi = 8 \sin \frac{\pi}{6} = 4} \\ \theta & = & \theta \\ z & = & {\rho \cos \varphi = 8 \cos \frac{\pi}{6} = 4\sqrt{3}.} \end{array}$$ Thus, cylindrical coordinates for the point are $$\left( {4,\frac{\pi}{3},4\sqrt{3}} \right).$$

title: Converting from Rectangular Coordinates
snippet: Converting from Rectangular Coordinates: Convert the rectangular coordinates \left( {-1,1,\sqrt{6}} \right) to both spherical and cylindrical coordinates. Start by converting from rectangular to spherical coordinates: \begin{array}{lccl}...
body_xml:
<example number="2.64" title="Converting from Rectangular Coordinates">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Convert the rectangular coordinates $$\left( {-1,1,\sqrt{6}} \right)$$ to both spherical and cylindrical coordinates.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Start by converting from rectangular to spherical coordinates:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lccl} \begin{array}{rll} \rho^{2} & = & {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = (-1)^{2} + 1^{2} + \left( \sqrt{6} \right)^{2} = 8} \\ \rho & = & {2\sqrt{2}} \end{array} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {\tan \theta} & = & \frac{1}{-1} \\ \theta & = & {\arctan (-1) = \frac{3\pi}{4}.} \end{array} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Because $$\left( {x,y} \right) = \left( {-1,1} \right),$$ then the correct choice for $$\theta$$ is $$\frac{3\pi}{4}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>There are actually two ways to identify $$\varphi.$$ We can use the equation $$\varphi = \arccos \left( \frac{z}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}} \right).$$ A more simple approach, however, is to use equation $$z = \rho \cos \varphi.$$ We know that $$z = \sqrt{6}$$ and $$\rho = 2\sqrt{2},$$ so</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\sqrt{6} = 2\sqrt{2} \cos \varphi, \text{so} \cos \varphi = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and therefore $$\varphi = \frac{\pi}{6}.$$ The spherical coordinates of the point are $$\left( {2\sqrt{2},\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{6}} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To find the cylindrical coordinates for the point, we need only find $$r:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$r = \rho \sin \varphi = 2\sqrt{2} \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right) = \sqrt{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The cylindrical coordinates for the point are $$\left( {\sqrt{2},\frac{3\pi}{4},\sqrt{6}} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Identifying Surfaces in the Spherical Coordinate System
snippet: Identifying Surfaces in the Spherical Coordinate System: Describe the surfaces with the given spherical equations. \theta = \frac{\pi}{3} \varphi = \frac{5\pi}{6} \rho = 6 \rho = \sin \theta \sin \varphi The variable \theta represents the...
body_xml:
<example number="2.65" title="Identifying Surfaces in the Spherical Coordinate System">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Describe the surfaces with the given spherical equations.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$$</item>
        <item>$$\varphi = \frac{5\pi}{6}$$</item>
        <item>$$\rho = 6$$</item>
        <item>$$\rho = \sin \theta \sin \varphi$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The variable $$\theta$$ represents the measure of the same angle in both the cylindrical and spherical coordinate systems. Points with coordinates $$\left( {\rho,\frac{\pi}{3},\varphi} \right)$$ lie on the plane that forms angle $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$$ with the positive x-axis. Because $$\rho > 0,$$ the surface described by equation $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$$ is the half-plane shown in Figure 2.101. Figure 2.101 The surface described by equation $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$$ is a half-plane.</item>
        <item>Equation $$\varphi = \frac{5\pi}{6}$$ describes all points in the spherical coordinate system that lie on a line from the origin forming an angle measuring $$\frac{5\pi}{6}$$ rad with the positive z-axis. These points form a half-cone (Figure 2.102). Because there is only one value for $$\varphi$$ that is measured from the positive z-axis, we do not get the full cone (with two pieces). Figure 2.102 The equation $$\varphi = \frac{5\pi}{6}$$ describes a cone. To find the equation in rectangular coordinates, use equation $$\varphi = \arccos \left( \frac{z}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}} \right).$$ $$\begin{array}{rll} \frac{5\pi}{6} & = & {\arccos \left( \frac{z}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}} \right)} \\ {\cos \frac{5\pi}{6}} & = & \frac{z}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}} \\ {- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} & = & \frac{z}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}} \\ \frac{3}{4} & = & \frac{z^{2}}{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \\ {\frac{3x^{2}}{4} + \frac{3y^{2}}{4} + \frac{3z^{2}}{4}} & = & z^{2} \\ {\frac{3x^{2}}{4} + \frac{3y^{2}}{4} - \frac{z^{2}}{4}} & = & 0. \end{array}$$ This is the equation of a cone centered on the z-axis.</item>
        <item>Equation $$\rho = 6$$ describes the set of all points $$6$$ units away from the origin—a sphere with radius $$6$$ (Figure 2.103). Figure 2.103 Equation $$\rho = 6$$ describes a sphere with radius $$6.$$</item>
        <item>To identify this surface, convert the equation from spherical to rectangular coordinates, using equations $$y = \rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta$$ and $$\rho^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}:$$ $$\begin{array}{rllccc} \rho & = & {\sin \theta \sin \varphi} & & & \\ \rho^{2} & = & {\rho \sin \theta \sin \varphi} & & & { \text{Multiply both sides of the equation by} \rho.} \\ {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} & = & y & & & \text{Substitute rectangular variables using the equations above.} \\ {x^{2} + y^{2} - y + z^{2}} & = & 0 & & & { \text{Subtract} y \text{from both sides of the equation.} } \\ {x^{2} + y^{2} - y + \frac{1}{4} + z^{2}} & = & \frac{1}{4} & & & \text{Complete the square.} \\ {x^{2} + \left( {y - \frac{1}{2}} \right)^{2} + z^{2}} & = & {\frac{1}{4}.} & & & \text{Rewrite the middle terms as a perfect square.} \end{array}$$ The equation describes a sphere centered at point $$\left( {0,\frac{1}{2},0} \right)$$ with radius $$\frac{1}{2}.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Converting Latitude and Longitude to Spherical Coordinates: The latitude of Columbus, Ohio, is 40^\circ N and the longitude is 83^\circ W, which means that Columbus is 40^\circ north of the equator. Imagine a ray from the center of Earth...

<example number="2.66" title="Converting Latitude and Longitude to Spherical Coordinates">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The latitude of Columbus, Ohio, is $$40^\circ$$ N and the longitude is $$83^\circ$$ W, which means that Columbus is $$40^\circ$$ north of the equator. Imagine a ray from the center of Earth through Columbus and a ray from the center of Earth through the equator directly south of Columbus. The measure of the angle formed by the rays is $$40^\circ.$$ In the same way, measuring from the prime meridian, Columbus lies $$83^\circ$$ to the west. Express the location of Columbus in spherical coordinates.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The radius of Earth is $$4000$$ mi, so $$\rho = 4000.$$ The intersection of the prime meridian and the equator lies on the positive x-axis. Movement to the west is then described with negative angle measures, which shows that $$\theta = -83^\circ,$$ Because Columbus lies $$40^\circ$$ north of the equator, it lies $$50^\circ$$ south of the North Pole, so $$\varphi = 50^\circ.$$ In spherical coordinates, Columbus lies at point $$\left( {4000,-83^\circ,50^\circ} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>
