title: Choosing the Best Coordinate System
snippet: Choosing the Best Coordinate System: In each of the following situations, we determine which coordinate system is most appropriate and describe how we would orient the coordinate axes. There could be more than one right answer for how the...
body_xml:
<example number="2.67" title="Choosing the Best Coordinate System">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>In each of the following situations, we determine which coordinate system is most appropriate and describe how we would orient the coordinate axes. There could be more than one right answer for how the axes should be oriented, but we select an orientation that makes sense in the context of the problem. Note: There is not enough information to set up or solve these problems; we simply select the coordinate system (Figure 2.105).</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find the center of gravity of a bowling ball.</item>
        <item>Determine the velocity of a submarine subjected to an ocean current.</item>
        <item>Calculate the pressure in a conical water tank.</item>
        <item>Find the volume of oil flowing through a pipeline.</item>
        <item>Determine the amount of leather required to make a football. Figure 2.105 (credit: (a) modification of work by scl hua, Wikimedia, (b) modification of work by DVIDSHUB, Flickr, (c) modification of work by Michael Malak, Wikimedia, (d) modification of work by Sean Mack, Wikimedia, (e) modification of work by Elvert Barnes, Flickr)</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Clearly, a bowling ball is a sphere, so spherical coordinates would probably work best here. The origin should be located at the physical center of the ball. There is no obvious choice for how the x-, y- and z-axes should be oriented. Bowling balls normally have a weight block in the center. One possible choice is to align the z-axis with the axis of symmetry of the weight block.</item>
        <item>A submarine generally moves in a straight line. There is no rotational or spherical symmetry that applies in this situation, so rectangular coordinates are a good choice. The z-axis should probably point upward. The x- and y-axes could be aligned to point east and north, respectively. The origin should be some convenient physical location, such as the starting position of the submarine or the location of a particular port.</item>
        <item>A cone has several kinds of symmetry. In cylindrical coordinates, a cone can be represented by equation $$z = kr,$$ where $$k$$ is a constant. In spherical coordinates, we have seen that surfaces of the form $$\varphi = c$$ are half-cones. Last, in rectangular coordinates, elliptic cones are quadric surfaces and can be represented by equations of the form $$z^{2} = \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}.$$ In this case, we could choose any of the three. However, the equation for the surface is more complicated in rectangular coordinates than in the other two systems, so we might want to avoid that choice. In addition, we are talking about a water tank, and the depth of the water might come into play at some point in our calculations, so it might be nice to have a component that represents height and depth directly. Based on this reasoning, cylindrical coordinates might be the best choice. Choose the z-axis to align with the axis of the cone. The orientation of the other two axes is arbitrary. The origin should be the bottom point of the cone.</item>
        <item>A pipeline is a cylinder, so cylindrical coordinates would be best the best choice. In this case, however, we would likely choose to orient our z-axis with the center axis of the pipeline. The x-axis could be chosen to point straight downward or to some other logical direction. The origin should be chosen based on the problem statement. Note that this puts the z-axis in a horizontal orientation, which is a little different from what we usually do. It may make sense to choose an unusual orientation for the axes if it makes sense for the problem.</item>
        <item>A football has rotational symmetry about a central axis, so cylindrical coordinates would work best. The z-axis should align with the axis of the ball. The origin could be the center of the ball or perhaps one of the ends. The position of the x-axis is arbitrary.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>A vector-valued function is a function of the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} } \text{or} \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + h(t)\mathbf{ \text{k} },$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where the component functions f, g, and h, are real-valued functions of the parameter t. Vector-valued functions are also written in the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {f(t),g(t)} \right\rangle \text{or} \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {f(t),g(t),h(t)} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In both cases, the first form of the function defines a two-dimensional vector-valued function; the second form describes a three-dimensional vector-valued function.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Evaluating Vector-Valued Functions and Determining Domains
snippet: Evaluating Vector-Valued Functions and Determining Domains: For each of the following vector-valued functions, evaluate \mathbf{ \text{r} }(0),\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right), \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{r} }\left(...
body_xml:
<example number="3.1" title="Evaluating Vector-Valued Functions and Determining Domains">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each of the following vector-valued functions, evaluate $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(0),\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right), \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right).$$ Do any of these functions have domain restrictions?</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\sin t\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$</item>
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 3\tan t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sec t\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 5t\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To calculate each of the function values, substitute the appropriate value of t into the function: $$\begin{array}{cll} {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(0)} & = & {4\cos (0)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\sin (0)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ & = & {4\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 0\mathbf{ \text{j} } = 4\mathbf{ \text{i} }} \\ {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)} & = & {4\cos \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ & = & {0\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\mathbf{ \text{j} } = 3\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)} & = & {4\cos \left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\sin \left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ & = & {4\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } = -2\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }.} \end{array}$$ To determine whether this function has any domain restrictions, consider the component functions separately. The first component function is $$f(t) = 4\cos t$$ and the second component function is $$g(t) = 3\sin t.$$ Neither of these functions has a domain restriction, so the domain of $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\sin t\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ is all real numbers.</item>
        <item>To calculate each of the function values, substitute the appropriate value of t into the function: $$\begin{array}{cll} {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(0)} & = & {3\tan (0)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sec (0)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 5(0)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & = & {0\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 0\mathbf{ \text{k} } = 4\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)} & = & {3\tan \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sec \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 5\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }, \text{which does not exist} } \\ {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)} & = & {3\tan \left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sec \left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 5\left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & = & {3\left( {- \sqrt{3}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4(-2)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{10\pi}{3}\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & = & {-3\sqrt{3}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 8\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{10\pi}{3}\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$ To determine whether this function has any domain restrictions, consider the component functions separately. The first component function is $$f(t) = 3\tan t,$$ the second component function is $$g(t) = 4\sec t,$$ and the third component function is $$h(t) = 5t.$$ The first two functions are not defined for odd multiples of $$\pi/2,$$ so the function is not defined for odd multiples of $$\pi/2.$$ Therefore, $$\text{dom} \left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} \right) = \left\{ {t\left| {t \neq \frac{\left( {2n + 1} \right)\pi}{2}} \right.} \right\},$$ where n is any integer.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.2" title="Graphing a Vector-Valued Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Create a graph of each of the following vector-valued functions:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The plane curve represented by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\sin t\mathbf{ \text{j} },$$ $$0 \leq t \leq 2\pi$$</item>
        <item>The plane curve represented by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos \cos 2t\textbf{i} + 3\sin \sin 2 t\textbf{j},$$ $$0 \leq t \leq \pi$$</item>
        <item>The space curve represented by $$\textbf{r}(t) = 4\cos t\textbf{i} + 4\sin t\textbf{j} + t\textbf{k},$$ $$0 \leq t \leq 4\pi$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>As with any graph, we start with a table of values. We then graph each of the vectors in the second column of the table in standard position and connect the terminal points of each vector to form a curve (Figure 3.2). This curve turns out to be an ellipse centered at the origin. t $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ t $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ 0 $$4\mathbf{ \text{i} }$$ $$\pi$$ $$-4\mathbf{ \text{i} }$$ $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ $$2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{5\pi}{4}$$ $$-2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$ $$3\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{3\pi}{2}$$ $$-3\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{3\pi}{4}$$ $$-2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{7\pi}{4}$$ $$2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$2\pi$$ $$4\mathbf{ \text{i} }$$ Table 3.1 Table of Values for $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 3\sin t\mathbf{ \text{j} },$$ $$0 \leq t \leq 2\pi$$ Figure 3.2 The graph of the first vector-valued function is an ellipse.</item>
        <item>The table of values for $$\textbf{r}(t) = 4\cos \cos 2t\textbf{i} + 3\sin \sin 2 t\textbf{j},$$ $$0 \leq t \leq \pi$$ is as follows: t $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ t $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ 0 $$4\mathbf{ \text{i} }$$ $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$ $$-4\mathbf{ \text{i} }$$ $$\frac{\pi}{8}$$ $$2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{5\pi}{8}$$ $$-2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ $$3\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{3\pi}{4}$$ $$-3\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{3\pi}{8}$$ $$-2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\frac{7\pi}{8}$$ $$2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ $$\pi$$ $$4\mathbf{ \text{i} }$$ Table 3.2 Table of Values for $$\textbf{r}(t) = 4\cos \left( { \text{2} t} \right)\textbf{i} + 3\sin \left( {2t} \right)\textbf{j},$$ $$0 \leq t \leq \pi$$ The graph of this curve is also an ellipse centered at the origin. Figure 3.3 The graph of the second vector-valued function is also an ellipse.</item>
        <item>We go through the same procedure for a three-dimensional vector function. t $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ t $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ 0 $$4\mathbf{ \text{i} }$$ $$\pi$$ $$-4\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \pi\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ $$\frac{\pi}{4}$$ $$2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{\pi}{4}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ $$\frac{5\pi}{4}$$ $$-2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{5\pi}{4}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ $$\frac{\pi}{2}$$ $$4\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{\pi}{2}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ $$\frac{3\pi}{2}$$ $$-4\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{3\pi}{2}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ $$\frac{3\pi}{4}$$ $$-2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{3\pi}{4}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ $$\frac{7\pi}{4}$$ $$2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 2\sqrt{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{7\pi}{4}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ $$2\pi$$ $$4\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\pi\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ Table 3.3 Table of Values for $$\textbf{r}(t) = 4\cos t\textbf{i} + 4\sin t\textbf{j} + t\textbf{k},$$ $$0 \leq t \leq 4\pi$$ The values then repeat themselves, except for the fact that the coefficient of k is always increasing (Figure 3.4). This curve is called a helix. Notice that if the k component is eliminated, then the function becomes $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \cos t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \sin t\mathbf{ \text{j} },$$ which is a unit circle centered at the origin. Figure 3.4 The graph of the third vector-valued function is a helix.</item>

    </solution>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="3.1" title="Limit of a Vector-Valued Function">
    <heading level="4">Limit of a Vector-Valued Function</heading>
    <paragraph>Let f, g, and h be functions of t. Then the limit of the vector-valued function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ as t approaches a is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\lbrack {\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(t)} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(t)} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} },$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>provided the limits $$\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(t) \text{and} \underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(t)$$ exist. Similarly, the limit of the vector-valued function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + h(t)\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ as t approaches a is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\lbrack {\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(t)} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(t)} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left\lbrack {\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }h(t)} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{k} },$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>provided the limits $$\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(t), \underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(t) \text{and} \underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }h(t)$$ exist.</paragraph>
  </note>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let f, g, and h be functions of t. Then, the vector-valued function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ is continuous at point $$t = a$$ if the following three conditions hold:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(a)$$ exists</item>
      <item>$$\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ exists</item>
      <item>$$\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \mathbf{ \text{r} }(a)$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Similarly, the vector-valued function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + h(t)\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ is continuous at point $$t = a$$ if the following three conditions hold:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(a)$$ exists</item>
      <item>$$\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ exists</item>
      <item>$$\underset{t\rightarrow a}{\lim }\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \mathbf{ \text{r} }(a)$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>The derivative of a vector-valued function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = \underset{ \text{Δ} t\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {t + \text{Δ} t} \right) - \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)}{ \text{Δ} t},$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>provided the limit exists. If $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)$$ exists, then r is differentiable at t. If $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)$$ exists for all t in an open interval $$\left( {a,b} \right),$$ then r is differentiable over the interval $$\left( {a,b} \right).$$ For the function to be differentiable over the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack,$$ the following two limits must exist as well:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(a) = \underset{ \text{Δ} t\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }\frac{\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {a + \text{Δ} t} \right) - \mathbf{ \text{r} }(a)}{ \text{Δ} t} \text{and} \mathbf{r^{\prime}}(b) = \underset{ \text{Δ} t\rightarrow 0^{-}}{\lim }\frac{\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {b + \text{Δ} t} \right) - \mathbf{ \text{r} }(b)}{ \text{Δ} t}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let’s use Equation 3.5:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} & {= \underset{ \text{Δ} t\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {t + \text{Δ} t} \right) - \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)}{ \text{Δ} t}} \\ & {= \underset{ \text{Δ} t\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left\lbrack {\left( {3\left( {t + \text{Δ} t} \right) + 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {\left( {t + \text{Δ} t} \right)^{2} - 4\left( {t + \text{Δ} t} \right) + 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\left( {3t + 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {t^{2} - 4t + 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right\rbrack}{ \text{Δ} t}} \\ & {= \underset{ \text{Δ} t\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left( {3t + 3 \text{Δ} t + 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {3t + 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {t^{2} + 2t \text{Δ} t + \left( { \text{Δ} t} \right)^{2} - 4t - 4 \text{Δ} t + 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } - \left( {t^{2} - 4t + 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }}{ \text{Δ} t}} \\ & {= \underset{ \text{Δ} t\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left( {3 \text{Δ} t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {2t \text{Δ} t + \left( { \text{Δ} t} \right)^{2} - 4 \text{Δ} t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }}{ \text{Δ} t}} \\ & {= \underset{ \text{Δ} t\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( {3\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {2t + \text{Δ} t - 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right)} \\ & {= 3\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {2t - 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <item>If $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + h(t)\mathbf{ \text{k} },$$ then $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = f^{\prime}(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g^{\prime}(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + h^{\prime}(t)\mathbf{ \text{k} }.$$</item>

<example number="3.5" title="Calculating the Derivative of Vector-Valued Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use Differentiation of Vector-Valued Functions to calculate the derivative of each of the following functions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left( {6t + 8} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {4t^{2} + 2t - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$</item>
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 3\cos t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sin t\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$</item>
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = e^{t}\sin t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + e^{t}\cos t\mathbf{ \text{j} } - e^{2t}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We use Differentiation of Vector-Valued Functions and what we know about differentiating functions of one variable.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The first component of $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left( {6t + 8} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {4t^{2} + 2t - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ is $$f(t) = 6t + 8.$$ The second component is $$g(t) = 4t^{2} + 2t - 3.$$ We have $$f^{\prime}(t) = 6$$ and $$g^{\prime}(t) = 8t + 2,$$ so the theorem gives $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = 6\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {8t + 2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }.$$</item>
        <item>The first component is $$f(t) = 3\cos t$$ and the second component is $$g(t) = 4\sin t.$$ We have $$f^{\prime}(t) = -3\sin t$$ and $$g^{\prime}(t) = 4\cos t,$$ so we obtain $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = -3\sin t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\cos t\mathbf{ \text{j} }.$$</item>
        <item>The first component of $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = e^{t}\sin t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + e^{t}\cos t\mathbf{ \text{j} } - e^{2t}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ is $$f(t) = e^{t}\sin t,$$ the second component is $$g(t) = e^{t}\cos t,$$ and the third component is $$h(t) = - e^{2t}.$$ We have $$f^{\prime}(t) = e^{t}\left( {\sin t + \cos t} \right),$$ $$g^{\prime}(t) = e^{t}\left( {\cos t - \sin t} \right),$$ and $$h^{\prime}(t) = -2e^{2t},$$ so the theorem gives $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = e^{t}\left( {\sin t + \cos t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + e^{t}\left( {\cos t - \sin t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } - 2e^{2t}\mathbf{ \text{k} }.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Properties of the Derivative of Vector-Valued Functions
snippet: Properties of the Derivative of Vector-Valued Functions: Properties of the Derivative of Vector-Valued Functions Let r and u be differentiable vector-valued functions of t, let f be a differentiable real-valued function of t, and let c be...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="3.3" title="Properties of the Derivative of Vector-Valued Functions">
    <heading level="4">Properties of the Derivative of Vector-Valued Functions</heading>
    <paragraph>Let r and u be differentiable vector-valued functions of t, let f be a differentiable real-valued function of t, and let c be a scalar.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lcrllcc} \text{i.} & & {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {c\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} \right\rbrack} & = & {c\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} & & \text{Scalar multiple} \\ \text{ii.} & & {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \pm \mathbf{ \text{u} }(t)} \right\rbrack} & = & {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) \pm \mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} & & \text{Sum and difference} \\ \text{iii.} & & {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {f(t)\mathbf{ \text{u} }(t)} \right\rbrack} & = & {f^{\prime}(t)\mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) + f(t)\mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} & & \text{Scalar product} \\ \text{iv.} & & {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{u} }(t)} \right\rbrack} & = & {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) + \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \cdot \mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} & & \text{Dot product} \\ \text{v.} & & {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \times \mathbf{ \text{u} }(t)} \right\rbrack} & = & {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) \times \mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) + \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \times \mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} & & \text{Cross product} \\ \text{vi.} & & {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {f(t)} \right)} \right\rbrack} & = & {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}\left( {f(t)} \right) \cdot f^{\prime}(t)} & & \text{Chain rule} \\ \text{vii.} & & { \text{If} \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} & = & {c, \text{then} \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \cdot \mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = 0.} & & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="3.6" title="Using the Properties of Derivatives of Vector-Valued Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Given the vector-valued functions</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left( {6t + 8} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {4t^{2} + 2t - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 5t\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) = \left( {t^{2} - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {2t + 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {t^{3} - 3t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} },$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>calculate each of the following derivatives using the properties of the derivative of vector-valued functions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{u} }(t)} \right\rbrack$$</item>
        <item>$$\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) \times \mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} \right\rbrack$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>We have $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = 6\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {8t + 2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 5\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ and $$\mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t) = 2t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {3t^{2} - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }.$$ Therefore, according to property iv.: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{u} }(t)} \right\rbrack} & {= \mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) + \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) \cdot \mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} \\ & {= \left( {6\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {8t + 2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 5\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right) \cdot \left( {\left( {t^{2} - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {2t + 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {t^{3} - 3t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right)} \\ & { + \left( {\left( {6t + 8} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {4t^{2} + 2t - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 5t\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right) \cdot \left( {2t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {3t^{2} - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right)} \\ & {= 6\left( {t^{2} - 3} \right) + \left( {8t + 2} \right)\left( {2t + 4} \right) + 5\left( {t^{3} - 3t} \right)} \\ & { + 2t\left( {6t + 8} \right) + 2\left( {4t^{2} + 2t - 3} \right) + 5t\left( {3t^{2} - 3} \right)} \\ & {= 20t^{3} + 42t^{2} + 26t - 16.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>First, we need to adapt property v. for this problem: $$\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) \times \mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} \right\rbrack = \mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t) \times \mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t) + \mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) \times \mathbf{ \text{u''} }(t).$$ Recall that the cross product of any vector with itself is zero. Furthermore, $$\mathbf{ \text{u''} }(t)$$ represents the second derivative of $$\mathbf{ \text{u} }(t):$$ $$\mathbf{ \text{u''} }(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} \right\rbrack = \frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {2t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {3t^{2} - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\rbrack = 2\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6t\mathbf{ \text{k} }.$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\frac{d}{dt}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) \times \mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} \right\rbrack} & {= \mathbf{0} + \left( {\left( {t^{2} - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {2t + 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {t^{3} - 3t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right) \times \left( {2\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6t\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right)} \\ & {= \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ {t^{2} - 3} & {2t + 4} & {t^{3} - 3t} \\ 2 & 0 & {6t} \end{matrix} \right|} \\ & {= 6t\left( {2t + 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {6t\left( {t^{2} - 3} \right) - 2\left( {t^{3} - 3t} \right)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } - 2\left( {2t + 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= \left( {12t^{2} + 24t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {12t - 4t^{3}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } - \left( {4t + 8} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let C be a curve defined by a vector-valued function r, and assume that $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)$$ exists when $$t = t_{0}.$$ A tangent vector v at $$t = t_{0}$$ is any vector such that, when the tail of the vector is placed at point $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( t_{0} \right)$$ on the graph, vector v is tangent to curve C. Vector $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}\left( t_{0} \right)$$ is an example of a tangent vector at point $$t = t_{0}.$$ Furthermore, assume that $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) \neq \mathbf{0}.$$ The principal unit tangent vector at t is defined to be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t) = \frac{\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)}{ \text{‖} {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \text{‖} },$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>provided $${ \text{‖} {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \text{‖} } \neq 0.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="3.7" title="Finding a Unit Tangent Vector">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the unit tangent vector for each of the following vector-valued functions:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \cos t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \sin t\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$</item>
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{u} }(t) = \left( {3t^{2} + 2t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {2 - 4t^{3}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {6t + 5} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\begin{array}{lrll} \text{First step:} & {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} & = & {{-sin} t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \cos t\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ \text{Second step:} & { \text{‖} {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \text{‖} } & = & {\sqrt{\left( {-\sin t} \right)^{2} + \left( {\cos t} \right)^{2}} = 1} \\ \text{Third step:} & {\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t)} & = & {\frac{\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)}{ \text{‖} {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \text{‖} } = \frac{ \text{−sin} t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \cos t\mathbf{ \text{j} }}{1} = \text{−sin} t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \cos t\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>$$\begin{array}{cccl} \text{First step:} & {\mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} & = & {\left( {6t + 2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 12t^{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ \text{Second step:} & { \text{‖} {\mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} \text{‖} } & = & \sqrt{\left( {6t + 2} \right)^{2} + \left( {-12t^{2}} \right)^{2} + 6^{2}} \\ & & = & \sqrt{144t^{4} + 36t^{2} + 24t + 40} \\ & & = & {2\sqrt{36t^{4} + 9t^{2} + 6t + 10}} \\ \text{Third step:} & {\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t)} & = & {\frac{\mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)}{ \text{‖} {\mathbf{u^{\prime}}(t)} \text{‖} } = \frac{\left( {6t + 2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 12t^{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{k} }}{2\sqrt{36t^{4} + 9t^{2} + 6t + 10}}} \\ & & = & {\frac{3t + 1}{\sqrt{36t^{4} + 9t^{2} + 6t + 10}}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{6t^{2}}{\sqrt{36t^{4} + 9t^{2} + 6t + 10}}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{3}{\sqrt{36t^{4} + 9t^{2} + 6t + 10}}\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let f, g, and h be integrable real-valued functions over the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack.$$</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The indefinite integral of a vector-valued function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ is $${\int{\left\lbrack {f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right\rbrack dt}} = \left\lbrack {{\int{f(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {{\int{g(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} }.$$ (3.7) The definite integral of a vector-valued function is $${\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \right\rbrack dt}} = \left\lbrack {{\int_{a}^{b}{f(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {{\int_{a}^{b}{g(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} }.$$ (3.8)</item>
      <item>The indefinite integral of a vector-valued function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + h(t)\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ is $${\int{\left\lbrack {f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + h(t)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\rbrack dt}} = \left\lbrack {{\int{f(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {{\int{g(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left\lbrack {{\int{h(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{k} }.$$ (3.9) The definite integral of the vector-valued function is $${\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {f(t)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + h(t)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\rbrack dt}} = \left\lbrack {{\int_{a}^{b}{f(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {{\int_{a}^{b}{g(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left\lbrack {{\int_{a}^{b}{h(t)dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{k} }.$$ (3.10)</item>
    </list>
  </note>

<example number="3.8" title="Integrating Vector-Valued Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate each of the following integrals:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$${\int\left\lbrack {\left( {3t^{2} + 2t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {3t - 6} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {6t^{3} + 5t^{2} - 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\rbrack} dt$$</item>
        <item>$${\int\left\lbrack {\left\langle {t,t^{2},t^{3}} \right\rangle \times \left\langle {t^{3},t^{2},t} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack} dt$$</item>
        <item>$$\int_{0}^{\pi/3}{\left\lbrack {\sin 2t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \tan t\mathbf{ \text{j} } + e^{-2t}\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\rbrack dt}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>We use the first part of the definition of the integral of a space curve: $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int\left\lbrack {\left( {3t^{2} + 2t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {3t - 6} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {6t^{3} + 5t^{2} - 4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\rbrack}dt} \\ \\ { = \left\lbrack {{\int{3t^{2} + 2t dt}}} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {{\int{3t - 6}}dt} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left\lbrack {{\int{6t^{3} + 5t^{2} - 4}}dt} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ { = \left( {t^{3} + t^{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {\frac{3}{2}t^{2} - 6t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {\frac{3}{2}t^{4} + \frac{5}{3}t^{3} - 4t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} } + \mathbf{ \text{C} }.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>First calculate $$\left\langle {t,t^{2},t^{3}} \right\rangle \times \left\langle {t^{3},t^{2},t} \right\rangle:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\left\langle {t,t^{2},t^{3}} \right\rangle \times \left\langle {t^{3},t^{2},t} \right\rangle} & {= \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ t & t^{2} & t^{3} \\ t^{3} & t^{2} & t \end{matrix} \right|} \\ & {= \left( {t^{2}(t) - t^{3}\left( t^{2} \right)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {t^{2} - t^{3}\left( t^{3} \right)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {t\left( t^{2} \right) - t^{2}\left( t^{3} \right)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= \left( {t^{3} - t^{5}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {t^{6} - t^{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {t^{3} - t^{5}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$ Next, substitute this back into the integral and integrate: $$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int\left\lbrack {\left\langle {t,t^{2},t^{3}} \right\rangle \times \left\langle {t^{3},t^{2},t} \right\rangle} \right\rbrack}dt} & {= {\int{\left( {t^{3} - t^{5}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {t^{6} - t^{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {t^{3} - t^{5}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} } dt}}} \\ & {= \left( {\frac{t^{4}}{4} - \frac{t^{6}}{6}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {\frac{t^{7}}{7} - \frac{t^{3}}{3}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {\frac{t^{4}}{4} - \frac{t^{6}}{6}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} } + \mathbf{ \text{C} }.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>Use the second part of the definition of the integral of a space curve: $$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{0}^{\pi/3}{\left\lbrack {\sin 2t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \tan t\mathbf{ \text{j} } + e^{-2t}\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\rbrack dt}} \\ \\ {= \left\lbrack {{\int_{0}^{\pi/3}{\sin 2t}}dt} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {{\int_{0}^{\pi/3}{\tan t}}dt} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left\lbrack {{\int_{0}^{\pi/3}e^{-2t}}dt} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ {= \left. \left( {- \frac{1}{2}\cos 2t} \right) \right|_{0}^{\pi/3}\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left. \left( {\ln \left( {\cos t} \right)} \right) \right|_{0}^{\pi/3}\mathbf{ \text{j} } - \left. \left( {\frac{1}{2}e^{-2t}} \right) \right|_{0}^{\pi/3}\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ {= \left( {- \frac{1}{2}\cos \frac{2\pi}{3} + \frac{1}{2}\cos 0} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {\ln \left( {\cos \frac{\pi}{3}} \right) - \ln \left( {\cos 0} \right)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } - \left( {\frac{1}{2}e^{-2\pi/3} - \frac{1}{2}e^{-2{(0)}}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ {= \left( {\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \left( {-\ln 2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } - \left( {\frac{1}{2}e^{-2\pi/3} - \frac{1}{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ {= \frac{3}{4}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {\ln 2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}e^{-2\pi/3}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="3.4" title="Arc-Length Formulas">
    <heading level="4">Arc-Length Formulas</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Plane curve: Given a smooth curve C defined by the function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t) \mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t) \mathbf{ \text{j} },$$ where t lies within the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack,$$ the arc length of C over the interval is $$s = {\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{ \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(t)} \right\rbrack^{2} + \left\lbrack {g^{\prime}(t)} \right\rbrack^{2}}}dt = {\int_{a}^{b}\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|} dt.$$ (3.11)</item>
      <item>Space curve: Given a smooth curve C defined by the function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = f(t) \mathbf{ \text{i} } + g(t) \mathbf{ \text{j} } + h(t) \mathbf{ \text{k} },$$ where t lies within the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack,$$ the arc length of C over the interval is $$s = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{ \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(t)} \right\rbrack^{2} + \left\lbrack {g^{\prime}(t)} \right\rbrack^{2} + \left\lbrack {h^{\prime}(t)} \right\rbrack^{2}}dt}} = {\int_{a}^{b}\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|} dt.$$ (3.12)</item>

body_xml:
<example number="3.9" title="Finding the Arc Length">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate the arc length for each of the following vector-valued functions:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left( {3t - 2} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {4t + 5} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} },1 \leq t \leq 5$$</item>
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {t\cos t,t\sin t,2t} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 2\pi$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Using Equation 3.11, $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = 3\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\mathbf{ \text{j} },$$ so $$\begin{array}{cl} s & {= {\int_{a}^{b}\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|} dt} \\ & {= {\int_{a}^{5}\sqrt{3^{2} + 4^{2}}}dt} \\ & {= {\int_{1}^{5}{5 dt}} = \left. {5t} \right|_{1}^{5} = 20.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>Using Equation 3.12, $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = \left\langle {\cos t - t\sin t,\sin t + t\cos t,2} \right\rangle,$$ so $$\begin{array}{cl} s & {= {\int_{a}^{b}\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|} dt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sqrt{\left( {\cos t - t\sin t} \right)^{2} + \left( {\sin t + t\cos t} \right)^{2} + 2^{2}}}dt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{\left( {\cos^{2}t - 2t\sin t\cos t + t^{2}\sin^{2}t} \right) + \left( {\sin^{2}t + 2t\sin t\cos t + t^{2}\cos^{2}t} \right) + 4} dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{\cos^{2}t + \sin^{2}t + t^{2}\left( {\cos^{2}t + \sin^{2}t} \right) + 4} dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{t^{2} + 5} dt}}.} \end{array}$$ Here we can use a table integration formula $${\int{\sqrt{u^{2} + a^{2}} du}} = \frac{u}{2}\sqrt{u^{2} + a^{2}} + \frac{a^{2}}{2}\ln \left| {u + \sqrt{u^{2} + a^{2}}} \right| + C,$$ so we obtain $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{t^{2} + 5} dt}} & {= \frac{1}{2}\left( {t\sqrt{t^{2} + 5} + 5\ln \left| {t + \sqrt{t^{2} + 5}} \right|} \right)_{0}^{2\pi}} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}\left( {2\pi\sqrt{4\pi^{2} + 5} + 5\ln \left( {2\pi + \sqrt{4\pi^{2} + 5}} \right)} \right) - \frac{5}{2}\ln \sqrt{5}} \\ & {\approx 25.343.} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="3.5" title="Arc-Length Function">
    <heading level="4">Arc-Length Function</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ describe a smooth curve for $$t \geq a.$$ Then the arc-length function is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$s(t) = {\int_{a}^{t}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(u)} \right\| du}}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Furthermore, $$\frac{ds}{dt} = \left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\| > 0.$$ If $$\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\| = 1$$ for all $$t \geq a,$$ then the parameter t represents the arc length from the starting point at $$t = a.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Finding an Arc-Length Parameterization: Find the arc-length parameterization for each of the following curves: \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sin t \mathbf{ \text{j} },t \geq 0 \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) =...
body_xml:
<example number="3.10" title="Finding an Arc-Length Parameterization">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the arc-length parameterization for each of the following curves:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sin t \mathbf{ \text{j} },t \geq 0$$</item>
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {t + 3, 2t - 4,2t} \right\rangle,t \geq 3$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>First we find the arc-length function using Equation 3.14: $$\begin{array}{cl} {s(t)} & {= {\int_{a}^{t}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(u)} \right\| du}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{t}{\left\| \left\langle {-4\sin u,4\cos u} \right\rangle \right\| du}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{t}{\sqrt{\left( {-4\sin u} \right)^{2} + \left( {4\cos u} \right)^{2}} du}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{t}{\sqrt{16\sin^{2}u + 16\cos^{2}u} du}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{t}{4 du}} = 4t,} \end{array}$$ which gives the relationship between the arc length s and the parameter t as $$s = 4t;$$ so, $$t = {s/4.}$$ Next we replace the variable t in the original function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sin t \mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ with the expression $$s/4$$ to obtain $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos \left( \frac{s}{4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sin \left( \frac{s}{4} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }.$$ This is the arc-length parameterization of $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t).$$ Since the original restriction on t was given by $$t \geq 0,$$ the restriction on s becomes $${s/4} \geq 0,$$ or $$s \geq 0.$$</item>
        <item>The arc-length function is given by Equation 3.14: $$\begin{array}{cl} {s(t)} & {= {\int_{a}^{t}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(u)} \right\| du}}} \\ & {= {\int_{3}^{t}{\left\| \left\langle {1,2,2} \right\rangle \right\| du}}} \\ & {= {\int_{3}^{t}{\sqrt{1^{2} + 2^{2} + 2^{2}} du}}} \\ & {= {\int_{3}^{t}{3 du}}} \\ & {= 3t - 9.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the relationship between the arc length s and the parameter t is $$s = 3t - 9,$$ so $$t = \frac{s}{3} + 3.$$ Substituting this into the original function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {t + 3, 2t - 4,2t} \right\rangle$$ yields $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(s) = \left\langle {\left( {\frac{s}{3} + 3} \right) + 3, 2\left( {\frac{s}{3} + 3} \right) - 4,2\left( {\frac{s}{3} + 3} \right)} \right\rangle = \left\langle {\frac{s}{3} + 6, \frac{2s}{3} + 2,\frac{2s}{3} + 6} \right\rangle.$$ This is an arc-length parameterization of $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t).$$ The original restriction on the parameter $$t$$ was $$t \geq 3,$$ so the restriction on s is $$\left( {s/3} \right) + 3 \geq 3,$$ or $$s \geq 0.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="3.6" title="Alternative Formulas for Curvature">
    <heading level="4">Alternative Formulas for Curvature</heading>
    <paragraph>If C is a smooth curve given by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t),$$ then the curvature $$\kappa$$ of C at t is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\kappa = \frac{\left\| {\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If C is a three-dimensional curve, then the curvature can be given by the formula</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\kappa = \frac{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) \times \mathbf{r^{''}}(t)} \right\|}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|^{3}}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If C is the graph of a function $$y = f(x)$$ and both $$y^{\prime}$$ and $$y^{''}$$ exist, then the curvature $$\kappa$$ at point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\kappa = \frac{\left| y^{''} \right|}{\left\lbrack {1 + \left( y^{\prime} \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack^{3/2}}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="3.11" title="Finding Curvature">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the curvature for each of the following curves at the given point:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 4\sin t \mathbf{ \text{j} } + 3t \mathbf{ \text{k} },t = \frac{4\pi}{3}$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = \sqrt{4x - x^{2}},x = 2$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>This function describes a helix. The curvature of the helix at $$t = {\left( {4\pi} \right)/3}$$ can be found by using Equation 3.15. First, calculate $$\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t):$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t)} & {= \frac{\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{\left\langle {-4\sin t,4\cos t,3} \right\rangle}{\sqrt{\left( {-4\sin t} \right)^{2} + \left( {4\cos t} \right)^{2} + 3^{2}}}} \\ & {= \left\langle {- \frac{4}{5}\sin t,\frac{4}{5}\cos t,\frac{3}{5}} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$ Next, calculate $$\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t):$$ $$\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t) = \left\langle {- \frac{4}{5}\cos t, - \frac{4}{5}\sin t,0} \right\rangle.$$ Last, apply Equation 3.15: $$\begin{array}{cl} \kappa & {= \frac{\left\| {\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|} = \frac{\left\| \left\langle {- \frac{4}{5}\cos t, - \frac{4}{5}\sin t,0} \right\rangle \right\|}{\left\| \left\langle {-4\sin t,4\cos t,3} \right\rangle \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{\sqrt{\left( {- \frac{4}{5}\cos t} \right)^{2} + \left( {- \frac{4}{5}\sin t} \right)^{2} + 0^{2}}}{\sqrt{\left( {-4\sin t} \right)^{2} + \left( {4\cos t} \right)^{2} + 3^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{4/5}{5} = \frac{4}{25}.} \end{array}$$ The curvature of this helix is constant at all points on the helix.</item>
        <item>This function describes a semicircle. To find the curvature of this graph, we must use Equation 3.16. First, we calculate $$y^{\prime}$$ and $$y^{''}:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} y & {= \sqrt{4x - x^{2}} = \left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{1/2}} \\ y^{\prime} & {= \frac{1}{2}\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{- {1/2}}\left( {4 - 2x} \right) = \left( {2 - x} \right)\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{- {1/2}}} \\ y^{''} & {= - \left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{- {1/2}} + \left( {2 - x} \right)\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{- {3/2}}\left( {4 - 2x} \right)} \\ & {= - \frac{4x - x^{2}}{\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2}} - \frac{\left( {2 - x} \right)^{2}}{\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}} \\ & {= \frac{x^{2} - 4x - \left( {4 - 4x + x^{2}} \right)}{\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}} \\ & {= - \frac{4}{\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}.} \end{array}$$ Then, we apply Equation 3.17: $$\begin{array}{cl} \kappa & {= \frac{\left| y^{''} \right|}{\left\lbrack {1 + \left( y^{\prime} \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack^{3/2}}} \\ & {= \frac{\left| {- \frac{4}{\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}} \right|}{\left\lbrack {1 + \left( {\left( {2 - x} \right)\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{- {1/2}}} \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack^{3/2}} = \frac{\left| \frac{4}{\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2}} \right|}{\left\lbrack {1 + \frac{\left( {2 - x} \right)^{2}}{4x - x^{2}}} \right\rbrack^{3/2}}} \\ & {= \frac{\left| \frac{4}{\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2}} \right|}{\left\lbrack \frac{4x - x^{2} + x^{2} - 4x + 4}{4x - x^{2}} \right\rbrack^{3/2}} = \left| \frac{4}{\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2}} \right| \cdot \frac{\left( {4x - x^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}{8}} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}.} \end{array}$$ The curvature of this circle is equal to the reciprocal of its radius. There is a minor issue with the absolute value in Equation 3.16; however, a closer look at the calculation reveals that the denominator is positive for any value of x.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let C be a three-dimensional smooth curve represented by r over an open interval I. If $$\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t) \neq \mathbf{0},$$ then the principal unit normal vector at t is defined to be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{N} }(t) = \frac{\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)}{\left\| {\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The binormal vector at t is defined as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{B} }(t) = \mathbf{ \text{T} }(t) \times \mathbf{ \text{N} }(t),$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t)$$ is the unit tangent vector.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding the Principal Unit Normal Vector and Binormal Vector
snippet: Finding the Principal Unit Normal Vector and Binormal Vector: For each of the following vector-valued functions, find the principal unit normal vector. Then, if possible, find the binormal vector. \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t \mathbf{...
body_xml:
<example number="3.12" title="Finding the Principal Unit Normal Vector and Binormal Vector">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each of the following vector-valued functions, find the principal unit normal vector. Then, if possible, find the binormal vector.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = 4\cos t \mathbf{ \text{i} } - 4\sin t \mathbf{ \text{j} }$$</item>
        <item>$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left( {6t + 2} \right) \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 5t^{2} \mathbf{ \text{j} } - 8t \mathbf{ \text{k} }$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>This function describes a circle. To find the principal unit normal vector, we first must find the unit tangent vector $$\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t):$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t)} & {= \frac{\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{-4\sin t \mathbf{ \text{i} } - 4\cos t \mathbf{ \text{j} }}{\sqrt{\left( {-4\sin t} \right)^{2} + \left( {-4\cos t} \right)^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{-4\sin t \mathbf{ \text{i} } - 4\cos t \mathbf{ \text{j} }}{\sqrt{16\sin^{2}t + 16\cos^{2}t}}} \\ & {= \frac{-4\sin t \mathbf{ \text{i} } - 4\cos t \mathbf{ \text{j} }}{\sqrt{16\left( {\sin^{2}t + \cos^{2}t} \right)}}} \\ & {= \frac{-4\sin t \mathbf{ \text{i} } - 4\cos t \mathbf{ \text{j} }}{4}} \\ & {= - \sin t \mathbf{ \text{i} } - \cos t \mathbf{ \text{j} }.} \end{array}$$ Next, we use Equation 3.18: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{N} }(t)} & {= \frac{\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)}{\left\| {\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{-\cos t \mathbf{ \text{i} } + \sin t \mathbf{ \text{j} }}{\sqrt{\left( {-\cos t} \right)^{2} + \left( {\sin t} \right)^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{-\cos t \mathbf{ \text{i} } + \sin t \mathbf{ \text{j} }}{\sqrt{\cos^{2}t + \sin^{2}t}}} \\ & {= - \cos t \mathbf{ \text{i} } + \sin t \mathbf{ \text{j} }.} \end{array}$$ Notice that the unit tangent vector and the principal unit normal vector are orthogonal to each other for all values of t: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }(t)} & {= \left\langle {-\sin t, - \cos t} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {-\cos t,\sin t} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \sin t\cos t - \cos t\sin t} \\ & {= 0.} \end{array}$$ Furthermore, the principal unit normal vector points toward the center of the circle from every point on the circle. Since $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ defines a curve in two dimensions, we cannot calculate the binormal vector.</item>
        <item>This function looks like this: To find the principal unit normal vector, we first find the unit tangent vector $$\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t):$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t)} & {= \frac{\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|}} \\ & {= \frac{6 \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 10t \mathbf{ \text{j} } - 8 \mathbf{ \text{k} }}{\sqrt{6^{2} + \left( {10t} \right)^{2} + (-8)^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{6 \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 10t \mathbf{ \text{j} } - 8 \mathbf{ \text{k} }}{\sqrt{36 + 100t^{2} + 64}}} \\ & {= \frac{6 \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 10t \mathbf{ \text{j} } - 8\mathbf{ \text{k} }}{\sqrt{100\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)}}} \\ & {= \frac{3 \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 5t \mathbf{ \text{j} } - 4\mathbf{ \text{k} }}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}} \\ & {= \frac{3}{5}\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{- {1/2}}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + t\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{- {1/2}}\mathbf{ \text{j} } - \frac{4}{5}\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{- {1/2}}\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$ Next, we calculate $$\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)$$ and $$\left\| {\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)} & {= \frac{3}{5}\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{- {3/2}}\left( {2t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{- {1/2}} - t\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{- {3/2}}\left( {2t} \right)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ & { - \frac{4}{5}\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{- {3/2}}\left( {2t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= - \frac{3t}{5\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3/2}}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \frac{1}{\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3/2}}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{4t}{5\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3/2}}\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ \left\| {\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)} \right\| & {= \sqrt{\left( {- \frac{3t}{5\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3/2}}} \right)^{2} + \left( {- \frac{1}{\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3/2}}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{4t}{5\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3/2}} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{\frac{9t^{2}}{25\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3}} + \frac{1}{\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3}} + \frac{16t^{2}}{25\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3}}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{\frac{25t^{2} + 25}{25\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3}}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{\frac{1}{\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{1}{t^{2} + 1}.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, according to Equation 3.18: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{N} }(t)} & {= \frac{\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)}{\left\| {\mathbf{T^{\prime}}(t)} \right\|}} \\ & {= \left( {- \frac{3t}{5\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3/2}}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \frac{1}{\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3/2}}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{4t}{5\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{3/2}}\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right)\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)} \\ & {= - \frac{3t}{5\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{1/2}}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \frac{5}{5\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{1/2}}\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \frac{4t}{5\left( {t^{2} + 1} \right)^{1/2}}\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= - \frac{3t \mathbf{ \text{i} } - 5\mathbf{ \text{j} } - 4t \mathbf{ \text{k} }}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}.} \end{array}$$ Once again, the unit tangent vector and the principal unit normal vector are orthogonal to each other for all values of t: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }(t)} & {= \left( \frac{3 \mathbf{ \text{i} } + 5t \mathbf{ \text{j} } - 4\mathbf{ \text{k} }}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right) \cdot \left( {- \frac{3t \mathbf{ \text{i} } - 5\mathbf{ \text{j} } - 4t \mathbf{ \text{k} }}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{3\left( {-3t} \right) - 5t(-5) - 4\left( {4t} \right)}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}} \\ & {= \frac{-9t + 25t - 16t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}} \\ & {= 0.} \end{array}$$ Last, since $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ represents a three-dimensional curve, we can calculate the binormal vector using Equation 3.17: $$\begin{matrix} {\textbf{B}(t)} & {= \textbf{T}(t) \times \textbf{N}(t)} \\ & {= \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ \frac{3}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} & {+ \frac{5t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}} & {- \frac{4}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}} \\ {- \frac{3t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}} & {+ \frac{5}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}} & \frac{4t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \end{matrix} \right|} \\ & {= \left( \left( + \frac{5t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right)\left( \frac{4t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right) - \left( - \frac{4}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right)\left( + \frac{5}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right) \right)\textbf{i}} \\ & { + \left( \left( \frac{3}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right)\left( \frac{4t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right) - \left( - \frac{4}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right)\left( - \frac{3t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right) \right)\textbf{j}} \\ & { + \left( \left( \frac{3}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right)\left( + \frac{5}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right) - \left( + \frac{5t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right)\left( - \frac{3t}{5\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}} \right) \right)\textbf{k}} \\ & {= \left( \frac{20t^{2} + 20}{25\left( t^{2} + 1 \right)} \right)\textbf{i} + \left( \frac{-15 - 15t^{2}}{25\left( t^{2} + 1 \right)} \right)\textbf{k}} \\ & {= 20\left( \frac{t^{2} + 1}{25\left( t^{2} + 1 \right)} \right)\textbf{i+}15\left( \frac{t^{2} + 1}{25\left( t^{2} + 1 \right)} \right)\textbf{k}} \\ & {= \frac{4}{5}\textbf{i+}\frac{3}{5}\textbf{k}.} \end{matrix}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Equation of an Osculating Circle
snippet: Finding the Equation of an Osculating Circle: Find an equation of the osculating circle of the curve defined by the function y = x^{3} - 3x + 1 at x = 1. Figure 3.9 shows the graph of y = x^{3} - 3x + 1. First, let’s calculate the...
body_xml: Find an equation of the osculating circle of the curve defined by the function $$y = x^{3} - 3x + 1$$ at $$x = 1.$$ Figure 3.9 shows the graph of $$y = x^{3} - 3x + 1.$$ First, let’s calculate the curvature at $$x = 1:$$ $$\kappa = \frac{\left| {f^{''}(x)} \right|}{\left( {1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}} \right)^{3/2}} = \frac{\left| {6x} \right|}{\left( {1 + \left\lbrack {3x^{2} - 3} \right\rbrack^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}.$$ This gives $$\kappa = 6.$$ Therefore, the radius of the osculating circle is given by $$R = \frac{1}{\kappa} = \frac{1}{6}.$$ Next, we then calculate the coordinates of the center of the circle. When $$x = 1,$$ the slope of the tangent line is zero. Therefore, the center of the osculating circle is directly above the point on the graph with coordinates $$\left( {1,-1} \right).$$ The center is located at $$\left( {1, - \frac{5}{6}} \right).$$ The formula for a circle with radius r and center $$\left( {h,k} \right)$$ is given by $$\left( {x - h} \right)^{2} + \left( {y - k} \right)^{2} = r^{2}.$$ Therefore, the equation of the osculating circle is $$\left( {x - 1} \right)^{2} + \left( {y + \frac{5}{6}} \right)^{2} = \frac{1}{36}.$$ The graph and its osculating circle appears in the following graph.

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Let \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) be a twice-differentiable vector-valued function of the parameter t that represents the position of an object as a function of time. The velocity vector \mathbf{ \text{v} }(t) of the object is given...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ be a twice-differentiable vector-valued function of the parameter t that represents the position of an object as a function of time. The velocity vector $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }(t)$$ of the object is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Velocity} = \mathbf{ \text{v} }(t) = \mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t).$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The acceleration vector $$\mathbf{ \text{a} }(t)$$ is defined to be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Acceleration} = \mathbf{ \text{a} }(t) = \mathbf{v^{\prime}}(t) = \mathbf{ \text{r''} }(t).$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The speed is defined to be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Speed} = v(t) = \left\| {\mathbf{ \text{v} }(t)} \right\| = \left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\| = \frac{ds}{dt}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="3.14" title="Studying Motion Along a Parabola">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A particle moves in a parabolic path defined by the vector-valued function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = t^{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \sqrt{5 - t^{2}}\mathbf{ \text{j} },$$ where t measures time in seconds.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find the velocity, acceleration, and speed as functions of time.</item>
        <item>Sketch the curve along with the velocity vector at time $$t = 1.$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>We use Equation 3.20, Equation 3.21, and Equation 3.22: $$\begin{array}{cll} {\mathbf{ \text{v} }(t)} & = & {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = 2t\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{t}{\sqrt{5 - t^{2}}}\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ {\mathbf{ \text{a} }(t)} & = & {\mathbf{v^{\prime}}(t) = 2\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 5\left( {5 - t^{2}} \right)^{- \frac{3}{2}}\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ {v(t)} & = & \left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\| \\ & = & \sqrt{\left( {2t} \right)^{2} + \left( {- \frac{t}{\sqrt{5 - t^{2}}}} \right)^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{4t^{2} + \frac{t^{2}}{5 - t^{2}}} \\ & = & {\sqrt{\frac{21t^{2} - 4t^{4}}{5 - t^{2}}}.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>The graph of $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = t^{2}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \sqrt{5 - t^{2}}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ is a portion of a parabola (Figure 3.11). The velocity vector at $$t = 1$$ is $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }(1) = \mathbf{r^{\prime}}(1) = 2(1)\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{1}{\sqrt{5 - (1)^{2}}}\mathbf{ \text{j} } = 2\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$ and the acceleration vector at $$t = 1$$ is $$\mathbf{ \text{a} }(1) = \mathbf{v^{\prime}}(1) = 2\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 5\left( {5 - (1)^{2}} \right)^{-{3/2}}\mathbf{ \text{j} } = 2\mathbf{ \text{i} } - \frac{5}{8}\mathbf{ \text{j} }.$$ Notice that the velocity vector is tangent to the path, as is always the case. Figure 3.11 This graph depicts the velocity vector at time $$t = 1$$ for a particle moving in a parabolic path.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="3.7" title="The Plane of the Acceleration Vector">
    <heading level="4">The Plane of the Acceleration Vector</heading>
    <paragraph>The acceleration vector $$\mathbf{ \text{a} }(t)$$ of an object moving along a curve traced out by a twice-differentiable function $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ lies in the plane formed by the unit tangent vector $$\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t)$$ and the principal unit normal vector $$\mathbf{ \text{N} }(t)$$ to C. Furthermore,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{a} }(t) = v^{\prime}(t)\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t) + \left\lbrack {v(t)} \right\rbrack^{2}\kappa\mathbf{ \text{N} }(t).$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Here, $$v(t)$$ is the speed of the object and $$\kappa$$ is the curvature of C traced out by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t).$$</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Tangential and Normal Components of Acceleration: Tangential and Normal Components of Acceleration Let \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) be a vector-valued function that denotes the position of an object as a function of time. Then \mathbf{ \text{a}...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="3.8" title="Tangential and Normal Components of Acceleration">
    <heading level="4">Tangential and Normal Components of Acceleration</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ be a vector-valued function that denotes the position of an object as a function of time. Then $$\mathbf{ \text{a} }(t) = \mathbf{ \text{r''} }(t)$$ is the acceleration vector. The tangential and normal components of acceleration $$a_{\mathbf{ \text{T} }}$$ and $$a_{\mathbf{ \text{N} }}$$ are given by the formulas</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a_{\mathbf{ \text{T} }} = \mathbf{ \text{a} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} } = \frac{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{a} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\|}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a_{\mathbf{ \text{N} }} = \mathbf{ \text{a} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} } = \frac{\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{v} } \times \mathbf{ \text{a} }} \right\|}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\|} = \sqrt{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{a} } \right\|^{2} - a_{\mathbf{ \text{T} }}^{2}}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>These components are related by the formula</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{a} }(t) = a_{\mathbf{ \text{T} }}\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t) + a_{\mathbf{ \text{N} }}\mathbf{ \text{N} }(t).$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Here $$\mathbf{ \text{T} }(t)$$ is the unit tangent vector to the curve defined by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t),$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{N} }(t)$$ is the unit normal vector to the curve defined by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t).$$</paragraph>
  </note>

    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Let’s start with Equation 3.23: $$\begin{array}{cll} {\mathbf{ \text{v} }(t)} & = & {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = 2t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {6t - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ {\mathbf{ \text{a} }(t)} & = & {\mathbf{v^{\prime}}(t) = 2\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ a_{\mathbf{ \text{T} }} & = & \frac{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{a} }}{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right\|} \\ & = & \frac{\left( {2t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {6t - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right) \cdot \left( {2\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right)}{\left\| {2t\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 2\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {6t - 3} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\|} \\ & = & \frac{4t + 6\left( {6t - 3} \right)}{\sqrt{\left( {2t} \right)^{2} + 2^{2} + \left( {6t - 3} \right)^{2}}} \\ & = & {\frac{40t - 18}{\sqrt{40t^{2} - 36t + 13}}.} \end{array}$$ Then we apply Equation 3.24: $$\begin{array}{cl} a_{\mathbf{ \text{N} }} & {= \sqrt{\left\| \mathbf{ \text{a} } \right\|^{2} - {a\mathbf{ \text{T} }}^{2}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{\left\| {2\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 6\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\|^{2} - \left( \frac{40t - 18}{\sqrt{40t^{2} - 36t + 13}} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{4 + 36 - \frac{\left( {40t - 18} \right)^{2}}{40t^{2} - 36t + 13}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{\frac{40\left( {40t^{2} - 36t + 13} \right) - \left( {1600t^{2} - 1440t + 324} \right)}{40t^{2} - 36t + 13}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{\frac{196}{40t^{2} - 36t + 13}}} \\ & {= \frac{14}{\sqrt{40t^{2} - 36t + 13}}.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>We must evaluate each of the answers from part a. at $$t = 2:$$ $$\begin{array}{cll} {a_{\mathbf{ \text{T} }}(2)} & = & \frac{40(2) - 18}{\sqrt{40(2)^{2} - 36(2) + 13}} \\ & = & {\frac{80 - 18}{\sqrt{160 - 72 + 13}} = \frac{62}{\sqrt{101}}} \\ {a_{\mathbf{ \text{N} }}(2)} & = & \frac{14}{\sqrt{40(2)^{2} - 36(2) + 13}} \\ & = & {\frac{14}{\sqrt{160 - 72 + 13}} = \frac{14}{\sqrt{101}}.} \end{array}$$ The units of acceleration are feet per second squared, as are the units of the normal and tangential components of acceleration.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Motion of a Cannonball
snippet: Motion of a Cannonball: During an Independence Day celebration, a cannonball is fired from a cannon on a cliff toward the water. The cannon is aimed at an angle of 30° above horizontal and the initial speed of the cannonball is 600...
body_xml:
<example number="3.16" title="Motion of a Cannonball">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>During an Independence Day celebration, a cannonball is fired from a cannon on a cliff toward the water. The cannon is aimed at an angle of 30° above horizontal and the initial speed of the cannonball is $$600 \text{ft/sec} .$$ The cliff is 100 ft above the water (Figure 3.17).</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find the maximum height of the cannonball.</item>
        <item>How long will it take for the cannonball to splash into the sea?</item>
        <item>How far out to sea will the cannonball hit the water? Figure 3.17 The flight of a cannonball (ignoring air resistance) is projectile motion.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We use the equation</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{s} }(t) = v_{0}t\cos \theta\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {v_{0}t\sin \theta - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>with $$\theta = 30^\circ,$$ $$g = 32{ \text{ft/sec} }^{2},$$ and $$v_{0} = 600$$ ft/sec. Then the position equation becomes</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{s} }(t)} & {= 600t\left( {\cos 30} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {600t\sin 30 - \frac{1}{2}(32)t^{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ & {= 300t\sqrt{3}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {300t - 16t^{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The cannonball reaches its maximum height when the vertical component of its velocity is zero, because the cannonball is neither rising nor falling at that point. The velocity vector is $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{v} }(t)} & {= \mathbf{s^{\prime}}(t)} \\ & {= 300\sqrt{3}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {300 - 32t} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the vertical component of velocity is given by the expression $$300 - 32t.$$ Setting this expression equal to zero and solving for t gives $$t = 9.375$$ sec. The height of the cannonball at this time is given by the vertical component of the position vector, evaluated at $$t = 9.375.$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{s} }(9.375)} & {= 300(9.375)\sqrt{3}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {300(9.375) - 16(9.375)^{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ & {= 4871.39\mathbf{ \text{i} } + 1406.25\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the maximum height of the cannonball is 1406.39 ft above the cannon, or 1506.39 ft above sea level.</item>
        <item>When the cannonball lands in the water, it is 100 ft below the cannon. Therefore, the vertical component of the position vector is equal to $$-100.$$ Setting the vertical component of $$\mathbf{ \text{s} }(t)$$ equal to $$-100$$ and solving, we obtain $$\begin{array}{cll} & & \\ {300t - 16t^{2}} & = & -100 \\ {16t^{2} - 300t - 100} & = & 0 \\ {4t^{2} - 75t - 25} & = & 0 \\ t & = & \frac{75 \pm \sqrt{(-75)^{2} - 4(4)(-25)}}{2(4)} \\ & = & \frac{75 \pm \sqrt{6025}}{8} \\ & = & {\frac{75 \pm 5\sqrt{241}}{8}.} \end{array}$$ The positive value of t that solves this equation is approximately 19.08. Therefore, the cannonball hits the water after approximately 19.08 sec.</item>
        <item>To find the distance out to sea, we simply substitute the answer from part (b) into $$\mathbf{ \text{s} }(t):$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{s} }(19.08)} & {= 300(19.08)\sqrt{3}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {300(19.08) - 16(19.08)^{2}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ & {= 9914.26\mathbf{ \text{i} } - 100.7424\mathbf{ \text{j} }.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the ball hits the water about 9914.26 ft away from the base of the cliff. Notice that the vertical component of the position vector is very close to $$-100,$$ which tells us that the ball just hit the water. Note that 9914.26 feet is not the true range of the cannon since the cannonball lands in the ocean at a location below the cannon. The range of the cannon would be determined by finding how far out the cannonball is when its height is 100 ft above the water (the same as the altitude of the cannon).</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Kepler’s Laws of Planetary Motion
snippet: Kepler’s Laws of Planetary Motion: Kepler’s Laws of Planetary Motion The path of any planet about the Sun is elliptical in shape, with the center of the Sun located at one focus of the ellipse (the law of ellipses). A line drawn from the...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="3.9" title="Kepler’s Laws of Planetary Motion">
    <heading level="4">Kepler’s Laws of Planetary Motion</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The path of any planet about the Sun is elliptical in shape, with the center of the Sun located at one focus of the ellipse (the law of ellipses).</item>
      <item>A line drawn from the center of the Sun to the center of a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals (the law of equal areas) (Figure 3.18).</item>
      <item>The ratio of the squares of the periods of any two planets is equal to the ratio of the cubes of the lengths of their semimajor orbital axes (the law of harmonies).</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Using Kepler’s Third Law for Nonheliocentric Orbits
snippet: Using Kepler’s Third Law for Nonheliocentric Orbits: Kepler’s third law of planetary motion can be modified to the case of one object in orbit around an object other than the Sun, such as the Moon around the Earth. In this case, Kepler’s...
body_xml:
<example number="3.17" title="Using Kepler’s Third Law for Nonheliocentric Orbits">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Kepler’s third law of planetary motion can be modified to the case of one object in orbit around an object other than the Sun, such as the Moon around the Earth. In this case, Kepler’s third law becomes</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}a^{3}}{G\left( {m + M} \right)},$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>where m is the mass of the Moon and M is the mass of Earth, a represents the length of the major axis of the elliptical orbit, and P represents the period.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Given that the mass of the Moon is $$7.35 \times 10^{22} \text{kg,}$$ the mass of Earth is $$5.97 \times 10^{24} \text{kg,}$$ $$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}{ \text{m} ^{3}/{ \text{kg} \cdot \sec^{2}}},$$ and the period of the moon is 27.3 days, let’s find the length of the major axis of the orbit of the Moon around Earth.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>It is important to be consistent with units. Since the universal gravitational constant contains seconds in the units, we need to use seconds for the period of the Moon as well:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$27.3 \text{days} \times \frac{24 \text{hr} }{1 \text{day} } \times \frac{3600\sec }{1 \text{hour} } = 2,358,720\sec .$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Substitute all the data into Equation 3.30 and solve for a:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cll} \left( {2,358,720\sec } \right)^{2} & = & \frac{4\pi^{2}a^{3}}{\left( {6.67 \times 10^{-11}\frac{ \text{m} ^{3}}{ \text{kg} \cdot \sec^{2}}} \right)\left( {7.35 x 10^{22} \text{kg} + 5.97 x 10^{24} \text{kg} } \right)} \\ {5.563 \times 10^{12}} & = & \frac{4\pi^{2}a^{3}}{\left( {6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{m} ^{3}} \right)\left( {6.04 x 10^{24}} \right)} \\ {\left( {5.563 \times 10^{12}} \right)\left( {6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{m} ^{3}} \right)\left( {6.04 \times 10^{24}} \right)} & = & {4\pi^{2}a^{3}} \\ a^{3} & = & {\frac{2.241 \times 10^{27}}{4\pi^{2}} \text{m} ^{3}} \\ a & = & {3.84 \times 10^{8} \text{m} } \\ & \approx & {384,000 \text{km.} } \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>According to solarsystem.nasa.gov, the actual average distance from the Moon to Earth is 384,400 km. This is calculated using reflectors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts back in the 1960s.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Chapter Opener: Halley’s Comet
snippet: Chapter Opener: Halley’s Comet: We now return to the chapter opener, which discusses the motion of Halley’s comet around the Sun. Kepler’s first law states that Halley’s comet follows an elliptical path around the Sun, with the Sun as one...
body_xml:
<example number="3.18" title="Chapter Opener: Halley’s Comet">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>We now return to the chapter opener, which discusses the motion of Halley’s comet around the Sun. Kepler’s first law states that Halley’s comet follows an elliptical path around the Sun, with the Sun as one focus of the ellipse. The period of Halley’s comet is approximately 76.1 years, depending on how closely it passes by Jupiter and Saturn as it passes through the outer solar system. Let’s use $$T = 76.1$$ years. What is the average distance of Halley’s comet from the Sun?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using the equation $$T^{2} = D^{3}$$ with $$T = 76.1,$$ we obtain $$D^{3} = 5791.21,$$ so $$D \approx 17.96$$ A.U. This comes out to approximately $$1.67 \times 10^{9}$$ mi.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>A natural question to ask is: What are the maximum (aphelion) and minimum (perihelion) distances from Halley’s Comet to the Sun? The eccentricity of the orbit of Halley’s Comet is 0.967 (Source: http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/cometfact.html). Recall that the formula for the eccentricity of an ellipse is $$e = {c/a},$$ where a is the length of the semimajor axis and c is the distance from the center to either focus. Therefore, $$0.967 = {c/17.96}$$ and $$c \approx 17.37$$ A.U. Subtracting this from a gives the perihelion distance $$p = a - c = 17.96 - 17.37 = 0.59$$ A.U. According to the National Space Science Data Center (Source: http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/cometfact.html), the perihelion distance for Halley’s comet is 0.587 A.U. To calculate the aphelion distance, we add</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P = a + c = 17.96 + 17.37 = 35.33 \text{A} \text{.U} .$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This is approximately $$3.3 \times 10^{9}$$ mi. The average distance from Pluto to the Sun is 39.5 A.U. (Source: http://www.oarval.org/furthest.htm), so it would appear that Halley’s Comet stays just within the orbit of Pluto.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

The range of $$f$$ is the set of all real numbers $$z$$ that has at least one ordered pair $$\left( {x,y} \right) \in D$$ such that $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = z$$ as shown in the following figure.</paragraph>
