title: Domains and Ranges for Functions of Two Variables
snippet: Domains and Ranges for Functions of Two Variables: Find the domain and range of each of the following functions: f\left( {x,y} \right) = 3x + 5y + 2 g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} This is an example of a linear function...
body_xml:
<example number="4.1" title="Domains and Ranges for Functions of Two Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the domain and range of each of the following functions:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 3x + 5y + 2$$</item>
        <item>$$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>This is an example of a linear function in two variables. There are no values or combinations of $$x$$ and $$y$$ that cause $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ to be undefined, so the domain of $$f$$ is $$\mathbb{R}^{2}.$$ To determine the range, first pick a value for $$z.$$ We need to find a solution to the equation $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = z,$$ or $$3x + 5y + 2 = z.$$ One such solution can be obtained by first setting $$y = 0,$$ which yields the equation $$3x + 2 = z.$$ The solution to this equation is $$x = \frac{z - 2}{3},$$ which gives the ordered pair $$\left( {\frac{z - 2}{3},0} \right)$$ as a solution to the equation $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = z$$ for any value of $$z.$$ Therefore, the range of the function is all real numbers, or $$\mathbb{R}.$$</item>
        <item>For the function $$g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ to have a real value, the quantity under the square root must be nonnegative: $$9 - x^{2} - y^{2} \geq 0.$$ This inequality can be written in the form $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 9.$$ Therefore, the domain of $$g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is $$\left\{ {\left( {x,y} \right) \in \left. \mathbb{R}^{2} \right|x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 9} \right\}.$$ The graph of this set of points can be described as a disk of radius $$3$$ centered at the origin. The domain includes the boundary circle as shown in the following graph. Figure 4.3 The domain of the function $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ is a closed disk of radius 3. To determine the range of $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ we start with a point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ on the boundary of the domain, which is defined by the relation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9.$$ It follows that $$x_{0}^{2} + y_{0}^{2} = 9$$ and $$g\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x_{0}^{2} - y_{0}^{2}} = \sqrt{9 - \left( {x_{0}^{2} + y_{0}^{2}} \right)} = \sqrt{9 - 9} = 0.$$ If $$x_{0}^{2} + y_{0}^{2} = 0$$ (in other words, $$x_{0} = y_{0} = 0),$$ then $$g\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x_{0}^{2} - y_{0}^{2}} = \sqrt{9 - \left( {x_{0}^{2} + y_{0}^{2}} \right)} = \sqrt{9 - 0} = 3.$$ This is the maximum value of the function. Given any value c between $$0 \text{and} 3,$$ we can find an entire set of points inside the domain of $$g$$ such that $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = c:$$ $$\begin{array}{rll} \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} & = & c \\ {9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} & = & c^{2} \\ {x^{2} + y^{2}} & = & {9 - c^{2}.} \end{array}$$ Since $$9 - c^{2} > 0,$$ this describes a circle of radius $$\sqrt{9 - c^{2}}$$ centered at the origin. Any point on this circle satisfies the equation $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = c.$$ Therefore, the range of this function can be written in interval notation as $$\left\lbrack {0,3} \right\rbrack.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Graphing Functions of Two Variables
snippet: Graphing Functions of Two Variables: Create a graph of each of the following functions: g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} + y^{2} In Example 4.1, we determined that the domain of g\left( {x,y}...
body_xml:
<example number="4.2" title="Graphing Functions of Two Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Create a graph of each of the following functions:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$</item>
        <item>$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} + y^{2}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>In Example 4.1, we determined that the domain of $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ is $$\left\{ {\left( {x,y} \right) \in \left. \mathbb{R}^{2} \right|x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 9} \right\}$$ and the range is $$\left\{ {z \in \left. \mathbb{R} \right|0 \leq z \leq 3} \right\}.$$ When $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$$ we have $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0.$$ Therefore any point on the circle of radius $$3$$ centered at the origin in the $$x,y \text{-plane}$$ maps to $$z = 0$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}.$$ If $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 8,$$ then $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 1,$$ so any point on the circle of radius $$2\sqrt{2}$$ centered at the origin in the $$x,y \text{-plane}$$ maps to $$z = 1$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}.$$ As $$x^{2} + y^{2}$$ gets closer to zero, the value of z approaches 3. When $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 0,$$ then $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 3.$$ This is the origin in the $$x,y \text{-plane} .$$ If $$x^{2} + y^{2}$$ is equal to any other value between $$0 \text{and} 9,$$ then $$g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ equals some other constant between $$0 \text{and} 3.$$ The surface described by this function is a hemisphere centered at the origin with radius $$3$$ as shown in the following graph. Figure 4.4 Graph of the hemisphere represented by the given function of two variables.</item>
        <item>This function also contains the expression $$x^{2} + y^{2}.$$ Setting this expression equal to various values starting at zero, we obtain circles of increasing radius. The minimum value of $$f(x,y) = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ is zero (attained when $$x = y = 0.).$$ When $$x = 0,$$ the function becomes $$z = y^{2},$$ and when $$y = 0,$$ then the function becomes $$z = x^{2}.$$ These are cross-sections of the graph, and are parabolas. Recall from Introduction to Vectors in Space that the name of the graph of $$f(x,y) = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ is a paraboloid. The graph of $$f$$ appears in the following graph. Figure 4.5 A paraboloid is the graph of the given function of two variables.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Nuts and Bolts: A profit function for a hardware manufacturer is given by f(x,y) = 16 - \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} - \left( {y - 2} \right)^{2}, where x is the number of nuts sold per month (measured in thousands) and y represents the...
body_xml: A profit function for a hardware manufacturer is given by $$f(x,y) = 16 - \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} - \left( {y - 2} \right)^{2},$$ where $$x$$ is the number of nuts sold per month (measured in thousands) and $$y$$ represents the number of bolts sold per month (measured in thousands). Profit is measured in thousands of dollars. Sketch a graph of this function. This function is a polynomial function in two variables. The domain of $$f$$ consists of $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ coordinate pairs that yield a nonnegative profit: $$\begin{array}{l} {16 - \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} - \left( {y - 2} \right)^{2} \geq 0} \\ {\left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} + \left( {y - 2} \right)^{2} \leq 16.} \end{array}$$ This is a disk of radius $$4$$ centered at $$\left( {3,2} \right).$$ A further restriction is that both $$x \text{and} y$$ must be nonnegative. When $$x = 3$$ and $$y = 2,$$ $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 16.$$ Note that it is possible for either value to be a noninteger; for example, it is possible to sell $$2.5$$ thousand nuts in a month. The domain, therefore, contains thousands of points, so we can consider all points within the disk. For any $$z < 16,$$ we can solve the equation $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = z:$$ $$\begin{array}{rll} & & \\ {16 - \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} - \left( {y - 2} \right)^{2}} & = & z \\ {\left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} + \left( {y - 2} \right)^{2}} & = & {16 - z.} \end{array}$$ Since $$z < 16,$$ we know that $$16 - z > 0,$$ so the previous equation describes a circle with radius $$\sqrt{16 - z}$$ centered at the point $$\left( {3,2} \right).$$ Therefore. the range of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is $$\left\{ {z \in \left. \mathbb{R} \right|z \leq 16} \right\}.$$ The graph of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is also a paraboloid, and this paraboloid points downward as shown.

snippet: Making a Contour Map: Given the function f\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{8 + 8x - 4y - 4x^{2} - y^{2}}, find the level curve corresponding to c = 0. Then create a contour map for this function. What are the domain and range of f? To find the...
body_xml: Given the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{8 + 8x - 4y - 4x^{2} - y^{2}},$$ find the level curve corresponding to $$c = 0.$$ Then create a contour map for this function. What are the domain and range of $$f?$$ To find the level curve for $$c = 0,$$ we set $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ and solve. This gives $$0 = \sqrt{8 + 8x - 4y - 4x^{2} - y^{2}}.$$ We then square both sides and multiply both sides of the equation by $$-1:$$ $$4x^{2} + y^{2} - 8x + 4y - 8 = 0.$$ Now, we rearrange the terms, putting the $$x$$ terms together and the $$y$$ terms together, and add $$8$$ to each side: $$4x^{2} - 8x + y^{2} + 4y = 8.$$ Next, we group the pairs of terms containing the same variable in parentheses, and factor $$4$$ from the first pair: $$4\left( {x^{2} - 2x} \right) + \left( {y^{2} + 4y} \right) = 8.$$ Then we complete the square in each pair of parentheses and add the correct value to the right-hand side: $$4\left( {x^{2} - 2x + 1} \right) + \left( {y^{2} + 4y + 4} \right) = 8 + 4(1) + 4.$$ Next, we factor the left-hand side and simplify the right-hand side: $$4\left( {x - 1} \right)^{2} + \left( {y + 2} \right)^{2} = 16.$$ Last, we divide both sides by $$16:$$ $$\frac{\left( {x - 1} \right)^{2}}{4} + \frac{\left( {y + 2} \right)^{2}}{16} = 1.$$ This equation describes an ellipse centered at $$\left( {1,-2} \right).$$ The graph of this ellipse appears in the following graph. We can repeat the same derivation for values of $$c$$ less than $$4.$$ Then, Equation 4.1 becomes $$\frac{4\left( {x - 1} \right)^{2}}{16 - c^{2}} + \frac{\left( {y + 2} \right)^{2}}{16 - c^{2}} = 1$$ for an arbitrary value of $$c.$$ Figure 4.10 shows a contour map for $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ using the values $$c = 0,1,2, \text{and} 3.$$ When $$c = 4,$$ the level curve is the point $$\left( {1,-2} \right).$$ $$\begin{array}{l} { \text{Domain:} \left( {x,y} \right) \text{inside the ellipse} \frac{(x - 1)^{2}}{4} + \frac{(y + 2)^{2}}{16} = 1} \\ { \text{Range:} \lbrack 0,4)} \end{array}$$

body_xml:
<example number="4.6" title="Domains for Functions of Three Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the domain of each of the following functions:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \frac{3x - 4y + 2z}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2} - z^{2}}}$$</item>
        <item>$$g\left( {x,y,t} \right) = \frac{\sqrt{2t - 4}}{x^{2} - y^{2}}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>For the function $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \frac{3x - 4y + 2z}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2} - z^{2}}}$$ to be defined (and be a real value), two conditions must hold: The denominator cannot be zero. The radicand cannot be negative. Combining these conditions leads to the inequality $$9 - x^{2} - y^{2} - z^{2} > 0.$$ Moving the variables to the other side and reversing the inequality gives the domain as $$\text{domain} (f) = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right) \in \left. \mathbb{R}^{3} \right|x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} < 9} \right\},$$ which describes a ball of radius $$3$$ centered at the origin. (Note: The surface of the ball is not included in this domain.)</item>
        <item>For the function $$g\left( {x,y,t} \right) = \frac{\sqrt{2t - 4}}{x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ to be defined (and be a real value), two conditions must hold: The radicand cannot be negative. The denominator cannot be zero. Since the radicand cannot be negative, this implies $$2t - 4 \geq 0,$$ and therefore that $$t \geq 2.$$ Since the denominator cannot be zero, $$x^{2} - y^{2} \neq 0,$$ or $$x^{2} \neq y^{2},$$ Which can be rewritten as $$y \neq \text{±} x$$ , which are the equations of two lines passing through the origin. Therefore, the domain of $$g$$ is $$\text{domain} (g) = \left\{ \left. \left( {x,y,t} \right) \right|y \neq \text{±} x,t \geq 2 \right\}.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a function of two variables, $$x$$ and $$y.$$ The limit of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ as $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ approaches $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ is $$L,$$ written</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({a,b})}}{\lim }f(x,y) = L$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>if for each $$\varepsilon > 0$$ there exists a small enough $$\delta > 0$$ such that for all points $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in a $$\delta$$ disk around $$\left( {a,b} \right),$$ except possibly for $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ itself, the value of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is no more than $$\varepsilon$$ away from $$L$$ (Figure 4.15). Using symbols, we write the following: For any $$\varepsilon > 0,$$ there exists a number $$\delta > 0$$ such that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left| {f\left( {x,y} \right) - L} \right| < \varepsilon \text{whenever} 0 < \sqrt{\left( {x - a} \right)^{2} + \left( {y - b} \right)^{2}} < \delta.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Limit laws for functions of two variables: Limit laws for functions of two variables Let f\left( {x,y} \right) and g\left( {x,y} \right) be defined for all \left( {x,y} \right) \neq \left( {a,b} \right) in a neighborhood around \left(...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="4.1" title="Limit laws for functions of two variables">
    <heading level="4">Limit laws for functions of two variables</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and $$g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be defined for all $$\left( {x,y} \right) \neq \left( {a,b} \right)$$ in a neighborhood around $$\left( {a,b} \right),$$ and assume the neighborhood is contained completely inside the domain of $$f.$$ Assume that $$L$$ and $$M$$ are real numbers such that $$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }f(x,y) = L$$ and $$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }g(x,y) = M,$$ and let $$c$$ be a constant. Then each of the following statements holds:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Constant Law:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }c = c$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Identity Laws:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }x = a$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }y = b$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Sum Law:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }\left( {f\left( {x,y} \right) + g\left( {x,y} \right)} \right) = L + M$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Difference Law:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }\left( {f\left( {x,y} \right) - g\left( {x,y} \right)} \right) = L - M$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Constant Multiple Law:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }\left( {cf\left( {x,y} \right)} \right) = cL$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Product Law:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }\left( {f\left( {x,y} \right)g\left( {x,y} \right)} \right) = LM$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Quotient Law:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x,y} \right)}{g\left( {x,y} \right)} = \frac{L}{M} \text{for} M \neq 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Power Law:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }\left( {f\left( {x,y} \right)} \right)^{n} = L^{n}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>for any positive integer $$n.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Root Law:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(a,b)}{\lim }\sqrt[n]{f\left( {x,y} \right)} = \sqrt[n]{L}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>for all $$L$$ if $$n$$ is odd and positive, and for $$L \geq 0$$ if $$n$$ is even and positive provided that $$f(x, y) \geq 0$$ for all $$(x, y) \neq (a, b)$$ in neighborhood of $$(a, b)$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding the Limit of a Function of Two Variables
snippet: Finding the Limit of a Function of Two Variables: Find each of the following limits: \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\left( {x^{2} - 2xy + 3y^{2} - 4x + 3y - 6} \right) \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim...
body_xml:
<example number="4.8" title="Finding the Limit of a Function of Two Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find each of the following limits:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\left( {x^{2} - 2xy + 3y^{2} - 4x + 3y - 6} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\frac{2x + 3y}{4x - 3y}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>First use the sum and difference laws to separate the terms: $$\begin{array}{l} \\ {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\left( {x^{2} - 2xy + 3y^{2} - 4x + 3y - 6} \right)} \\ {= \left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }x^{2}} \right) - \left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }2xy} \right) + \left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }3y^{2}} \right) - \left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }4x} \right)} \\ {{+ \left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }3y} \right)} - \left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }6} \right).} \end{array}$$ Next, use the constant multiple law on the second, third, fourth, and fifth limits: $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ {= \left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }x^{2}} \right) - 2\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }xy} \right) + 3\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }y^{2}} \right) - 4\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }x} \right)} \\ { + 3\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }y} \right) - \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }6.} \end{array}$$ Now, use the power law on the first and third limits, and the product law on the second limit: $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ \\ {= \left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }x} \right)^{2} - 2\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }x} \right)\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }y} \right) + 3\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }y} \right)^{2}} \\ { - 4\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }x} \right) + 3\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }y} \right) - \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }6.} \end{array}$$ Last, use the identity laws on the first six limits and the constant law on the last limit: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\left( {x^{2} - 2xy + 3y^{2} - 4x + 3y - 6} \right)} & {= (2)^{2} - 2(2)(-1) + 3(-1)^{2} - 4(2) + 3(-1) - 6} \\ & {= -6.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>Before applying the quotient law, we need to verify that the limit of the denominator is nonzero. Using the difference law, constant multiple law, and identity law, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\left( {4x - 3y} \right)} & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }4x - \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }3y} \\ & {= 4\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }x} \right) - 3\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }y} \right)} \\ & {= 4(2) - 3(-1) = 11.} \end{array}$$ Since the limit of the denominator is nonzero, the quotient law applies. We now calculate the limit of the numerator using the difference law, constant multiple law, and identity law: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\left( {2x + 3y} \right)} & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }2x + \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }3y} \\ & {= 2\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }x} \right) + 3\left( {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }y} \right)} \\ & {= 2(2) + 3(-1)} \\ & {= 1.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, according to the quotient law we have $$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\frac{2x + 3y}{4x - 3y} = \frac{\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\left( {2x + 3y} \right)}{\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-1})}}{\lim }\left( {4x - 3y} \right)} = \frac{1}{11}.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>

title: Limits That Fail to Exist
snippet: Limits That Fail to Exist: Show that neither of the following limits exist: \underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\frac{2xy}{3x^{2} + y^{2}} \underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\frac{4xy^{2}}{x^{2} + 3y^{4}} The domain of the function...
body_xml:
<example number="4.9" title="Limits That Fail to Exist">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Show that neither of the following limits exist:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\frac{2xy}{3x^{2} + y^{2}}$$</item>
        <item>$$\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\frac{4xy^{2}}{x^{2} + 3y^{4}}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The domain of the function $$f(x,y) = \frac{2xy}{3x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ consists of all points in the $$xy \text{-plane}$$ except for the point $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ (Figure 4.16). To show that the limit does not exist as $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ approaches $$\left( {0,0} \right),$$ we note that it is impossible to satisfy the definition of a limit of a function of two variables because of the fact that the function takes different values along different lines passing through point $$\left( {0,0} \right).$$ First, consider the line $$y = 0$$ in the $$xy \text{-plane.}$$ Substituting $$y = 0$$ into $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ gives $$f\left( {x,0} \right) = \frac{2x(0)}{3x^{2} + 0^{2}} = 0$$ for any value of $$x.$$ Therefore the value of $$f$$ remains constant for any point on the $$x \text{-axis,}$$ and as $$y$$ approaches zero, the function remains fixed at zero. Next, consider the line $$y = x.$$ Substituting $$y = x$$ into $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ gives $$f\left( {x,x} \right) = \frac{2x(x)}{3x^{2} + x^{2}} = \frac{2x^{2}}{4x^{2}} = \frac{1}{2}.$$ This is true for any point on the line $$y = x.$$ If we let $$x$$ approach zero while staying on this line, the value of the function remains fixed at $$\frac{1}{2},$$ regardless of how small $$x$$ is. Choose a value for $$\varepsilon$$ that is less than $$1/2$$ —say, $$1/4.$$ Then, no matter how small a $$\delta$$ disk we draw around $$\left( {0,0} \right),$$ the values of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ for points inside that $$\delta$$ disk will include both $$0$$ and $$\frac{1}{2}.$$ Therefore, the definition of limit at a point is never satisfied and the limit fails to exist. Figure 4.16 Graph of the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = {\left( {2xy} \right)/\left( {3x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)}.$$ Along the line $$y = 0,$$ the function is equal to zero; along the line $$y = x,$$ the function is equal to $$\frac{1}{2}.$$ In a similar fashion to a., we can approach the origin along any straight line passing through the origin. If we try the $$x \text{-axis}$$ (i.e., $$y = 0),$$ then the function remains fixed at zero. The same is true for the $$y \text{-axis.}$$ Suppose we approach the origin along a straight line of slope $$k.$$ The equation of this line is $$y = kx.$$ Then the limit becomes $$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\frac{4xy^{2}}{x^{2} + 3y^{4}}} & {= \underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\frac{4x\left( {kx} \right)^{2}}{x^{2} + 3\left( {kx} \right)^{4}}} \\ & {= \underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\frac{4k^{2}x^{3}}{x^{2} + 3k^{4}x^{4}}} \\ & {= \underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\frac{4k^{2}x}{1 + 3k^{4}x^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\left( {4k^{2}x} \right)}{\underset{(x,y)\rightarrow(0,0)}{\lim }\left( {1 + 3k^{4}x^{2}} \right)}} \\ & {= 0} \end{array}$$ regardless of the value of $$k.$$ It would seem that the limit is equal to zero. What if we chose a curve passing through the origin instead? For example, we can consider the parabola given by the equation $$x = y^{2}.$$ Substituting $$y^{2}$$ in place of $$x$$ in $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ gives $$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}{\lim }\frac{4xy^{2}}{x^{2} + 3y^{4}}} & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}{\lim }\frac{4\left( y^{2} \right)y^{2}}{\left( y^{2} \right)^{2} + 3y^{4}}} \\ & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}{\lim }\frac{4y^{4}}{y^{4} + 3y^{4}}} \\ & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}{\lim }1} \\ & {= 1.} \end{array}$$ By the same logic in a., it is impossible to find a $$\delta$$ disk around the origin that satisfies the definition of the limit for any value of $$\varepsilon < 1.$$ Therefore, $$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({0,0})}}{\lim }\frac{4xy^{2}}{x^{2} + 3y^{4}}$$ does not exist.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

Using symbols, we can write: For any $$\varepsilon > 0,$$ there exists a number $$\delta > 0$$ such that</paragraph>

title: Demonstrating Continuity for a Function of Two Variables
snippet: Demonstrating Continuity for a Function of Two Variables: Show that the function f(x,y) = \frac{3x + 2y}{x + y + 1} is continuous at point \left( {5,-3} \right). There are three conditions to be satisfied, per the definition of continuity....
body_xml:
<example number="4.11" title="Demonstrating Continuity for a Function of Two Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Show that the function $$f(x,y) = \frac{3x + 2y}{x + y + 1}$$ is continuous at point $$\left( {5,-3} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>There are three conditions to be satisfied, per the definition of continuity. In this example, $$a = 5$$ and $$b = -3.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f\left( {a,b} \right)$$ exists. This is true because the domain of the function $$f$$ consists of those ordered pairs for which the denominator is nonzero (i.e., $$x + y + 1 \neq 0).$$ Point $$\left( {5,-3} \right)$$ satisfies this condition. Furthermore, $$f\left( {a,b} \right) = f\left( {5,-3} \right) = \frac{3(5) + 2(-3)}{5 + (-3) + 1} = \frac{15 - 6}{2 + 1} = 3.$$</item>
        <item>$$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({a,b})}}{\lim }f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ exists. This is also true: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({a,b})}}{\lim }f\left( {x,y} \right)} & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({5,-3})}}{\lim }\frac{3x + 2y}{x + y + 1}} \\ & {= \frac{\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({5,-3})}}{\lim }\left( {3x + 2y} \right)}{\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({5,-3})}}{\lim }\left( {x + y + 1} \right)}} \\ & {= \frac{15 - 6}{5 - 3 + 1}} \\ & {= 3.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>$$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({a,b})}}{\lim }f\left( {x,y} \right) = f\left( {a,b} \right).$$ This is true because we have just shown that both sides of this equation equal three.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}} \right)$$ be a point in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}.$$ Then, a $$\delta$$ ball in three dimensions consists of all points in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ lying at a distance of less than $$\delta$$ from $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}} \right)$$ —that is,</paragraph>

    <paragraph>To define a $$\delta$$ ball in higher dimensions, add additional terms under the radical to correspond to each additional dimension. For example, given a point $$P = \left( {w_{0},x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}} \right)$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{4},$$ a $$\delta$$ ball around $$P$$ can be described by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left\{ \left( {w,x,y,z} \right) \in \mathbb{R}^{4} \middle| \sqrt{\left( {w - w_{0}} \right)^{2} + \left( {x - x_{0}} \right)^{2} + \left( {y - y_{0}} \right)^{2} + \left( {z - z_{0}} \right)^{2}} < \delta \right\}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Finding the Limit of a Function of Three Variables: Find \underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }\frac{x^{2}y - 3z}{2x + 5y - z}. Before we can apply the quotient law, we need to verify that the limit of the denominator is...

<example number="4.13" title="Finding the Limit of a Function of Three Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find $$\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }\frac{x^{2}y - 3z}{2x + 5y - z}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Before we can apply the quotient law, we need to verify that the limit of the denominator is nonzero. Using the difference law, the identity law, and the constant law,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }\left( {2x + 5y - z} \right)} & {= 2\left( {\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }x} \right) + 5\left( {\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }y} \right) - \left( {\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }z} \right)} \\ & {= 2(4) + 5(1) - (-3)} \\ & {= 16.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since this is nonzero, we next find the limit of the numerator. Using the product law, difference law, constant multiple law, and identity law,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }\left( {x^{2}y - 3z} \right)} & {= \left( {\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }x} \right)^{2}\left( {\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }y} \right) - 3\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }z} \\ & {= \left( 4^{2} \right)(1) - 3(-3)} \\ & {= 16 + 9} \\ & {= 25.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Last, applying the quotient law:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }\frac{x^{2}y - 3z}{2x + 5y - z}} & {= \frac{\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }\left( {x^{2}y - 3z} \right)}{\underset{{({x,y,z})}\rightarrow{({4,1,-3})}}{\lim }\left( {2x + 5y - z} \right)}} \\ & {= \frac{25}{16}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ be a function of two variables. Then the partial derivative of $$f$$ with respect to $$x,$$ written as $${{\partial f}/{\partial x}},$$ or $$f_{x},$$ is defined as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x + h,y} \right) - f\left( {x,y} \right)}{h}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The partial derivative of $$f$$ with respect to $$y,$$ written as $${{\partial f}/{\partial y}},$$ or $$f_{y},$$ is defined as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \underset{k\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x,y + k} \right) - f\left( {x,y} \right)}{k}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Calculating Partial Derivatives from the Definition
snippet: Calculating Partial Derivatives from the Definition: Use the definition of the partial derivative as a limit to calculate {\partial f}/{\partial x} and {\partial f}/{\partial y} for the function f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2}...
body_xml:
<example number="4.14" title="Calculating Partial Derivatives from the Definition">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the definition of the partial derivative as a limit to calculate $${\partial f}/{\partial x}$$ and $${\partial f}/{\partial y}$$ for the function</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4x + 5y - 12.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, calculate $$f\left( {x + h,y} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {f\left( {x + h,y} \right)} & {= \left( {x + h} \right)^{2} - 3\left( {x + h} \right)y + 2y^{2} - 4\left( {x + h} \right) + 5y - 12} \\ & {= x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 3xy - 3hy + 2y^{2} - 4x - 4h + 5y - 12.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, substitute this into Equation 4.12 and simplify:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x + h,y} \right) - f\left( {x,y} \right)}{h}} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left( {x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 3xy - 3hy + 2y^{2} - 4x - 4h + 5y - 12} \right) - \left( {x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4x + 5y - 12} \right)}{h}} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 3xy - 3hy + 2y^{2} - 4x - 4h + 5y - 12 - x^{2} + 3xy - 2y^{2} + 4x - 5y + 12}{h}} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{2xh + h^{2} - 3hy - 4h}{h}} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{h\left( {2x + h - 3y - 4} \right)}{h}} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( {2x + h - 3y - 4} \right)} \\ & {= 2x - 3y - 4.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To calculate $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y},$$ first calculate $$f\left( {x,y + k} \right):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {f(x,y + k)} & {= x^{2} - 3x(y + k) + 2(y + k)^{2} - 4x + 5(y + k) - 12} \\ & {= x^{2} - 3xy - 3xk + 2y^{2} + 4yk + 2k^{2} - 4x + 5y + 5k - 12.} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, substitute this into Equation 4.13 and simplify:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} & {= \underset{k\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f(x,y + k) - f(x,y)}{k}} \\ & {= \underset{k\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left( {x^{2} - 3xy - 3xk + 2y^{2} + 4yk + 2k^{2} - 4x + 5y + 5k - 12} \right) - \left( {x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4x + 5y - 12} \right)}{k}} \\ & {= \underset{k\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} - 3xy - 3xk + 2y^{2} + 4yk + 2k^{2} - 4x + 5y + 5k - 12 - x^{2} + 3xy - 2y^{2} + 4x - 5y + 12}{k}} \\ & {= \underset{k\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{-3xk + 4yk + 2k^{2} + 5k}{k}} \\ & {= \underset{k\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{h\left( {-3x + 4y + 2k + 5} \right)}{k}} \\ & {= \underset{k\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( {-3x + 4y + 2k + 5} \right)} \\ & {= -3x + 4y + 5.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Calculating Partial Derivatives: Calculate both partial derivatives for the following functions by holding the opposite variable constant then differentiating: f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4x + 5y - 12 g\left( {x,y}...
body_xml:
<example number="4.15" title="Calculating Partial Derivatives">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate both partial derivatives for the following functions by holding the opposite variable constant then differentiating:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4x + 5y - 12$$</item>
        <item>$$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sin \left( {x^{2}y - 2x + 4} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To calculate $${{\partial f}/{\partial x}},$$ treat the variable $$y$$ as a constant. Then differentiate $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ with respect to $$x$$ using the sum, difference, and power rules: $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4x + 5y - 12} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack x^{2} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {3xy} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {2y^{2}} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {4x} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {5y} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\lbrack 12\rbrack} \\ & {= 2x - 3y + 0 - 4 + 0 - 0} \\ & {= 2x - 3y - 4.} \end{array}$$ The derivatives of the third, fifth, and sixth terms are all zero because they do not contain the variable $$x,$$ so they are treated as constant terms. The derivative of the second term is equal to the coefficient of $$x,$$ which is $$-3y.$$ Calculating $${{\partial f}/{\partial y}}:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4x + 5y - 12} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack x^{2} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {3xy} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {2y^{2}} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {4x} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {5y} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\lbrack 12\rbrack} \\ & {= -3x + 4y - 0 + 5 - 0} \\ & {= -3x + 4y + 5.} \end{array}$$ These are the same answers obtained in Example 4.14.</item>
        <item>To calculate $${{\partial g}/{\partial x}},$$ treat the variable y as a constant. Then differentiate $$g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ with respect to x using the chain rule and power rule: $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial g}{\partial x} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {\sin \left( {x^{2}y - 2x + 4} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \cos \left( {x^{2}y - 2x + 4} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {x^{2}y - 2x + 4} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \left( {2xy - 2} \right)\cos \left( {x^{2}y - 2x + 4} \right).} \end{array}$$ To calculate $${{\partial g}/{\partial y}},$$ treat the variable $$x$$ as a constant. Then differentiate $$g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ with respect to $$y$$ using the chain rule and power rule: $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial g}{\partial y} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {\sin \left( {x^{2}y - 2x + 4} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \cos \left( {x^{2}y - 2x + 4} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {x^{2}y - 2x + 4} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= x^{2}\cos \left( {x^{2}y - 2x + 4} \right).} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Partial Derivatives from a Contour Map: Use a contour map to estimate {\partial g}/{\partial x} at the point \left( {\sqrt{5},0} \right) for the function g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}. The following graph represents a...
body_xml: Use a contour map to estimate $${\partial g}/{\partial x}$$ at the point $$\left( {\sqrt{5},0} \right)$$ for the function $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}.$$ The following graph represents a contour map for the function $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}.$$ The inner circle on the contour map corresponds to $$c = 2$$ and the next circle out corresponds to $$c = 1.$$ The first circle is given by the equation $$2 = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}};$$ the second circle is given by the equation $$1 = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}.$$ The first equation simplifies to $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 5$$ and the second equation simplifies to $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 8.$$ The $$x \text{-intercept}$$ of the first circle is $$\left( {\sqrt{5},0} \right)$$ and the $$x \text{-intercept}$$ of the second circle is $$\left( {2\sqrt{2},0} \right).$$ We can estimate the value of $${\partial g}/{\partial x}$$ evaluated at the point $$\left( {\sqrt{5},0} \right)$$ using the slope formula: $$\left. \frac{\partial g}{\partial x} \right|_{{({x,y})} = {({\sqrt{5},0})}} \approx \frac{g\left( {\sqrt{5},0} \right) - g\left( {2\sqrt{2},0} \right)}{\sqrt{5} - 2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2 - 1}{\sqrt{5} - 2\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5} - 2\sqrt{2}} \approx -1.688.$$ To calculate the exact value of $${\partial g}/{\partial x}$$ evaluated at the point $$\left( {\sqrt{5},0} \right),$$ we start by finding $${\partial g}/{\partial x}$$ using the chain rule. First, we rewrite the function as $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} = \left( {9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} \right)^{1/2}$$ and then differentiate with respect to $$x$$ while holding $$y$$ constant: $$\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{2}\left( {9 - x^{2} - y^{2}} \right)^{-1/2}\left( {-2x} \right) = - \frac{x}{\sqrt{9 - x^{2} - y^{2}}}.$$ Next, we evaluate this expression using $$x = \sqrt{5}$$ and $$y = 0:$$ $$\left. \frac{\partial g}{\partial x} \right|_{{({x,y})} = {({\sqrt{5},0})}} = - \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{9 - \left( \sqrt{5} \right)^{2} - (0)^{2}}} = - \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{4}} = - \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2} \approx -1.118.$$ The estimate for the partial derivative corresponds to the slope of the secant line passing through the points $$\left( {\sqrt{5},0,g\left( {\sqrt{5},0} \right)} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2\sqrt{2},0,g\left( {2\sqrt{2},0} \right)} \right).$$ It represents an approximation to the slope of the tangent line to the surface through the point $$\left( {\sqrt{5},0,g\left( {\sqrt{5},0} \right)} \right),$$ which is parallel to the $$x \text{-axis} .$$

snippet: Definition: Let f\left( {x,y,z} \right) be a function of three variables. Then, the partial derivative of f with respect to x, written as {{\partial f}/{\partial x}}, or f_{x}, is defined to be \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} =...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ be a function of three variables. Then, the partial derivative of $$f$$ with respect to x, written as $${{\partial f}/{\partial x}},$$ or $$f_{x},$$ is defined to be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x + h,y,z} \right) - f\left( {x,y,z} \right)}{h}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The partial derivative of $$f$$ with respect to $$y,$$ written as $${{\partial f}/{\partial y}},$$ or $$f_{y},$$ is defined to be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \underset{k\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x,y + k,z} \right) - f\left( {x,y,z} \right)}{k}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The partial derivative of $$f$$ with respect to $$z,$$ written as $${{\partial f}/{\partial z}},$$ or $$f_{z},$$ is defined to be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial z} = \underset{m\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x,y,z + m} \right) - f\left( {x,y,z} \right)}{m}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Calculating Partial Derivatives for a Function of Three Variables
snippet: Calculating Partial Derivatives for a Function of Three Variables: Use the limit definition of partial derivatives to calculate {\partial f}/{\partial x} for the function f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4xz + 5yz^{2} - 12x...
body_xml:
<example number="4.17" title="Calculating Partial Derivatives for a Function of Three Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the limit definition of partial derivatives to calculate $${\partial f}/{\partial x}$$ for the function</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4xz + 5yz^{2} - 12x + 4y - 3z.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, find $${\partial f}/{\partial y}$$ and $${\partial f}/{\partial z}$$ by setting the other two variables constant and differentiating accordingly.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We first calculate $${\partial f}/{\partial x}$$ using Equation 4.14, then we calculate the other two partial derivatives by holding the remaining variables constant. To use the equation to find $${{\partial f}/{\partial x}},$$ we first need to calculate $$f\left( {x + h,y,z} \right):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {f\left( {x + h,y,z} \right)} & {= \left( {x + h} \right)^{2} - 3\left( {x + h} \right)y + 2y^{2} - 4\left( {x + h} \right)z + 5yz^{2} - 12\left( {x + h} \right) + 4y - 3z} \\ & {= x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 3xy - 3xh + 2y^{2} - 4xz - 4hz + 5yz^{2} - 12x - 12h + 4y - 3z} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and recall that $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4zx + 5yz^{2} - 12x + 4y - 3z.$$ Next, we substitute these two expressions into the equation:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left\lbrack \frac{x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 3xy - 3hy + 2y^{2} - 4xz - 4hz + 5yz^{2} - 12x - 12h + 4y - 3z}{h} \right.} \\ & \left. - \frac{x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4xz + 5yz^{2} - 12x + 4y - 3z}{h} \right\rbrack \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left\lbrack \frac{2xh + h^{2} - 3hy - 4hz - 12h}{h} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left\lbrack \frac{h\left( {2x + h - 3y - 4z - 12} \right)}{h} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( {2x + h - 3y - 4z - 12} \right)} \\ & {= 2x - 3y - 4z - 12.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then we find $${\partial f}/{\partial y}$$ by holding $$x \text{and} z$$ constant. Therefore, any term that does not include the variable $$y$$ is constant, and its derivative is zero. We can apply the sum, difference, and power rules for functions of one variable:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4xz + 5yz^{2} - 12x + 4y - 3z} \right\rbrack} \\ {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack x^{2} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {3xy} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {2y^{2}} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {4xz} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {5yz^{2}} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {12x} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {4y} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {3z} \right\rbrack} \\ {= 0 - 3x + 4y - 0 + 5z^{2} - 0 + 4 - 0} \\ {= -3x + 4y + 5z^{2} + 4.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To calculate $${{\partial f}/{\partial z}},$$ we hold x and y constant and apply the sum, difference, and power rules for functions of one variable:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack {x^{2} - 3xy + 2y^{2} - 4xz + 5yz^{2} - 12x + 4y - 3z} \right\rbrack} \\ {= \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack x^{2} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack {3xy} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack {2y^{2}} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack {4xz} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack {5yz^{2}} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack {12x} \right\rbrack + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack {4y} \right\rbrack - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack {3z} \right\rbrack} \\ {= 0 - 0 + 0 - 4x + 10yz - 0 + 0 - 3} \\ {= -4x + 10yz - 3.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Calculating Partial Derivatives for a Function of Three Variables
snippet: Calculating Partial Derivatives for a Function of Three Variables: Calculate the three partial derivatives of the following functions. f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \frac{x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}}{x - 3yz} g\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \sin \left(...
body_xml:
<example number="4.18" title="Calculating Partial Derivatives for a Function of Three Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate the three partial derivatives of the following functions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \frac{x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}}{x - 3yz}$$</item>
        <item>$$g\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \sin \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) + \cos \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>In each case, treat all variables as constants except the one whose partial derivative you are calculating.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack \frac{x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}}{x - 3yz} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}} \right)\left( {x - 3yz} \right) - \left( {x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {x - 3yz} \right)}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{\left( {2xy - 4z} \right)\left( {x - 3yz} \right) - \left( {x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}} \right)(1)}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{2x^{2}y - 6xy^{2}z - 4xz + 12yz^{2} - x^{2}y + 4xz - y^{2}}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{x^{2}y - 6xy^{2}z - 4xz + 12yz^{2} + 4xz - y^{2}}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack \frac{x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}}{x - 3yz} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}} \right)\left( {x - 3yz} \right) - \left( {x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {x - 3yz} \right)}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{\left( {x^{2} + 2y} \right)\left( {x - 3yz} \right) - \left( {x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}} \right)\left( {-3z} \right)}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{x^{3} - 3x^{2}yz + 2xy - 6y^{2}z + 3x^{2}yz - 12xz^{2} + 3y^{2}z}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{x^{3} + 2xy - 3y^{2}z - 12xz^{2}}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack \frac{x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}}{x - 3yz} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left( {x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}} \right)\left( {x - 3yz} \right) - \left( {x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left( {x - 3yz} \right)}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{\left( {-4x} \right)\left( {x - 3yz} \right) - \left( {x^{2}y - 4xz + y^{2}} \right)\left( {-3y} \right)}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{-4x^{2} + 12xyz + 3x^{2}y^{2} - 12xyz + 3y^{3}}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \frac{-4x^{2} + 3x^{2}y^{2} + 3y^{3}}{\left( {x - 3yz} \right)^{2}}} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {\sin \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) + \cos \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \left( {\cos \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right)} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) - \left( {\sin \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \\ & {= 2xy \cos \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) - 2x \sin \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {\sin \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) + \cos \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \left( {\cos \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right)} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) - \left( {\sin \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \\ & {= x^{2}\cos \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) + z \sin \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left\lbrack {\sin \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) + \cos \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \left( {\cos \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right)} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) - \left( {\sin \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \right)\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \\ & {= -\cos \left( {x^{2}y - z} \right) + y \sin \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Calculating Second Partial Derivatives
snippet: Calculating Second Partial Derivatives: Calculate all four second partial derivatives for the function f\left( {x,y} \right) = xe^{-3y} + \sin \left( {2x - 5y} \right). To calculate {\partial^{2}f}/{dx^{2}} and {{\partial^{2}f}/{\partial...
body_xml:
<example number="4.19" title="Calculating Second Partial Derivatives">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate all four second partial derivatives for the function</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = xe^{-3y} + \sin \left( {2x - 5y} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To calculate $${\partial^{2}f}/{dx^{2}}$$ and $${{\partial^{2}f}/{\partial y\partial x}},$$ we first calculate $${{\partial f}/{\partial x}}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = e^{-3y} + 2 \cos \left( {2x - 5y} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To calculate $${{\partial^{2}f}/{dx^{2}}},$$ differentiate $${\partial f}/{\partial x}$$ with respect to $$x:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {e^{-3y} + 2 \cos \left( {2x - 5y} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= -4 \sin \left( {2x - 5y} \right).} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To calculate $${{\partial^{2}f}/{\partial y\partial x}},$$ differentiate $${\partial f}/{\partial x}$$ with respect to $$y:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y\partial x} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {e^{-3y} + 2 \cos \left( {2x - 5y} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= -3e^{-3y} + 10 \sin \left( {2x - 5y} \right).} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To calculate $${\partial^{2}f}/{\partial x\partial y}$$ and $${{\partial^{2}f}/{dy^{2}}},$$ first calculate $${{\partial f}/{\partial y}}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -3xe^{-3y} - 5 \cos \left( {2x - 5y} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To calculate $${{\partial^{2}f}/{\partial x\partial y}},$$ differentiate $${\partial f}/{\partial y}$$ with respect to $$x:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {-3xe^{-3y} - 5 \cos \left( {2x - 5y} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= -3e^{-3y} + 10 \sin \left( {2x - 5y} \right).} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To calculate $${{\partial^{2}f}/{\partial y^{2}}},$$ differentiate $${\partial f}/{\partial y}$$ with respect to $$y:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {-3xe^{-3y} - 5 \cos \left( {2x - 5y} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= 9xe^{-3y} - 25 \sin \left( {2x - 5y} \right).} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: A Solution to the Wave Equation
snippet: A Solution to the Wave Equation: Verify that u\left( {x,y,t} \right) = 5 \sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right) is a solution to the wave equation u_{tt} = 4\left( {u_{xx} + u_{yy}} \right)....
body_xml:
<example number="4.20" title="A Solution to the Wave Equation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Verify that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$u\left( {x,y,t} \right) = 5 \sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>is a solution to the wave equation</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$u_{tt} = 4\left( {u_{xx} + u_{yy}} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, we calculate $$u_{tt},u_{xx},$$ and $$u_{yy}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cll} u_{tt} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left\lbrack \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \right\rbrack} \\ & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left\lbrack {5 \sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\left( {-10\pi \sin \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left\lbrack {-50\pi \sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\sin \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & = & {-500\pi^{2}\sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \\ u_{xx} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \right\rbrack} \\ & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\lbrack {15\pi \cos \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & = & {-45\pi^{2}\sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \\ u_{yy} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \right\rbrack} \\ & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {5 \sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\left( {4\pi \cos \left( {4\pi y} \right)} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left\lbrack {20\pi \sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\cos \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & = & {-80\pi^{2}\sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right).} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, we substitute each of these into the right-hand side of Equation 4.20 and simplify:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {4\left( {u_{xx} + u_{yy}} \right)} & {= 4\left( {-45\pi^{2}\sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right) + - 80\pi^{2}\sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \right)} \\ & {= 4\left( {-125\pi^{2}\sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \right)} \\ & {= -500\pi^{2}\sin \left( {3\pi x} \right)\sin \left( {4\pi y} \right)\cos \left( {10\pi t} \right)} \\ & {= u_{tt}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This verifies the solution.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Finding a Tangent Plane: Find an equation of the tangent plane to the surface defined by the function f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} - 3xy + 8y^{2} + 2x - 4y + 4 at point \left( {2,-1} \right). First, we must calculate f_{x}\left( {x,y}...
body_xml: Find an equation of the tangent plane to the surface defined by the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} - 3xy + 8y^{2} + 2x - 4y + 4$$ at point $$\left( {2,-1} \right).$$ First, we must calculate $$f_{x}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and $$f_{y}\left( {x,y} \right),$$ then use Equation 4.24 with $$x_{0} = 2$$ and $$y_{0} = -1:$$ $$\begin{array}{rll} {f_{x}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {4x - 3y + 2} \\ {f_{y}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {-3x + 16y - 4} \\ {f\left( {2,-1} \right)} & = & {2(2)^{2} - 3(2)(-1) + 8(-1)^{2} + 2(2) - 4(-1) + 4 = 34.} \\ {f_{x}\left( {2,-1} \right)} & = & {4(2) - 3(-1) + 2 = 13} \\ {f_{y}\left( {2,-1} \right)} & = & {-3(2) + 16(-1) - 4 = -26.} \end{array}$$ Then Equation 4.24 becomes $$\begin{array}{l} {z = f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) + f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {x - x_{0}} \right) + f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {y - y_{0}} \right)} \\ {z = 34 + 13\left( {x - 2} \right) - 26\left( {y - (-1)} \right)} \\ {z = 34 + 13x - 26 - 26y - 26} \\ {z = 13x - 26y - 18.} \end{array}$$ (See the following figure).

body_xml:
<example number="4.22" title="Finding Another Tangent Plane">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find an equation of the tangent plane to the surface defined by the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \sin \left( {2x} \right)\cos \left( {3y} \right)$$ at the point $$\left( {{\pi/3},{\pi/4}} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, calculate $$f_{x}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and $$f_{y}\left( {x,y} \right),$$ then use Equation 4.24 with $$x_{0} = {\pi/3}$$ and $$y_{0} = {\pi/4}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {f_{x}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {2 \cos \left( {2x} \right)\cos \left( {3y} \right)} \\ {f_{y}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {-3 \sin \left( {2x} \right)\sin \left( {3y} \right)} \\ {f\left( {\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{4}} \right)} & = & {\sin \left( {2\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right)} \right)\cos \left( {3\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right)} \right) = \left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)\left( {- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} \right) = - \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}} \\ {f_{x}\left( {\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{4}} \right)} & = & {2 \cos \left( {2\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right)} \right)\cos \left( {3\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right)} \right) = 2\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)\left( {- \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} \right) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} \\ {f_{y}\left( {\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{4}} \right)} & = & {-3 \sin \left( {2\left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right)} \right)\sin \left( {3\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right)} \right) = -3\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right)\left( \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \right) = - \frac{3\sqrt{6}}{4}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then Equation 4.24 becomes</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \\ {z = f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) + f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {x - x_{0}} \right) + f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {y - y_{0}} \right)} \\ \\ {z = - \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left( {x - \frac{\pi}{3}} \right) - \frac{3\sqrt{6}}{4}\left( {y - \frac{\pi}{4}} \right)} \\ {z = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}x - \frac{3\sqrt{6}}{4}y - \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4} - \frac{\pi\sqrt{2}}{6} + \frac{3\pi\sqrt{6}}{16}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="4.23" title="Using a Tangent Plane Approximation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Given the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{41 - 4x^{2} - y^{2}},$$ approximate $$f\left( {2.1,2.9} \right)$$ using point $$\left( {2,3} \right)$$ for $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$ What is the approximate value of $$f\left( {2.1,2.9} \right)$$ to four decimal places?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To apply Equation 4.25, we first must calculate $$f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right),$$ $$f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right),$$ and $$f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ using $$x_{0} = 2$$ and $$y_{0} = 3:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)} & = & {f\left( {2,3} \right) = \sqrt{41 - 4(2)^{2} - (3)^{2}} = \sqrt{41 - 16 - 9} = \sqrt{16} = 4} \\ {f_{x}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {- \frac{4x}{\sqrt{41 - 4x^{2} - y^{2}}} \text{so} f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = - \frac{4(2)}{\sqrt{41 - 4(2)^{2} - (3)^{2}}} = -2} \\ {f_{y}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {- \frac{y}{\sqrt{41 - 4x^{2} - y^{2}}} \text{so} f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = - \frac{3}{\sqrt{41 - 4(2)^{2} - (3)^{2}}} = - \frac{3}{4}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now we substitute these values into Equation 4.25:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {L\left( {x,y} \right)} & {= f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) + f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {x - x_{0}} \right) + f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {y - y_{0}} \right)} \\ & {= 4 - 2\left( {x - 2} \right) - \frac{3}{4}\left( {y - 3} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{41}{4} - 2x - \frac{3}{4}y.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Last, we substitute $$x = 2.1$$ and $$y = 2.9$$ into $$L\left( {x,y} \right):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$L\left( {2.1,2.9} \right) = \frac{41}{4} - 2(2.1) - \frac{3}{4}(2.9) = 10.25 - 4.2 - 2.175 = 3.875.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The approximate value of $$f\left( {2.1,2.9} \right)$$ to four decimal places is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {2.1,2.9} \right) = \sqrt{41 - 4(2.1)^{2} - (2.9)^{2}} = \sqrt{14.95} \approx 3.8665,$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>which corresponds to a $$0.2\%$$ error in approximation.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>A function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is differentiable at a point $$P\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ if, for all points $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in a $$\delta$$ disk around $$P,$$ we can write</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) + f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {x - x_{0}} \right) + f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)\left( {y - y_{0}} \right) + E\left( {x,y} \right),$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where the error term $$E$$ satisfies</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({x_{0},y_{0}})}}{\lim }\frac{E\left( {x,y} \right)}{\sqrt{\left( {x - x_{0}} \right)^{2} + \left( {y - y_{0}} \right)^{2}}} = 0.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Demonstrating Differentiability
snippet: Demonstrating Differentiability: Show that the function f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} - 4y is differentiable at point \left( {2,-3} \right). First, we calculate f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right),f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right), \text{and}...
body_xml:
<example number="4.24" title="Demonstrating Differentiability">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Show that the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} - 4y$$ is differentiable at point $$\left( {2,-3} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, we calculate $$f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right),f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right), \text{and} f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ using $$x_{0} = 2$$ and $$y_{0} = -3,$$ then we use Equation 4.26:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {f\left( {2,-3} \right)} & = & {2(2)^{2} - 4(-3) = 8 + 12 = 20} \\ {f_{x}\left( {2,-3} \right)} & = & {4(2) = 8} \\ {f_{y}\left( {2,-3} \right)} & = & -4. \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore $$m_{1} = 8$$ and $$m_{2} = -4,$$ and Equation 4.26 becomes</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {f\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {f\left( {2,-3} \right) + f_{x}\left( {2,-3} \right)\left( {x - 2} \right) + f_{y}\left( {2,-3} \right)\left( {y + 3} \right) + E\left( {x,y} \right)} \\ {2x^{2} - 4y} & = & {20 + 8\left( {x - 2} \right) - 4\left( {y + 3} \right) + E\left( {x,y} \right)} \\ {2x^{2} - 4y} & = & {20 + 8x - 16 - 4y - 12 + E\left( {x,y} \right)} \\ {2x^{2} - 4y} & = & {8x - 4y - 8 + E\left( {x,y} \right)} \\ {E\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {2x^{2} - 8x + 8.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, we calculate $$\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({x_{0},y_{0}})}}{\lim }\frac{E\left( {x,y} \right)}{\sqrt{\left( {x - x_{0}} \right)^{2} + \left( {y - y_{0}} \right)^{2}}}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({x_{0},y_{0}})}}{\lim }\frac{E\left( {x,y} \right)}{\sqrt{\left( {x - x_{0}} \right)^{2} + \left( {y - y_{0}} \right)^{2}}}} & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-3})}}{\lim }\frac{2x^{2} - 8x + 8}{\sqrt{\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2} + \left( {y + 3} \right)^{2}}}} \\ & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-3})}}{\lim }\frac{2\left( {x^{2} - 4x + 4} \right)}{\sqrt{\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2} + \left( {y + 3} \right)^{2}}}} \\ & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-3})}}{\lim }\frac{2\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2}}{\sqrt{\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2} + \left( {y + 3} \right)^{2}}}} \\ & {\leq \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-3})}}{\lim }\frac{2\left( {\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2} + \left( {y + 3} \right)^{2}} \right)}{\sqrt{\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2} + \left( {y + 3} \right)^{2}}}} \\ & {= \underset{{({x,y})}\rightarrow{({2,-3})}}{\lim }2\sqrt{\left( {x - 2} \right)^{2} + \left( {y + 3} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= 0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$E\left( {x,y} \right) \geq 0$$ for any value of $$x \text{or} y,$$ the original limit must be equal to zero. Therefore, $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} - 4y$$ is differentiable at point $$\left( {2,-3} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="4.25" title="Approximation by Differentials">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the differential $$dz$$ of the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 3x^{2} - 2xy + y^{2}$$ and use it to approximate $$\text{Δ} z$$ at point $$\left( {2,-3} \right).$$ Use $$\text{Δ} x = 0.1$$ and $$\text{Δ} y = -0.05.$$ What is the exact value of $$\text{Δ} z?$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, we must calculate $$f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right),f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right), \text{and} f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)$$ using $$x_{0} = 2$$ and $$y_{0} = -3:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)} & = & {f\left( {2,-3} \right) = 3(2)^{2} - 2(2)(-3) + (-3)^{2} = 12 + 12 + 9 = 33} \\ {f_{x}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {6x - 2y} \\ {f_{y}\left( {x,y} \right)} & = & {-2x + 2y} \\ {f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)} & = & {f_{x}\left( {2,-3} \right) = 6(2) - 2(-3) = 12 + 6 = 18} \\ {f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)} & = & {f_{y}\left( {2,-3} \right) = -2(2) + 2(-3) = -4 - 6 = -10.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, we substitute these quantities into Equation 4.27:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {dz = f_{x}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)dx + f_{y}\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)dy} \\ {dz = 18(0.1) - 10(-0.05) = 1.8 + 0.5 = 2.3.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This is the approximation to $$\text{Δ} z = f\left( {x_{0} + \text{Δ} x,y_{0} + \text{Δ} y} \right) - f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right).$$ The exact value of $$\text{Δ} z$$ is given by</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} { \text{Δ} z} & {= f\left( {x_{0} + \text{Δ} x,y_{0} + \text{Δ} y} \right) - f\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)} \\ & {= f\left( {2 + 0.1,-3 - 0.05} \right) - f\left( {2,-3} \right)} \\ & {= f\left( {2.1,-3.05} \right) - f\left( {2,-3} \right)} \\ & {= 2.3425.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="4.8" title="Chain Rule for One Independent Variable">
    <heading level="4">Chain Rule for One Independent Variable</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose that $$x = g(t)$$ and $$y = h(t)$$ are differentiable functions of $$t$$ and $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a differentiable function of $$x \text{and} y.$$ Then $$z = f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)$$ is a differentiable function of $$t$$ and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dt},$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where the ordinary derivatives are evaluated at $$t$$ and the partial derivatives are evaluated at $$\left( {x,y} \right).$$</paragraph>

snippet: Using the Chain Rule: Calculate {dz}/{dt} for each of the following functions: z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = 4x^{2} + 3y^{2},x = x(t) = \sin t,y = y(t) = \cos t z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{x^{2} - y^{2}},x = x(t) = e^{2t},y = y(t) =...
body_xml:
<example number="4.26" title="Using the Chain Rule">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate $${dz}/{dt}$$ for each of the following functions:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = 4x^{2} + 3y^{2},x = x(t) = \sin t,y = y(t) = \cos t$$</item>
        <item>$$z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = \sqrt{x^{2} - y^{2}},x = x(t) = e^{2t},y = y(t) = e^{-t}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>To use the chain rule, we need four quantities— $${{\partial z}/{\partial x}},{{\partial z}/{\partial y}},{{dx}/{dt}},$$ and $${{dy}/{dt}}:$$ $$\begin{array}{lccl} {\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 8x} & & & {\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = 6y} \\ {\frac{dx}{dt} = \cos t} & & & {\frac{dy}{dt} = -\sin t} \end{array}$$ Now, we substitute each of these into Equation 4.29: $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{dz}{dt} & {= \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dt}} \\ & {= \left( {8x} \right)\left( {\cos t} \right) + \left( {6y} \right)\left( {-\sin t} \right)} \\ & {= 8x \cos t - 6y \sin t.} \end{array}$$ This answer has three variables in it. To reduce it to one variable, use the fact that $$x(t) = \sin t \text{and} y(t) = \cos t.$$ We obtain $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{dz}{dt} & {= 8x \cos t - 6y \sin t} \\ & {= 8\left( {\sin t} \right)\cos t - 6\left( {\cos t} \right)\sin t} \\ & {= 2 \sin t \cos t.} \end{array}$$ This derivative can also be calculated by first substituting $$x(t)$$ and $$y(t)$$ into $$f\left( {x,y} \right),$$ then differentiating with respect to $$t:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} z & {= f\left( {x,y} \right)} \\ & {= f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)} \\ & {= 4\left( {x(t)} \right)^{2} + 3\left( {y(t)} \right)^{2}} \\ & {= 4\sin^{2}t + 3\cos^{2}t.} \end{array}$$ Then $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{dz}{dt} & {= 2(4 \sin t)(\cos t) + 2(3 \cos t)(-\sin t)} \\ & {= 8 \sin t \cos t - 6 \sin t \cos t} \\ & {= 2 \sin t \cos t,} \end{array}$$ which is the same solution. However, it may not always be this easy to differentiate in this form.</item>
        <item>To use the chain rule, we again need four quantities— $${{\partial z}/{\partial x}},{{\partial z}/{dy}},{{dx}/{dt}},$$ and $${{dy}/{dt}}:$$ $$\begin{matrix} {\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} - y^{2}}}} & & & {\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \frac{-y}{\sqrt{x^{2} - y^{2}}}} \\ {\frac{dx}{dt} = 2e^{2t}} & & & {\frac{dy}{dt} = -e^{-t}.} \end{matrix}$$ We substitute each of these into Equation 4.29: $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{dz}{dt} & {= \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dt}} \\ & {= \left( \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} - y^{2}}} \right)\left( {2e^{2t}} \right) + \left( \frac{-y}{\sqrt{x^{2} - y^{2}}} \right)\left( {-e^{-t}} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{2xe^{2t} + ye^{-t}}{\sqrt{x^{2} - y^{2}}}.} \end{array}$$ To reduce this to one variable, we use the fact that $$x(t) = e^{2t}$$ and $$y(t) = e^{-t}.$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{dz}{dt} & {= \frac{2xe^{2t} + ye^{-t}}{\sqrt{x^{2} - y^{2}}}} \\ & {= \frac{2\left( e^{2t} \right)e^{2t} + \left( e^{-t} \right)e^{-t}}{\sqrt{e^{4t} - e^{-2t}}}} \\ & {= \frac{2e^{4t} + e^{-2t}}{\sqrt{e^{4t} - e^{-2t}}}.} \end{array}$$ To eliminate negative exponents, we multiply the top by $$e^{2t}$$ and the bottom by $$\sqrt{e^{4t}}:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{dz}{dt} & {= \frac{2e^{4t} + e^{-2t}}{\sqrt{e^{4t} - e^{-2t}}} \cdot \frac{e^{2t}}{\sqrt{e^{4t}}}} \\ & {= \frac{2e^{6t} + 1}{\sqrt{e^{8t} - e^{2t}}}} \\ & {= \frac{2e^{6t} + 1}{\sqrt{e^{2t}\left( {e^{6t} - 1} \right)}}} \\ & {= \frac{2e^{6t} + 1}{e^{t}\sqrt{e^{6t} - 1}}.} \end{array}$$ Again, this derivative can also be calculated by first substituting $$x(t)$$ and $$y(t)$$ into $$f\left( {x,y} \right),$$ then differentiating with respect to $$t:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} z & {= f\left( {x,y} \right)} \\ & {= f\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)} \\ & {= \sqrt{\left( {x(t)} \right)^{2} - \left( {y(t)} \right)^{2}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{e^{4t} - e^{-2t}}} \\ & {= \left( {e^{4t} - e^{-2t}} \right)^{1/2}.} \end{array}$$ Then $$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{dz}{dt} & {= \frac{1}{2}\left( {e^{4t} - e^{-2t}} \right)^{-{1/2}}\left( {4e^{4t} + 2e^{-2t}} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{2e^{4t} + e^{-2t}}{\sqrt{e^{4t} - e^{-2t}}}.} \end{array}$$ This is the same solution.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="4.9" title="Chain Rule for Two Independent Variables">
    <heading level="4">Chain Rule for Two Independent Variables</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose $$x = g\left( {u,v} \right)$$ and $$y = h\left( {u,v} \right)$$ are differentiable functions of $$u$$ and $$v,$$ and $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a differentiable function of $$x \text{and} y.$$ Then, $$z = f\left( {g\left( {u,v} \right),h\left( {u,v} \right)} \right)$$ is a differentiable function of $$u \text{and} v,$$ and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial u} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial v} = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Using the Chain Rule for Two Variables: Calculate {\partial z}/{\partial u} and {\partial z}/{\partial v} using the following functions: z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = 3x^{2} - 2xy + y^{2},x = x\left( {u,v} \right) = 3u + 2v,y = y\left( {u,v}...
body_xml:
<example number="4.27" title="Using the Chain Rule for Two Variables">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate $${\partial z}/{\partial u}$$ and $${\partial z}/{\partial v}$$ using the following functions:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = 3x^{2} - 2xy + y^{2},x = x\left( {u,v} \right) = 3u + 2v,y = y\left( {u,v} \right) = 4u - v.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To implement the chain rule for two variables, we need six partial derivatives— $${{\partial z}/{\partial x}},{{\partial z}/{\partial y,{{\partial x}/{\partial u,{{\partial x}/{\partial v,{{\partial y}/{\partial u}}}}}}}},$$ and $${{\partial y}/{\partial v}}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lccl} {\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 6x - 2y} & & & {\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -2x + 2y} \\ {\frac{\partial x}{\partial u} = 3} & & & {\frac{\partial x}{\partial v} = 2} \\ {\frac{\partial y}{\partial u} = 4} & & & {\frac{\partial y}{\partial v} = -1.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To find $${{\partial z}/{\partial u}},$$ we use Equation 4.31:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial z}{\partial u} & {= \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial u} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}} \\ & {= 3\left( {6x - 2y} \right) + 4\left( {-2x + 2y} \right)} \\ & {= 10x + 2y.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, we substitute $$x\left( {u,v} \right) = 3u + 2v$$ and $$y\left( {u,v} \right) = 4u - v:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial z}{\partial u} & {= 10x + 2y} \\ & {= 10\left( {3u + 2v} \right) + 2\left( {4u - v} \right)} \\ & {= 38u + 18v.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To find $${{\partial z}/{\partial v}},$$ we use Equation 4.32:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial z}{\partial v} & {= \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}} \\ & {= 2\left( {6x - 2y} \right) + (-1)\left( {-2x + 2y} \right)} \\ & {= 14x - 6y.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then we substitute $$x\left( {u,v} \right) = 3u + 2v$$ and $$y\left( {u,v} \right) = 4u - v:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \frac{\partial z}{\partial v} & {= 14x - 6y} \\ & {= 14\left( {3u + 2v} \right) - 6\left( {4u - v} \right)} \\ & {= 18u + 34v.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>
