title: Finding a Volume with Triple Integrals in Two Ways
snippet: Finding a Volume with Triple Integrals in Two Ways: Let E be the region bounded below by the r\theta -plane, above by the sphere x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4, and on the sides by the cylinder x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 (Figure 5.54). Set up a triple...
body_xml:
<example number="5.46" title="Finding a Volume with Triple Integrals in Two Ways">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let E be the region bounded below by the $$r\theta$$ -plane, above by the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4,$$ and on the sides by the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ (Figure 5.54). Set up a triple integral in cylindrical coordinates to find the volume of the region using the following orders of integration, and in each case find the volume and check that the answers are the same:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$dz dr d\theta$$</item>
        <item>$$dr dz d\theta.$$ Figure 5.54 Finding a cylindrical volume with a triple integral in cylindrical coordinates.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Note that the equation for the sphere is $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4 \text{or} r^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ and the equation for the cylinder is $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1 \text{or} r^{2} = 1.$$ Thus, we have for the region $$E$$ $$E = \left\{ {\left. \left( {r,\theta,z} \right) \right|0 \leq z \leq \sqrt{4 - r^{2}},0 \leq r \leq 1,0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi} \right\}$$ Hence the integral for the volume is $$\begin{array}{cl} {V(E)} & {= {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{r = 0}^{r = 1} {\int\limits_{z = 0}^{z = \sqrt{4 - r^{2}}}{r dz dr d\theta}}}}} \\ & {= {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{r = 0}^{r = 1}\left\lbrack \left. {rz} \right|_{z = 0}^{z = \sqrt{4 - r^{2}}} \right\rbrack}}dr d\theta = {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{r = 0}^{r = 1}\left( {r\sqrt{4 - r^{2}}} \right)}}dr d\theta} \\ & {= {\int\limits_{0}^{2\pi}{\left( {\frac{8}{3} - \sqrt{3}} \right)d\theta = 2\pi\left( {\frac{8}{3} - \sqrt{3}} \right)}} \text{cubic units} .} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>Since the sphere is $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4,$$ which is $$r^{2} + z^{2} = 4,$$ and the cylinder is $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1,$$ which is $$r^{2} = 1,$$ we have $$1 + z^{2} = 4,$$ that is, $$z^{2} = 3.$$ Thus we have two regions, since the sphere and the cylinder intersect at $$\left( {1,\sqrt{3}} \right)$$ in the $$rz$$ -plane $$E_{1} = \left\{ {\left. \left( {r,\theta,z} \right) \right|0 \leq r \leq \sqrt{4 - z^{2}},\sqrt{3} \leq z \leq 2,0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi} \right\}$$ and $$E_{2} = \left\{ {\left. \left( {r,\theta,z} \right) \right|0 \leq r \leq 1,0 \leq z \leq \sqrt{3},0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi} \right\}.$$ Hence the integral for the volume is $$\begin{array}{cl} {V(E)} & {= {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{z = \sqrt{3}}^{z = 2} {\int\limits_{r = 0}^{r = \sqrt{4 - r^{2}}}{r dr dz d\theta}}}} + {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{z = 0}^{z = \sqrt{3}} {\int\limits_{r = 0}^{r = 1}{r dr dz d\theta}}}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{3}\pi + \left( {\frac{16}{3} - 3\sqrt{3}} \right)\pi = 2\pi\left( {\frac{8}{3} - \sqrt{3}} \right) \text{cubic units} .} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>The triple integral in spherical coordinates is the limit of a triple Riemann sum,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{l,m,n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{l}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}{f(\rho_{ijk}^{*},\theta_{ijk}^{*},\varphi_{ijk}^{*}){(\rho_{ijk}^{*})}^{2}\sin \varphi_{ijk}^{*} \text{Δ} \rho \text{Δ} \theta \text{Δ} \varphi}}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>provided the limit exists.</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Fubini’s Theorem for Spherical Coordinates: Fubini’s Theorem for Spherical Coordinates If f\left( {\rho,\theta,\varphi} \right) is continuous on a spherical solid box B = \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {\alpha,\beta}...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="5.13" title="Fubini’s Theorem for Spherical Coordinates">
    <heading level="4">Fubini’s Theorem for Spherical Coordinates</heading>
    <paragraph>If $$f\left( {\rho,\theta,\varphi} \right)$$ is continuous on a spherical solid box $$B = \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {\alpha,\beta} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {\gamma,\psi} \right\rbrack,$$ then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\iiint\limits_{B}f(\rho,\theta,\varphi)\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\rho d\varphi d\theta = \int\limits_{\theta = \alpha}^{\theta = \beta} \int\limits_{\varphi = \gamma}^{\varphi = \psi} \int\limits_{\rho = a}^{\rho = b}f(\rho,\theta,\varphi)\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\rho d\varphi d\theta.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This iterated integral may be replaced by other iterated integrals by integrating with respect to the three variables in other orders.</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Evaluating a Triple Integral in Spherical Coordinates: Evaluate the iterated triple integral {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/2} {\int\limits_{p = 0}^{\rho = 1}{\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\rho...
body_xml:
<example number="5.47" title="Evaluating a Triple Integral in Spherical Coordinates">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate the iterated triple integral $${\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/2} {\int\limits_{p = 0}^{\rho = 1}{\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\rho d\varphi d\theta}}}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>As before, in this case the variables in the iterated integral are actually independent of each other and hence we can integrate each piece and multiply:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int\limits_{0}^{2\pi} {\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} {\int\limits_{0}^{1}{\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\rho d\varphi d\theta}}}} = {\int\limits_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta}}{\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2}{\sin \varphi d\varphi{\int\limits_{0}^{1}{\rho^{2}d\rho}}}} = \left( {2\pi} \right)(1)\left( \frac{1}{3} \right) = \frac{2\pi}{3}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml: Set up an integral for the volume of the region bounded by the cone $$z = \sqrt{3\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)}$$ and the hemisphere $$z = \sqrt{4 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ (see the figure below). Using the conversion formulas from rectangular coordinates to spherical coordinates, we have: For the cone: $$z = \sqrt{3\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)}$$ or $$\rho \cos \varphi = \sqrt{3}\rho \sin \varphi$$ or $$\tan \varphi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$ or $$\varphi = \frac{\pi}{6}.$$ For the sphere: $$z = \sqrt{4 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ or $$z^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ or $$\rho^{2} = 4$$ or $$\rho = 2.$$ Thus, the triple integral for the volume is $$V(E) = {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/6} {\int\limits_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = 2}{\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\rho d\varphi d\theta}}}}.$$

title: Interchanging Order of Integration in Spherical Coordinates
snippet: Interchanging Order of Integration in Spherical Coordinates: Let E be the region bounded below by the cone z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} and above by the sphere z = x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} (Figure 5.59). Set up a triple integral in spherical...
body_xml:
<example number="5.49" title="Interchanging Order of Integration in Spherical Coordinates">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$E$$ be the region bounded below by the cone $$z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ and above by the sphere $$z = x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}$$ (Figure 5.59). Set up a triple integral in spherical coordinates and find the volume of the region using the following orders of integration:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$d\rho d\theta d\theta,$$</item>
        <item>$$d\varphi d\rho d\theta.$$ Figure 5.59 A region bounded below by a cone and above by a sphere.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Use the conversion formulas to write the equations of the sphere and cone in spherical coordinates. For the sphere: $$\begin{array}{rll} {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} & = & z \\ \rho^{2} & = & {\rho \cos \varphi} \\ \rho & = & {\cos \varphi.} \end{array}$$ For the cone: $$\begin{matrix} z & = & \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} \\ {\rho \cos \varphi} & = & \sqrt{\rho^{2}\sin^{2}\varphi \cos^{2} \text{θ} + \rho^{2}\sin^{2}\varphi \sin^{2} \text{θ} } \\ {\rho \cos \varphi} & = & \sqrt{\rho^{2}\sin^{2}\varphi\left( \cos^{2} \text{θ} + \sin^{2} \text{θ} \right)} \\ {\rho \cos \varphi} & = & {\rho \sin \varphi} \\ {\cos \varphi} & = & {\sin \varphi} \\ \varphi & = & {\pi/4.} \end{matrix}$$ Hence the integral for the volume of the solid region $$E$$ becomes $$V(E) = {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/4} {\int\limits_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = \cos \varphi}{\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\rho d\varphi d\theta}}}}.$$</item>
        <item>Consider the $$\varphi\rho$$ -plane. Note that the ranges for $$\varphi$$ and $$\rho$$ (from part a.) are $$\begin{array}{l} {0 \leq \varphi \leq \pi/4} \\ {0 \leq \rho \leq \cos \varphi.} \end{array}$$ The curve $$\rho = \cos \varphi$$ meets the line $$\varphi = \pi/4$$ at the point $$\left( {\pi/4,\sqrt{2}/2} \right).$$ Thus, to change the order of integration, we need to use two pieces: $$\begin{array}{lcclccl} \begin{array}{l} {0 \leq \rho \leq \sqrt{2}/2} \\ {0 \leq \varphi \leq \pi/4} \end{array} & & & \text{and} & & & \begin{array}{rll} {\sqrt{2}/2} & \leq & {\rho \leq 1} \\ 0 & \leq & {\varphi \leq \cos^{-1}\rho.} \end{array} \end{array}$$ Hence the integral for the volume of the solid region $$E$$ becomes $$V(E) = {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = \sqrt{2}/2} {\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/4}{\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\varphi d\rho d\theta}}}} + {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = 2\pi} {\int\limits_{\rho = \sqrt{2}/2}^{\rho = 1} {\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \cos^{-1}\rho}{\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\varphi d\rho d\theta}}}}.$$ In each case, the integration results in $$V(E) = \frac{\pi}{8}.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="5.50" title="Converting from Rectangular Coordinates to Cylindrical Coordinates">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Convert the following integral into cylindrical coordinates:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int\limits_{y = -1}^{y = 1} {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = \sqrt{1 - y^{2}}} {\int\limits_{z = x^{2} + y^{2}}^{z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}{xyz dz dx dy}}}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The ranges of the variables are</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {- 1} & \leq & {y \leq 1} \\ 0 & \leq & {x \leq \sqrt{1 - y^{2}}} \\ {x^{2} + y^{2}} & \leq & {z \leq \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The first two inequalities describe the right half of a circle of radius $$1.$$ Therefore, the ranges for $$\theta$$ and $$r$$ are</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$- \frac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2} \text{and} 0 \leq r \leq 1.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The limits of $$z$$ are $$r^{2} \leq z \leq r,$$ hence</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int\limits_{y = -1}^{y = 1} {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = \sqrt{1 - y^{2}}} {\int\limits_{z = x^{2} + y^{2}}^{z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}{xyz dz dx dy}}}} = {\int\limits_{\theta = -{\pi/2}}^{\theta = {\pi/2}} {\int\limits_{r = 0}^{r = 1} {\int\limits_{z = r^{2}}^{z = r}{r\left( {r \cos \theta} \right)\left( {r \sin \theta} \right)z dz dr d\theta}}}}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Converting from Rectangular Coordinates to Spherical Coordinates
snippet: Converting from Rectangular Coordinates to Spherical Coordinates: Convert the following integral into spherical coordinates: {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 3} {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = \sqrt{9 - y^{2}}} {\int\limits_{z = \sqrt{x^{2} +...
body_xml:
<example number="5.51" title="Converting from Rectangular Coordinates to Spherical Coordinates">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Convert the following integral into spherical coordinates:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 3} {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = \sqrt{9 - y^{2}}} {\int\limits_{z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}^{z = \sqrt{18 - x^{2} - y^{2}}}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)dz dx dy}}}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The ranges of the variables are</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} 0 & \leq & {y \leq 3} \\ 0 & \leq & {x \leq \sqrt{9 - y^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} & \leq & {z \leq \sqrt{18 - x^{2} - y^{2}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The first two ranges of variables describe a quarter disk in the first quadrant of the $$xy$$ -plane. Hence the range for $$\theta$$ is $$0 \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The lower bound $$z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ is the upper half of a cone and the upper bound $$z = \sqrt{18 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ is the upper half of a sphere. Therefore, we have $$0 \leq \rho \leq \sqrt{18},$$ which is $$0 \leq \rho \leq 3\sqrt{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>For the ranges of $$\varphi,$$ we need to find where the cone and the sphere intersect, so solve the equation</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {r^{2} + z^{2}} & = & 18 \\ {\left( \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{2} + z^{2}} & = & 18 \\ {z^{2} + z^{2}} & = & 18 \\ {2z^{2}} & = & 18 \\ z^{2} & = & 9 \\ z & = & 3. \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This gives</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {3\sqrt{2} \cos \varphi} & = & 3 \\ {\cos \varphi} & = & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \varphi & = & {\frac{\pi}{4}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Putting this together, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 3} {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = \sqrt{9 - y^{2}}} {\int\limits_{z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}^{z = \sqrt{18 - x^{2} - y^{2}}}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)dz dx dy}}}} = {\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/4} {\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = \pi/2} {\int\limits_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = 3\sqrt{2}}{\rho^{4}\sin \varphi d\rho d\theta}}}} d\varphi.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example title="Checkpoint" number="5.32">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use rectangular, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates to set up triple integrals for finding the volume of the region inside the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ but outside the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1.$$</paragraph>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Rectangular: $$\int x=-2x=2\int y=-4-x2y=4-x2\int z=-4-x2-y2z=4-x2-y2dzdydx-\int x=-1x=1\int y=-1-x2y=1-x2\int z=-4-x2-y2z=4-x2-y2dzdydx.\int x=-2x=2\int y=-4-x2y=4-x2\int z=-4-x2-y2z=4-x2-y2dzdydx-\int x=-1x=1\int y=-1-x2y=1-x2\int z=-4-x2-y2z=4-x2-y2dzdydx.$$ Cylindrical: $$\int \theta =0\theta =2\pi \int r=1r=2\int z=-4-r2z=4-r2rdzdrd\theta .\int \theta =0\theta =2\pi \int r=1r=2\int z=-4-r2z=4-r2rdzdrd\theta .$$ Spherical: $$\int \phi =\pi /6\phi =5\pi /6\int \theta =0\theta =2\pi \int ρ=csc\phi ρ=2ρ2sin\phi dρd\theta d\phi .\int \phi =\pi /6\phi =5\pi /6\int \theta =0\theta =2\pi \int ρ=csc\phi ρ=2ρ2sin\phi dρd\theta d\phi .$$</paragraph>

snippet: Chapter Opener: Finding the Volume of l’Hemisphèric: Find the volume of the spherical planetarium in l’Hemisphèric in Valencia, Spain, which is five stories tall and has a radius of approximately 50 ft, using the equation x^{2} + y^{2} +...
body_xml: Find the volume of the spherical planetarium in l’Hemisphèric in Valencia, Spain, which is five stories tall and has a radius of approximately $$50$$ ft, using the equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = r^{2}.$$ We calculate the volume of the ball in the first octant, where $$x \geq 0,y \geq 0,$$ and $$z \geq 0,$$ using spherical coordinates, and then multiply the result by $$8$$ for symmetry. Since we consider the region $$D$$ as the first octant in the integral, the ranges of the variables are $$0 \leq \varphi \leq \frac{\pi}{2},0 \leq \rho \leq r,0 \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}.$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{cl} V & {= {\iiint\limits_{D}{dx dy dz = 8{\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = \pi/2} {\int\limits_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = r} {\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/2}{\rho^{2}\sin \theta}}}}}} d\varphi d\rho d\theta} \\ & {= 8{\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/2}{d\varphi{\int\limits_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = r}{\rho^{2}d\rho}}}}{\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = \pi/2}{\sin \theta d\theta}}} \\ & {= 8\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)\left( \frac{r^{3}}{3} \right)(1)} \\ & {= \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}.} \end{array}$$ This exactly matches with what we knew. So for a sphere with a radius of approximately $$50$$ ft, the volume is $$\frac{4}{3}\pi{(50)}^{3} \approx 523,600{ \text{ft} }^{3}.$$

snippet: Finding the Volume of an Ellipsoid: Find the volume of the ellipsoid \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{z^{2}}{c^{2}} = 1. We again use symmetry and evaluate the volume of the ellipsoid using spherical coordinates. As...
body_xml:
<example number="5.53" title="Finding the Volume of an Ellipsoid">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the volume of the ellipsoid $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{z^{2}}{c^{2}} = 1.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We again use symmetry and evaluate the volume of the ellipsoid using spherical coordinates. As before, we use the first octant $$x \geq 0,y \geq 0,$$ and $$z \geq 0$$ and then multiply the result by $$8.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In this case the ranges of the variables are</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$0 \leq \varphi \leq \frac{\pi}{2},0,0 \leq \rho \leq 1, \text{and} 0 \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Also, we need to change the rectangular to spherical coordinates in this way:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x = a\rho \cos \varphi \sin \theta,y = b\rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta, \text{and} z = c\rho \cos \theta.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then the volume of the ellipsoid becomes</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} V & {= {\iiint\limits_{D}{dx dy dz}}} \\ & {= 8{\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = \pi/2} {\int\limits_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = 1} {\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/2}{abc\rho^{2}\sin \theta}}}} d\varphi d\rho d\theta} \\ & {= 8abc{\int\limits_{\varphi = 0}^{\varphi = \pi/2}{d\varphi{\int\limits_{\rho = 0}^{\rho = 1}{\rho^{2}d\rho{\int\limits_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = \pi/2}{\sin \theta d\theta}}}}}}} \\ & {= 8abc\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right)\left( \frac{1}{3} \right)(1)} \\ & {= \frac{4}{3}\pi abc.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Finding the Volume of the Space Inside an Ellipsoid and Outside a Sphere: Find the volume of the space inside the ellipsoid \frac{x^{2}}{75^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{80^{2}} + \frac{z^{2}}{90^{2}} = 1 and outside the sphere x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}...
body_xml:
<example number="5.54" title="Finding the Volume of the Space Inside an Ellipsoid and Outside a Sphere">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the volume of the space inside the ellipsoid $$\frac{x^{2}}{75^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{80^{2}} + \frac{z^{2}}{90^{2}} = 1$$ and outside the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 50^{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This problem is directly related to the l’Hemisphèric structure. The volume of space inside the ellipsoid and outside the sphere might be useful to find the expense of heating or cooling that space. We can use the preceding two examples for the volume of the sphere and ellipsoid and then substract.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>First we find the volume of the ellipsoid using $$a = 75 \text{ft,}$$ $$b = 80 \text{ft,}$$ and $$c = 90 \text{ft}$$ in the result from Example 5.53. Hence the volume of the ellipsoid is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$V_{ \text{ellipsoid} } = \frac{4}{3}\pi(75)(80)(90) \approx 2,262,000{ \text{ft} }^{3}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>From Example 5.52, the volume of the sphere is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$V_{ \text{sphere} } \approx 523,600{ \text{ft} }^{3}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the volume of the space inside the ellipsoid $$\frac{x^{2}}{75^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{80^{2}} + \frac{z^{2}}{90^{2}} = 1$$ and outside the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 50^{2}$$ is approximately</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$V_{ \text{Hemisferic} } = V_{ \text{ellipsoid} } - V_{ \text{sphere} } = 1,738,400{ \text{ft} }^{3}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Finding the Total Mass of a Lamina: Consider a triangular lamina R with vertices \left( {0,0} \right),\left( {0,3} \right), \left( {3,0} \right) and with density \rho\left( {x,y} \right) = xy{ \text{kg/m} }^{2}. Find the total mass. A...
body_xml: Consider a triangular lamina $$R$$ with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right),\left( {0,3} \right),$$ $$\left( {3,0} \right)$$ and with density $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = xy{ \text{kg/m} }^{2}.$$ Find the total mass. A sketch of the region $$R$$ is always helpful, as shown in the following figure. Using the expression developed for mass, we see that $$\begin{array}{cl} m & {= {\iint\limits_{R}{dm = {\iint\limits_{R}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}}}dA = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 3} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 3 - x}{xy dy dx = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 3}\left\lbrack \left. {x\frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right|_{y = 0}^{y = 3 - x} \right\rbrack}}}}dx} \\ & {= {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 3}\frac{1}{2}}x\left( {3 - x} \right)^{2}dx = \left. \left\lbrack {\frac{9x^{2}}{4} - x^{3} + \frac{x^{4}}{8}} \right\rbrack \right|_{x = 0}^{x = 3}} \\ & {= \frac{27}{8}.} \end{array}$$ The computation is straightforward, giving the answer $$m = \frac{27}{8} \text{kg} .$$

<example number="5.56" title="Finding Moments">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Consider the same triangular lamina $$R$$ with vertices $${\left( {0,0} \right),\left( {0,3} \right),} \left( {3,0} \right)$$ and with density $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = xy.$$ Find the moments $$M_{x}$$ and $$M_{y}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Use double integrals for each moment and compute their values:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$M_{x} = {\iint\limits_{R}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 3} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 3 - x}{xy^{2} dy dx}}}}} = \frac{81}{20},$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$M_{y} = {\iint\limits_{R}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 3} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 3 - x}{x^{2} yd y dx}}}}} = \frac{81}{20}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The computation is quite straightforward.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Center of Mass
snippet: Finding the Center of Mass: Again consider the same triangular region R with vertices \left( {0,0} \right),\left( {0,3} \right), \left( {3,0} \right) and with density function \rho\left( {x,y} \right) = xy. Find the center of mass. Using...
body_xml:
<example number="5.57" title="Finding the Center of Mass">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Again consider the same triangular region $$R$$ with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right),\left( {0,3} \right),$$ $$\left( {3,0} \right)$$ and with density function $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = xy.$$ Find the center of mass.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using the formulas we developed, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} = \frac{81/20}{27/8} = \frac{6}{5},$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} = \frac{81/20}{27/8} = \frac{6}{5}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the center of mass is the point $$\left( {\frac{6}{5},\frac{6}{5}} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>If we choose the density $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ instead to be uniform throughout the region (i.e., constant), such as the value 1 (any constant will do), then we can compute the centroid,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ \\ \\ {x_{c} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{x dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{dA}} = \frac{9/2}{9/2} = 1,} \\ {y_{c} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{y dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{dA}} = \frac{9/2}{9/2} = 1.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Notice that the center of mass $$\left( {\frac{6}{5},\frac{6}{5}} \right)$$ is not exactly the same as the centroid $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ of the triangular region. This is due to the variable density of $$R.$$ If the density is constant, then we just use $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = c$$ (constant). This value cancels out from the formulas, so for a constant density, the center of mass coincides with the centroid of the lamina.</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Finding Mass, Moments, and Center of Mass: Find the mass, moments, and the center of mass of the lamina of density \rho\left( {x,y} \right) = x + y occupying the region R under the curve y = x^{2} in the interval 0 \leq x \leq 2 (see the...
body_xml: Find the mass, moments, and the center of mass of the lamina of density $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = x + y$$ occupying the region $$R$$ under the curve $$y = x^{2}$$ in the interval $$0 \leq x \leq 2$$ (see the following figure). First we compute the mass $$m.$$ We need to describe the region between the graph of $$y = x^{2}$$ and the vertical lines $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 2:$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} m & {= {\iint\limits_{R}{dm}} = {\iint\limits_{R}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 2} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = x^{2}}{\left( {x + y} \right)dy dx = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 2}\left\lbrack \left. {xy + \frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right|_{y = 0}^{y = x^{2}} \right\rbrack}}}}}}dx} \\ & {= {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 2}\left\lbrack {x^{3} + \frac{x^{4}}{2}} \right\rbrack}dx = \left. \left\lbrack {\frac{x^{4}}{4} + \frac{x^{5}}{10}} \right\rbrack \right|_{x = 0}^{x = 2} = \frac{36}{5}.} \end{array}$$ Now compute the moments $$M_{x}$$ and $$M_{y}:$$ $$M_{x} = {\iint\limits_{R}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 2} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = x^{2}}{y\left( {x + y} \right)dy dx = \frac{80}{7}}}},$$ $$M_{y} = {\iint\limits_{R}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 2} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = x^{2}}{x\left( {x + y} \right)dy dx = \frac{176}{15}}}}.$$ Finally, evaluate the center of mass, $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ \\ {\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} = \frac{176/15}{36/5} = \frac{44}{27},} \\ {\overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} = \frac{80/7}{36/5} = \frac{100}{63}.} \end{array}$$ Hence the center of mass is $$(\overset{-}{x},\overset{-}{y}) = \left( {\frac{44}{27},\frac{100}{63}} \right).$$

snippet: Finding a Centroid: Find the centroid of the region under the curve y = e^{x} over the interval 1 \leq x \leq 3 (see the following figure). To compute the centroid, we assume that the density function is constant and hence it cancels out:...
body_xml: Find the centroid of the region under the curve $$y = e^{x}$$ over the interval $$1 \leq x \leq 3$$ (see the following figure). To compute the centroid, we assume that the density function is constant and hence it cancels out: $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ \\ \\ {x_{c} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{x dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{dA}} \text{and} y_{c} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{y dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{dA}},} \\ {x_{c} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{x dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{dA}} = \frac{\int\limits_{x = 1}^{x = 3} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = e^{x}}{x dy dx}}}{\int\limits_{x = 1}^{x = 3} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = e^{x}}{dy dx}}} = \frac{\int\limits_{x = 1}^{x = 3}{xe^{x}dx}}{\int\limits_{x = 1}^{x = 3}{e^{x}dx}} = \frac{2e^{3}}{e^{3} - e} = \frac{2e^{2}}{e^{2} - 1},} \\ {y_{c} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{\iint\limits_{R}{y dA}}{\iint\limits_{R}{dA}} = \frac{\int\limits_{x = 1}^{x = 3} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = e^{x}}{y dy dx}}}{\int\limits_{x = 1}^{x = 3} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = e^{x}}{dy dx}}} = \frac{\int\limits_{x = 1}^{x = 3}{\frac{e^{2x}}{2}dx}}{\int\limits_{x = 1}^{x = 3}{e^{x}dx}} = \frac{\frac{1}{4}e^{2}\left( {e^{4} - 1} \right)}{e\left( {e^{2} - 1} \right)} = \frac{1}{4}e\left( {e^{2} + 1} \right).} \end{array}$$ Thus the centroid of the region is $$\left( {x_{c},y_{c}} \right) = \left( {\frac{2e^{2}}{e^{2} - 1},\frac{1}{4}e\left( {e^{2} + 1} \right)} \right).$$

<example number="5.60" title="Finding Moments of Inertia for a Triangular Lamina">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the triangular region $$R$$ with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right),\left( {2,2} \right),$$ and $$\left( {2,0} \right)$$ and with density $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ as in previous examples. Find the moments of inertia.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using the expressions established above for the moments of inertia, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cll} I_{x} & = & {{\iint\limits_{R}{y^{2}\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 2} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = x}{xy^{3}dy dx}}} = \frac{8}{3},} \\ I_{y} & = & {{\iint\limits_{R}{x^{2}\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 2} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = x}{x^{3}y dy dx}}} = \frac{16}{3},} \\ I_{0} & = & {{\iint\limits_{R}\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)}\rho(x,y)dA = {\int\limits_{0}^{2} {\int\limits_{0}^{x}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)xy dy dx}}}} \\ & = & {I_{x} + I_{y} = 8.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: If we have a solid object Q with a density function \rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) at any point \left( {x,y,z} \right) in space, then its mass is m = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}dV. Its moments about the xy...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>If we have a solid object $$Q$$ with a density function $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ at any point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ in space, then its mass is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$m = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}dV.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Its moments about the $$xy \text{-plane,}$$ the $$xz \text{-plane,}$$ and the $$yz \text{-plane}$$ are</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{M_{xy} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{z\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}dV,} {M_{xz} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{y\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}dV,}} \\ {M_{yz} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{x\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}dV.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If the center of mass of the object is the point $$\left( {\overset{-}{x},\overset{-}{y},\overset{-}{z}} \right),$$ then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M_{yz}}{m}, \overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{xz}}{m},\overset{-}{z} = \frac{M_{xy}}{m}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Also, if the solid object is homogeneous (with constant density), then the center of mass becomes the centroid of the solid. Finally, the moments of inertia about the $$yz \text{-plane,}$$ the $$xz \text{-plane,}$$ and the $$xy \text{-plane}$$ are</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \\ {I_{x} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}\left( {y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)}\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV,} \\ {I_{y} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}\left( {x^{2} + z^{2}} \right)}\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV,} \\ {I_{z} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)}\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding the Mass of a Solid
snippet: Finding the Mass of a Solid: Suppose that Q is a solid region bounded by x + 2y + 3z = 6 and the coordinate planes and has density \rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz. Find the total mass. The region Q is a tetrahedron (Figure 5.70)...
body_xml: Suppose that $$Q$$ is a solid region bounded by $$x + 2y + 3z = 6$$ and the coordinate planes and has density $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz.$$ Find the total mass. The region $$Q$$ is a tetrahedron (Figure 5.70) meeting the axes at the points $$\left( {6,0,0} \right),\left( {0,3,0} \right),$$ and $$\left( {0,0,2} \right).$$ To find the limits of integration, let $$z = 0$$ in the slanted plane $$z = \frac{1}{3}\left( {6 - x - 2y} \right).$$ Then for $$x$$ and $$y$$ find the projection of $$Q$$ onto the $$xy \text{-plane,}$$ which is bounded by the axes and the line $$x + 2y = 6.$$ Hence the mass is $$m = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 6} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 1/2{({6 - x})}} {\int\limits_{z = 0}^{z = 1/3{({6 - x - 2y})}}{x^{2}yz dz dy dx = \frac{108}{35} \approx 3.086}}}}}}.$$

title: Finding the Center of Mass of a Solid
snippet: Finding the Center of Mass of a Solid: Suppose Q is a solid region bounded by the plane x + 2y + 3z = 6 and the coordinate planes with density \rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz (see Figure 5.70). Find the center of mass using decimal...
body_xml:
<example number="5.63" title="Finding the Center of Mass of a Solid">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose $$Q$$ is a solid region bounded by the plane $$x + 2y + 3z = 6$$ and the coordinate planes with density $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz$$ (see Figure 5.70). Find the center of mass using decimal approximation. Use the mass found in Example 5.62</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have used this tetrahedron before and know the limits of integration, so we can proceed to the computations right away. First, we need to find the moments about the $$xy \text{-plane,}$$ the $$xz \text{-plane,}$$ and the $$yz \text{-plane:}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ \\ {M_{xy} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{z\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}dV = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 6} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 1/2{({6 - x})}} {\int\limits_{z = 0}^{z = 1/3{({6 - x - 2y})}}{x^{2}yz^{2}dz dy dx = \frac{54}{35}}}}} \approx 1.543,} \\ {M_{xz} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{y\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}dV = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 6} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 1/2{({6 - x})}} {\int\limits_{z = 0}^{z = 1/3{({6 - x - 2y})}}{x^{2}y^{2}z dz dy dx = \frac{81}{35}}}}} \approx 2.314,} \\ {M_{yz} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{x\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}dV = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 6} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = 1/2{({6 - x})}} {\int\limits_{z = 0}^{z = 1/3{({6 - x - 2y})}}{x^{3}yz dz dy dx = \frac{243}{35}}}}} \approx 6.943.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Hence the center of mass is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ \\ {\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M_{yz}}{m},\overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{xz}}{m},\overset{-}{z} = \frac{M_{xy}}{m},} \\ {\overset{-}{x} = \frac{M_{yz}}{m} = \frac{243/35}{108/35} = \frac{243}{108} = 2.25,} \\ {\overset{-}{y} = \frac{M_{xz}}{m} = \frac{81/35}{108/35} = \frac{81}{108} = 0.75,} \\ {\overset{-}{z} = \frac{M_{xy}}{m} = \frac{54/35}{108/35} = \frac{54}{108} = 0.5.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The center of mass for the tetrahedron $$Q$$ is the point $$\left( {2.25,0.75,0.5} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Moments of Inertia of a Solid
snippet: Finding the Moments of Inertia of a Solid: Suppose that Q is a solid region and is bounded by x + 2y + 3z = 6 and the coordinate planes with density \rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz (see Figure 5.70). Find the moments of inertia of the...
body_xml:
<example number="5.64" title="Finding the Moments of Inertia of a Solid">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose that $$Q$$ is a solid region and is bounded by $$x + 2y + 3z = 6$$ and the coordinate planes with density $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz$$ (see Figure 5.70). Find the moments of inertia of the tetrahedron $$Q$$ about the $$yz \text{-plane,}$$ the $$xz \text{-plane,}$$ and the $$xy \text{-plane} .$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Once again, we can almost immediately write the limits of integration and hence we can quickly proceed to evaluating the moments of inertia. Using the formula stated before, the moments of inertia of the tetrahedron $$Q$$ about the $$xy \text{-plane,}$$ the $$xz \text{-plane,}$$ and the $$yz \text{-plane}$$ are</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{r} \\ {I_{x} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{\left( {y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV}},} \\ {I_{y} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{\left( {x^{2} + z^{2}} \right)\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV}},} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${I_{z} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV}}} \text{with} {\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz.}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Proceeding with the computations, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ {I_{x} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{\left( {y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)x^{2}yz dV}} = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 6} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = \frac{1}{2}{({6 - x})}} {\int\limits_{z = 0}^{z = \frac{1}{3}{({6 - x - 2y})}}\left( {y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)}}}x^{2}yz dz dy dx = \frac{117}{35} \approx 3.343,} \\ {I_{y} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{\left( {x^{2} + z^{2}} \right)x^{2}yz dV}} = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 6} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = \frac{1}{2}{({6 - x})}} {\int\limits_{z = 0}^{z = \frac{1}{3}{({6 - x - 2y})}}\left( {x^{2} + z^{2}} \right)}}}x^{2}yz dz dy dx = \frac{684}{35} \approx 19.543,} \\ {I_{z} = {\iiint\limits_{Q}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)x^{2}yz dV}} = {\int\limits_{x = 0}^{x = 6} {\int\limits_{y = 0}^{y = \frac{1}{2}{({6 - x})}} {\int\limits_{z = 0}^{z = \frac{1}{3}{({6 - x - 2y})}}\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)}}}x^{2}yz dz dy dx = \frac{729}{35} \approx 20.829.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, the moments of inertia of the tetrahedron $$Q$$ about the $$yz \text{-plane,}$$ the $$xz \text{-plane,}$$ and the $$xy \text{-plane}$$ are $$117/35,684/35, \text{and} 729/35,$$ respectively.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

unit_title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals
title: Determining How the Transformation Works
snippet: Determining How the Transformation Works: Suppose a transformation T is defined as T\left( {r,\theta} \right) = \left( {x,y} \right) where x = r \cos \theta,y = r \sin \theta. Find the image of the polar rectangle G = \left\{ {\left....
body_xml: Suppose a transformation $$T$$ is defined as $$T\left( {r,\theta} \right) = \left( {x,y} \right)$$ where $$x = r \cos \theta,y = r \sin \theta.$$ Find the image of the polar rectangle $$G = \left\{ {\left. \left( {r,\theta} \right) \right|0 < r \leq 1,0 \leq \theta \leq \pi/2} \right\}$$ in the $$r\theta \text{-plane}$$ to a region $$R$$ in the $$xy \text{-plane} .$$ Show that $$T$$ is a one-to-one transformation in $$G$$ and find $$T^{-1}\left( {x,y} \right).$$ Since $$r$$ varies from 0 to 1 in the $$r\theta \text{-plane} ,$$ we have a circular disc of radius 0 to 1 in the $$xy \text{-plane} .$$ Because $$\theta$$ varies from 0 to $$\pi \text{/2}$$ in the $$r\theta \text{-plane} ,$$ we end up getting a quarter circle of radius $$1$$ in the first quadrant of the $$xy \text{-plane}$$ (Figure 5.72). Hence $$R$$ is a quarter circle bounded by $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ in the first quadrant. In order to show that $$T$$ is a one-to-one transformation, assume $$T\left( {r_{1},\theta_{1}} \right) = T\left( {r_{2},\theta_{2}} \right)$$ and show as a consequence that $$\left( {r_{1},\theta_{1}} \right) = \left( {r_{2},\theta_{2}} \right).$$ In this case, we have $$\begin{matrix} {T\left( r_{1},\theta_{1} \right)} & = & {T\left( r_{2},\theta_{2} \right),} \\ \left( x_{1},y_{1} \right) & = & {\left( x_{2},y_{2} \right),} \\ \left( r_{1}\cos \theta_{1},r_{1}\sin \theta_{1} \right) & = & {\left( r_{2}\cos \theta_{2},r_{2}\sin \theta_{2} \right),} \\ {r_{1}\cos \theta_{1}} & = & {r_{2}\cos \theta_{2}} \\ {r_{1}\sin \theta_{1}} & = & {r_{2}\sin \theta_{2}} \end{matrix}$$ Dividing, we obtain $$\begin{array}{rll} \frac{r_{1}\cos \theta_{1}}{r_{1}\sin \theta_{1}} & = & \frac{r_{2}\cos \theta_{2}}{r_{2}\sin \theta_{2}} \\ \frac{\cos \theta_{1}}{\sin \theta_{1}} & = & \frac{\cos \theta_{2}}{\sin \theta_{2}} \\ {\cot \theta_{1}} & = & {\cot \theta_{2}} \\ \theta_{1} & = & \theta_{2} \end{array}$$ since the cotangent function is one-one function in the interval $$0 \leq \theta \leq \pi/2.$$ Also, since $$0 < r \leq 1,$$ we have $$r_{1} = r_{2},\theta_{1} = \theta_{2}.$$ Therefore, $$\left( {r_{1},\theta_{1}} \right) = \left( {r_{2},\theta_{2}} \right)$$ and $$T$$ is a one-to-one transformation from $$G$$ into $$R.$$ To find $$T^{-1}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ solve for $$r,\theta$$ in terms of $$x,y.$$ We already know that $$r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ and $$\tan \theta = \frac{y}{x}.$$ Thus $$T^{-1}\left( {x,y} \right) = \left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ is defined as $$r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ and $$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{y}{x} \right).$$

snippet: Finding the Image under TT: Let the transformation T be defined by T\left( {u,v} \right) = \left( {x,y} \right) where x = u^{2} - v^{2} and y = uv. Find the image of the triangle in the uv \text{-plane} with vertices \left( {0,0}...
body_xml: Let the transformation $$T$$ be defined by $$T\left( {u,v} \right) = \left( {x,y} \right)$$ where $$x = u^{2} - v^{2}$$ and $$y = uv.$$ Find the image of the triangle in the $$uv \text{-plane}$$ with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right),\left( {0,1} \right),$$ and $$\left( {1,1} \right).$$ The triangle and its image are shown in Figure 5.73. To understand how the sides of the triangle transform, call the side that joins $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ side $$A,$$ the side that joins $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ side $$B,$$ and the side that joins $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ side $$C.$$ For the side $$A: u = 0,0 \leq v \leq 1$$ transforms to $$x = -v^{2},y = 0$$ so this is the side $$A\prime$$ that joins $$\left( {-1,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,0} \right).$$ For the side $$B: u = v,0 \leq u \leq 1$$ transforms to $$x = 0,y = u^{2}$$ so this is the side $$B^{\prime}$$ that joins $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,1} \right).$$ For the side $$C: 0 \leq u \leq 1,v = 1$$ transforms to $$x = u^{2} - 1,y = u$$ (hence $$x = y^{2} - 1)$$ so this is the side $$C^{\prime}$$ that makes the upper half of the parabolic arc joining $$\left( {-1,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,1} \right).$$ All the points in the entire region of the triangle in the $$uv \text{-plane}$$ are mapped inside the parabolic region in the $$xy \text{-plane} .$$

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>The Jacobian of the $$C^{1}$$ transformation $$T\left( {u,v} \right) = \left( {g\left( {u,v} \right),h\left( {u,v} \right)} \right)$$ is denoted by $$J\left( {u,v} \right)$$ and is defined by the $$2 \times 2$$ determinant</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$J\left( {u,v} \right) = \left| \frac{\partial\left( {x,y} \right)}{\partial\left( {u,v} \right)} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{lll} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} \\ \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{array} \right| = \left( {\frac{\partial x}{\partial u} \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} - \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}} \right).$$</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="5.67" title="Finding the Jacobian">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the Jacobian of the transformation given in Example 5.65.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The transformation in the example is $$T\left( {r,\theta} \right) = \left( {r \cos \theta,r \sin \theta} \right)$$ where $$x = r \cos \theta$$ and $$y = r \sin \theta.$$ Thus the Jacobian is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {J\left( {r,\theta} \right)} & {= \frac{\partial\left( {x,y} \right)}{\partial\left( {r,\theta} \right)} = \left| \begin{array}{lll} \frac{\partial x}{\partial r} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial r} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta} \end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{llr} {\cos \theta} & & {- r \sin \theta} \\ {\sin \theta} & & {r \cos \theta} \end{array} \right|} \\ & {= r \cos^{2}\theta + r \sin^{2}\theta = r\left( {\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta} \right) = r.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="5.68" title="Finding the Jacobian">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the Jacobian of the transformation given in Example 5.66.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The transformation in the example is $$T\left( {u,v} \right) = \left( {u^{2} - v^{2},uv} \right)$$ where $$x = u^{2} - v^{2}$$ and $$y = uv.$$ Thus the Jacobian is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$J\left( {u,v} \right) = \frac{\partial\left( {x,y} \right)}{\partial\left( {u,v} \right)} = \left| \begin{array}{lll} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{lll} {2u} & & v \\ {- 2v} & & u \end{array} \right| = 2u^{2} + 2v^{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>$$J ( u , v ) = \partial ( x , y ) \partial ( u , v ) = | \partial x \partial u \partial x \partial v \partial y \partial u \partial y \partial v | = | 1 1 0 2 | = 2 J ( u , v ) = \partial ( x , y ) \partial ( u , v ) = | \partial x \partial u \partial x \partial v \partial y \partial u \partial y \partial v | = | 1 1 0 2 | = 2$$</paragraph>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="5.14" title="Change of Variables for Double Integrals">
    <heading level="4">Change of Variables for Double Integrals</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$T\left( {u,v} \right) = \left( {x,y} \right)$$ where $$x = g\left( {u,v} \right)$$ and $$y = h\left( {u,v} \right)$$ be a one-to-one $$C^{1}$$ transformation, with a nonzero Jacobian on the interior of the region $$S$$ in the $$uv \text{-plane;}$$ it maps $$S$$ into the region $$R$$ in the $$xy \text{-plane} .$$ If $$f$$ is continuous on $$R,$$ then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\iint\limits_{R}{f\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = {\iint\limits_{S}{f\left( {g\left( {u,v} \right),h\left( {u,v} \right)} \right)}}\left| \frac{\partial\left( {x,y} \right)}{\partial\left( {u,v} \right)} \right|du dv.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Changing Variables from Rectangular to Polar Coordinates
snippet: Changing Variables from Rectangular to Polar Coordinates: Consider the integral {\int\limits_{0}^{2} {\int\limits_{0}^{\sqrt{2x - x^{2}}}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} dy dx}}}. Use the change of variables x = r \cos \theta and y = r \sin \theta,...
body_xml: Consider the integral $${\int\limits_{0}^{2} {\int\limits_{0}^{\sqrt{2x - x^{2}}}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} dy dx}}}.$$ Use the change of variables $$x = r \cos \theta$$ and $$y = r \sin \theta,$$ and find the resulting integral. First we need to find the region of integration. This region is bounded below by $$y = 0$$ and above by $$y = \sqrt{2x - x^{2}}$$ (see the following figure). Squaring and collecting terms, we find that the region is the upper half of the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} - 2x = 0,$$ that is, $$y^{2} + \left( {x - 1} \right)^{2} = 1.$$ In polar coordinates, the circle is $$r = 2 \cos \theta$$ so the region of integration in polar coordinates is bounded by $$0 \leq r \leq 2 \cos \theta$$ and $$0 \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}.$$ The Jacobian is $$J\left( {r,\theta} \right) = r,$$ as shown in Example 5.67. Since $$r \geq 0,$$ we have $$\left| {J\left( {r,\theta} \right)} \right| = r.$$ The integrand $$\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ changes to $$r$$ in polar coordinates, so the double iterated integral is $${\int\limits_{0}^{2} {\int\limits_{0}^{\sqrt{2x - x^{2}}}\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}}dy dx = {\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} {\int\limits_{0}^{2 \cos \theta}{r\left| {J\left( {r,\theta} \right)} \right|}}}dr d\theta = {\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} {\int\limits_{0}^{2 \cos \theta}r^{2}}}dr d\theta.$$

title: Changing Variables
snippet: Changing Variables: Consider the integral {\iint\limits_{R}\left( {x - y} \right)}dy dx, where R is the parallelogram joining the points \left( {1,2} \right), \left( {3,4} \right),\left( {4,3} \right), and \left( {6,5} \right) (Figure...
body_xml: Consider the integral $${\iint\limits_{R}\left( {x - y} \right)}dy dx,$$ where $$R$$ is the parallelogram joining the points $$\left( {1,2} \right),$$ $$\left( {3,4} \right),\left( {4,3} \right),$$ and $$\left( {6,5} \right)$$ (Figure 5.77). Make appropriate changes of variables, and write the resulting integral. First, we need to understand the region over which we are to integrate. The sides of the parallelogram are $$x - y + 1 = 0,x - y - 1 = 0,$$ $$x - 3y + 5 = 0, \text{and} x - 3y + 9 = 0$$ (Figure 5.78). Another way to look at them is $$x - y = -1,x - y = 1,$$ $$x - 3y = -5,$$ and $$x - 3y = - 9.$$ Clearly the parallelogram is bounded by the lines $$y = x + 1,y = x - 1,y = \frac{1}{3}\left( {x + 5} \right),$$ and $$y = \frac{1}{3}\left( {x + 9} \right).$$ Notice that if we were to make $$u = x - y$$ and $$v = x - 3y,$$ then the limits on the integral would be $$-1 \leq u \leq 1$$ and $$-9 \leq v \leq - 5.$$ To solve for $$x$$ and $$y,$$ we multiply the first equation by $$3$$ and subtract the second equation, $$3u - v = \left( {3x - 3y} \right) - \left( {x - 3y} \right) = 2x.$$ Then we have $$x = \frac{3u - v}{2}.$$ Moreover, if we simply subtract the second equation from the first, we get $$u - v = \left( {x - y} \right) - \left( {x - 3y} \right) = 2y$$ and $$y = \frac{u - v}{2}.$$ Thus, we can choose the transformation $$T\left( {u,v} \right) = \left( {\frac{3u - v}{2},\frac{u - v}{2}} \right)$$ and compute the Jacobian $$J\left( {u,v} \right).$$ We have $$J\left( {u,v} \right) = \frac{\partial\left( {x,y} \right)}{\partial\left( {u,v} \right)} = \left| \begin{array}{lll} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{lll} {3/2} & & {- 1/2} \\ {1/2} & & {- 1/2} \end{array} \right| = - \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = - \frac{1}{2}.$$ Therefore, $$\left| {J\left( {u,v} \right)} \right| = \frac{1}{2}.$$ Also, the original integrand becomes $$x - y = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {3u - v - u + v} \right\rbrack = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {3u - u} \right\rbrack = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {2u} \right\rbrack = u.$$ Therefore, by the use of the transformation $$T,$$ the integral changes to $${\iint\limits_{R}{\left( {x - y} \right)dy dx = {\int\limits_{-9}^{-5} {\int\limits_{-1}^{1}{J\left( {u,v} \right)u du dv = {\int\limits_{-9}^{-5} {\int\limits_{-1}^{1}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)}}}}}}}u du dv,$$ which is much simpler to compute. In fact, it is easily found to be zero. And this is just one example of why we transform integrals like this.

title: Evaluating an Integral
snippet: Evaluating an Integral: Using the change of variables u = x - y and v = x + y, evaluate the integral {\iint\limits_{R}{\left( {x - y} \right)e^{x^{2} - y^{2}}dA}}, where R is the region bounded by the lines x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 and the...
body_xml: Using the change of variables $$u = x - y$$ and $$v = x + y,$$ evaluate the integral $${\iint\limits_{R}{\left( {x - y} \right)e^{x^{2} - y^{2}}dA}},$$ where $$R$$ is the region bounded by the lines $$x + y = 1$$ and $$x + y = 3$$ and the curves $$x^{2} - y^{2} = -1$$ and $$x^{2} - y^{2} = 1$$ (see the first region in Figure 5.79). As before, first find the region $$R$$ and picture the transformation so it becomes easier to obtain the limits of integration after the transformations are made (Figure 5.79). Given $$u = x - y$$ and $$v = x + y,$$ we have $$x = \frac{u + v}{2}$$ and $$y = \frac{v - u}{2}$$ and hence the transformation to use is $$T\left( {u,v} \right) = \left( {\frac{u + v}{2},\frac{v - u}{2}} \right).$$ The lines $$x + y = 1$$ and $$x + y = 3$$ become $$v = 1$$ and $$v = 3,$$ respectively. The curves $$x^{2} - y^{2} = 1$$ and $$x^{2} - y^{2} = -1$$ become $$uv = 1$$ and $$uv = -1,$$ respectively. Thus we can describe the region $$S$$ (see the second region Figure 5.79) as $$S = \left\{ {\left. \left( {u,v} \right) \right|1 \leq v \leq 3,\frac{-1}{v} \leq u \leq \frac{1}{v}} \right\}.$$ The Jacobian for this transformation is $$J\left( {u,v} \right) = \frac{\partial\left( {x,y} \right)}{\partial\left( {u,v} \right)} = \left| \begin{array}{lll} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{lll} {1/2} & & {- 1/2} \\ {1/2} & & {1/2} \end{array} \right| = \frac{1}{2}.$$ Therefore, by using the transformation $$T,$$ the integral changes to $${\iint\limits_{R}\left( {x - y} \right)}e^{x^{2} - y^{2}}dA = \frac{1}{2}{\int\limits_{1}^{3} {\int\limits_{-1/v}^{1/v}{ue^{uv}du dv}}}.$$ Doing the evaluation, we have $$\frac{1}{2}{\int\limits_{1}^{3} {\int\limits_{-1/v}^{1/v}{ue^{uv}du dv}}} = \frac{2}{3e} \approx 0.245.$$

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: The Jacobian determinant J\left( {u,v,w} \right) in three variables is defined as follows: J(u,v,w) = \left| \begin{array}{lclcl} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>The Jacobian determinant $$J\left( {u,v,w} \right)$$ in three variables is defined as follows:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$J(u,v,w) = \left| \begin{array}{lclcl} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial u} \\ \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial v} \\ \frac{\partial x}{\partial w} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial w} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial w} \end{array} \right|.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This is also the same as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$J(u,v,w) = \left| \begin{array}{lclcl} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial w} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial w} \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial v} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial w} \end{array} \right|.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The Jacobian can also be simply denoted as $$\frac{\partial\left( {x,y,z} \right)}{\partial\left( {u,v,w} \right)}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="5.15" title="Change of Variables for Triple Integrals">
    <heading level="4">Change of Variables for Triple Integrals</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$T\left( {u,v,w} \right) = \left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ where $$x = g\left( {u,v,w} \right),y = h\left( {u,v,w} \right),$$ and $$z = k\left( {u,v,w} \right),$$ be a one-to-one $$C^{1}$$ transformation, with a nonzero Jacobian, that maps the region $$G$$ in the $$uvw \text{-space}$$ into the region $$R$$ in the $$xyz \text{-space} .$$ As in the two-dimensional case, if $$F$$ is continuous on $$R,$$ then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\iiint\limits_{R}{F\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV}} & {= {\iiint\limits_{G}{F\left( {g\left( {u,v,w} \right),h\left( {u,v,w} \right),k\left( {u,v,w} \right)} \right)\left| \frac{\partial\left( {x,y,z} \right)}{\partial\left( {u,v,w} \right)} \right|}}du dv dw} \\ & {= {\iiint\limits_{G}{H\left( {u,v,w} \right)}}\left| {J\left( {u,v,w} \right)} \right|du dv dw.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

unit_title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals
title: Obtaining Formulas in Triple Integrals for Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates
snippet: Obtaining Formulas in Triple Integrals for Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates: Derive the formula in triple integrals for cylindrical and spherical coordinates. For cylindrical coordinates, the transformation is T\left( {r,\theta,z}...
body_xml:
<example number="5.72" title="Obtaining Formulas in Triple Integrals for Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Derive the formula in triple integrals for</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>cylindrical and</item>
        <item>spherical coordinates.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>For cylindrical coordinates, the transformation is $$T\left( {r,\theta,z} \right) = \left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ from the Cartesian $$r\theta z \text{-plane}$$ to the Cartesian $$xyz \text{-plane}$$ (Figure 5.81). Here $$x = r \cos \theta,$$ $$y = r \sin \theta,$$ and $$z = z.$$ The Jacobian for the transformation is $$\begin{array}{cl} {J\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)} & {= \frac{\partial\left( {x,y,z} \right)}{\partial\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)} = \left| \begin{array}{lllll} \frac{\partial x}{\partial r} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial r} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial r} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial\theta} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial z} \end{array} \right|} \\ & {= \left| \begin{array}{clcll} {\cos \theta} & & {- r \sin \theta} & & 0 \\ {\sin \theta} & & {r \cos \theta} & & 0 \\ 0 & & 0 & & 1 \end{array} \right| = r \cos^{2}\theta + r \sin^{2}\theta = r\left( {\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta} \right) = r.} \end{array}$$ We know that $$r \geq 0,$$ so $$\left| {J\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)} \right| = r.$$ Then the triple integral is $${\iiint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)dV = {\iiint\limits_{G}{f\left( {r \cos \theta,r \sin \theta,z} \right)}}}}r dr d\theta dz.$$ Figure 5.81 The transformation from rectangular coordinates to cylindrical coordinates can be treated as a change of variables from region $$G$$ in $$r\theta z \text{-space}$$ to region $$D$$ in $$xyz \text{-space} .$$</item>
        <item>For spherical coordinates, the transformation is $$T\left( {\rho,\theta,\varphi} \right) = \left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ from the Cartesian $$p\theta\varphi \text{-plane}$$ to the Cartesian $$xyz \text{-plane}$$ (Figure 5.82). Here $$x = \rho \sin \varphi \cos \theta,$$ $$y = \rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta,$$ and $$z = \rho \cos \varphi.$$ The Jacobian for the transformation is $$J\left( {\rho,\theta,\varphi} \right) = \frac{\partial\left( {x,y,z} \right)}{\partial\left( {\rho,\theta,\varphi} \right)} = \left| \begin{array}{lllll} \frac{\partial x}{\partial\rho} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial\varphi} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial\rho} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial\varphi} \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial\rho} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial\theta} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial\varphi} \end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{clcll} {\sin \varphi \cos \theta} & & {\rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta} & & {\rho \cos \varphi \cos \theta} \\ {\sin \varphi \sin \theta} & & {\rho \sin \varphi \cos \theta} & & {\rho \cos \varphi \sin \theta} \\ {\cos \phi} & & 0 & & {- \rho \sin \varphi} \end{array} \right|.$$ Expanding the determinant with respect to the third row: $$\begin{matrix} \\ \\ {= \cos \varphi\left| \begin{array}{lll} {- \rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta} & & {\rho \cos \varphi \cos \theta} \\ {\rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta} & & {\rho \cos \varphi \sin \theta} \end{array} \right| - \rho \sin \varphi\left| \begin{array}{lll} {\sin \varphi \cos \theta} & & {- \rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta} \\ {\sin \varphi \sin \theta} & & {\rho \sin \varphi \cos \theta} \end{array} \right|} \\ {= \cos \varphi\left( {-\rho^{2}\sin \varphi \cos \varphi \sin^{2}\theta - \rho^{2}\sin \varphi \cos \varphi \cos^{2}\theta} \right)} \\ { - \rho \sin \varphi\left( {\rho \sin^{2}\varphi \cos^{2}\theta + \rho \sin^{2}\varphi \sin^{2}\theta} \right)} \\ {= -\rho^{2}\sin \varphi \cos^{2}\varphi\left( {\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta} \right) - \rho^{2}\sin \varphi \sin^{2}\varphi\left( {\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta} \right)} \\ {= -\rho^{2}\sin \varphi \cos^{2}\varphi - \rho^{2}\sin \varphi \sin^{2}\varphi} \\ {= -\rho^{2}\sin \varphi\left( {\cos^{2}\varphi + \sin^{2}\varphi} \right) = -\rho^{2}\sin \varphi.} \end{matrix}$$ Since $$0 \leq \varphi \leq \pi,$$ we must have $$\sin \varphi \geq 0.$$ Thus $$\left| {J\left( {\rho,\theta,\varphi} \right)} \right| = \left| {-\rho^{2}\sin \varphi} \right| = \rho^{2}\sin \varphi.$$ Figure 5.82 The transformation from rectangular coordinates to spherical coordinates can be treated as a change of variables from region $$G$$ in $$\rho\theta\varphi \text{-space}$$ to region $$D$$ in $$xyz \text{-space} .$$ Then the triple integral becomes $${\iiint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)}}dV = {\iiint\limits_{G}{f\left( {\rho \sin \varphi \cos \theta,\rho \sin \varphi \sin \theta,\rho \cos \varphi} \right)}}\rho^{2}\sin \varphi d\rho d\varphi d\theta.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Evaluating a Triple Integral with a Change of Variables
snippet: Evaluating a Triple Integral with a Change of Variables: Evaluate the triple integral {\int\limits_{0}^{3} {\int\limits_{0}^{4} {\int\limits_{y/2}^{{({y/2})} + 1}\left( {x + \frac{z}{3}} \right)}}}dx dy dz in xyz \text{-space} by using the...
body_xml:
Evaluate the triple integral $${\int\limits_{0}^{3} {\int\limits_{0}^{4} {\int\limits_{y/2}^{{({y/2})} + 1}\left( {x + \frac{z}{3}} \right)}}}dx dy dz$$ in $$xyz \text{-space}$$ by using the transformation $$u = \left( {2x - y} \right)/2,v = y/2, \text{and} w = z/3.$$ Then integrate over an appropriate region in $$uvw \text{-space} .$$ As before, some kind of sketch of the region $$G$$ in $$xyz \text{-space}$$ over which we have to perform the integration can help identify the region $$D$$ in $$uvw \text{-space}$$ (Figure 5.83). Clearly $$G$$ in $$xyz \text{-space}$$ is bounded by the planes $$x = y/2,x = \left( {y/2} \right) + 1,y = 0,$$ $$y = 4,$$ $$z = 0, \text{and} z = 4.$$ We also know that we have to use $$u = \left( {2x - y} \right)/2,v = y/2, \text{and} w = z/3$$ for the transformations. We need to solve for $$x,y, \text{and} z.$$ Here we find that $$x = u + v,$$ $$y = 2v,$$ and $$z = 3w.$$ Using elementary algebra, we can find the corresponding surfaces for the region $$G$$ and the limits of integration in $$uvw \text{-space} .$$ It is convenient to list these equations in a table. Equations in $$xyz$$ for the region $$D$$ Corresponding equations in $$uvw$$ for the region $$G$$ Limits for the integration in $$uvw$$ $$x = y/2$$ $$u + v = 2v/2 = v$$ $$u = 0$$ $$x = y/2$$ $$u + v = \left( {2v/2} \right) + 1 = v + 1$$ $$u = 1$$ $$y = 0$$ $$2v = 0$$ $$v = 0$$ $$y = 4$$ $$2v = 4$$ $$v = 2$$ $$z = 0$$ $$3w = 0$$ $$w = 0$$ $$z = 3$$ $$3w = 3$$ $$w = 1$$
Now we can calculate the Jacobian for the transformation: $$J(u,v,w) = \left| \begin{array}{lclcl} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} & & \frac{\partial x}{\partial w} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} & & \frac{\partial y}{\partial w} \\ \frac{\partial z}{\partial u} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial v} & & \frac{\partial z}{\partial w} \end{array} \right| = \left| \begin{array}{lclcl} 1 & & 1 & & 0 \\ 0 & & 2 & & 0 \\ 0 & & 0 & & 3 \end{array} \right| = 6.$$ The function to be integrated becomes $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x + \frac{z}{3} = u + v + \frac{3w}{3} = u + v + w.$$ We are now ready to put everything together and complete the problem. $$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ \\ \\ { {\int\limits_{0}^{3} {\int\limits_{0}^{4} {\int\limits_{y/2}^{{({y/2})} + 1}\left( {x + \frac{z}{3}} \right)}}}dx dy dz} \\ \\ {= {\int\limits_{0}^{1} {\int\limits_{0}^{2} {\int\limits_{0}^{1}\left( {u + v + w} \right)}}}\left| {J\left( {u,v,w} \right)} \right|du dv dw = {\int\limits_{0}^{1} {\int\limits_{0}^{2} {\int\limits_{0}^{1}\left( {u + v + w} \right)}}}|6|du dv dw} \\ {= 6{\int\limits_{0}^{1} {\int\limits_{0}^{2} {\int\limits_{0}^{1}\left( {u + v + w} \right)}}}du dv dw = 6{\int\limits_{0}^{1} {\int\limits_{0}^{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{u^{2}}{2} + vu + wu} \right\rbrack}}_{0}^{1}dv dw} \\ {= 6{\int\limits_{0}^{1} {\int\limits_{0}^{2}\left( {\frac{1}{2} + v + w} \right)}}dv dw = 6{\int\limits_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}v + \frac{v^{2}}{2} + wv} \right\rbrack}_{0}^{2}dw} \\ {= 6{\int\limits_{0}^{1}\left( {3 + 2w} \right)}dw = 6\left\lbrack {3w + w^{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = 24.} \end{array}$$

body_xml:
Sketch the vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {y,-x} \right\rangle.$$ Create a table (see the one that follows) using a representative sample of points in a plane and their corresponding vectors. Figure 6.6 shows the resulting vector field. $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right)$$ $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right)$$ $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right)$$ $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {0,-1} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {2,0} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {0,-2} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {1,-1} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {1,0} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {2,0} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {-1,1} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {1,1} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {-1,0} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {0,1} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {-2,0} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {0,2} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {-1,-1} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {-1,1} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {0,-1} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {-1,0} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {0,-2} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {-2,0} \right\rangle$$ $$\left( {1,-1} \right)$$ $$\left\langle {-1,-1} \right\rangle$$
Note that vector $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {a,b} \right) = \left\langle {b,-a} \right\rangle$$ points clockwise and is perpendicular to radial vector $$\left\langle {a,b} \right\rangle.$$ (We can verify this assertion by computing the dot product of the two vectors: $$\left\langle {a,b} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {-b,a} \right\rangle = -ab + ab = 0.)$$ Furthermore, vector $$\left\langle {b,-a} \right\rangle$$ has length $$r = \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}.$$ Thus, we have a complete description of this rotational vector field: the vector associated with point $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ is the vector with length r tangent to the circle with radius r, and it points in the clockwise direction. Sketches such as that in Figure 6.6 are often used to analyze major storm systems, including hurricanes and cyclones. In the northern hemisphere, storms rotate counterclockwise; in the southern hemisphere, storms rotate clockwise. (This is an effect caused by Earth’s rotation about its axis and is called the Coriolis Effect.)

How fast is the fluid moving at point $$\left( {1,-1} \right)?$$ (Assume the units of speed are meters per second.)</paragraph>
    </problem>

      <paragraph>To find the velocity of the fluid at point $$\left( {1,-1} \right),$$ substitute the point into v:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{v} }\left( {1,-1} \right) = - \frac{2(-1)}{1 + 1}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \frac{2(1)}{1 + 1}\mathbf{ \text{j} } = \mathbf{ \text{i} } + \mathbf{ \text{j} }.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The speed of the fluid at $$\left( {1,-1} \right)$$ is the magnitude of this vector. Therefore, the speed is $$\left| \middle| \left. \mathbf{ \text{i} } + \mathbf{ \text{j} } \right| \right| = \sqrt{2}$$ m/sec.</paragraph>

body_xml: Describe vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {1,1,z} \right\rangle.$$ For this vector field, the x and y components are constant, so every point in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ has an associated vector with x and y components equal to one. To visualize F, we first consider what the field looks like in the xy-plane. In the xy-plane, $$z = 0.$$ Hence, each point of the form $$\left( {a,b,0} \right)$$ has vector $$\left\langle {1,1,0} \right\rangle$$ associated with it. For points not in the xy-plane but slightly above it, the associated vector has a small but positive z component, and therefore the associated vector points slightly upward. For points that are far above the xy-plane, the z component is large, so the vector is almost vertical. Figure 6.7 shows this vector field.

title: Describing a Gravitational Vector Field
snippet: Describing a Gravitational Vector Field: Newton’s law of gravitation states that \mathbf{ \text{F} } = -G\frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\mathbf{\hat{r}}, where G is the universal gravitational constant. It describes the gravitational field...
body_xml: Newton’s law of gravitation states that $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = -G\frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\mathbf{\hat{r}},$$ where G is the universal gravitational constant. It describes the gravitational field exerted by an object (object 1) of mass $$m_{1}$$ located at the origin on another object (object 2) of mass $$m_{2}$$ located at point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right).$$ Field F denotes the gravitational force that object 1 exerts on object 2, r is the distance between the two objects, and $$\mathbf{\hat{r}}$$ indicates the unit vector from the first object to the second. The minus sign shows that the gravitational force attracts toward the origin; that is, the force of object 1 is attractive. Sketch the vector field associated with this equation. Since object 1 is located at the origin, the distance between the objects is given by $$r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}.$$ The unit vector from object 1 to object 2 is $$\mathbf{\hat{r}} = \frac{\left\langle {x,y,z} \right\rangle}{\left| \left| \left\langle {x,y,z} \right\rangle \right| \right|},$$ and hence $$\mathbf{\hat{r}} = \left\langle {\frac{x}{r},\frac{y}{r},\frac{z}{r}} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore, gravitational vector field F exerted by object 1 on object 2 is $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = -Gm_{1}m_{2}\left\langle {\frac{x}{r^{3}},\frac{y}{r^{3}},\frac{z}{r^{3}}} \right\rangle.$$ This is an example of a radial vector field in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}.$$ Figure 6.8 shows what this gravitational field looks like for a large mass at the origin. Note that the magnitudes of the vectors increase as the vectors get closer to the origin.

<example title="Checkpoint" number="6.7">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The mass of asteroid 1 is 750,000 kg and the mass of asteroid 2 is 130,000 kg. Assume asteroid 1 is located at the origin, and asteroid 2 is located at $$\left( {15,-5,10} \right),$$ measured in units of 10 to the eighth power kilometers. Given that the universal gravitational constant is $$G = 6.67384 \times 10^{-11}{ \text{m} }^{3} \text{kg} ^{-1} \text{s} ^{-2},$$ find the gravitational force vector that asteroid 1 exerts on asteroid 2.</paragraph>

title: The Cross-Partial Property of Conservative Vector Fields
snippet: The Cross-Partial Property of Conservative Vector Fields: The Cross-Partial Property of Conservative Vector Fields Let F be a vector field in two or three dimensions such that the component functions of F have continuous first-order...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="6.2" title="The Cross-Partial Property of Conservative Vector Fields">
    <heading level="4">The Cross-Partial Property of Conservative Vector Fields</heading>
    <paragraph>Let F be a vector field in two or three dimensions such that the component functions of F have continuous first-order partial derivatives on the domain of F.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {P(x,y),Q(x,y)} \right\rangle$$ is a conservative vector field in $$\mathbb{R}^{2},$$ then $$\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}.$$ If $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {P\left( {x,y,z} \right),Q\left( {x,y,z} \right),R\left( {x,y,z} \right)} \right\rangle$$ is a conservative vector field in $$\mathbb{R}^{3},$$ then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x},\frac{\partial Q}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial R}{\partial y}, \text{and} \frac{\partial R}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial z}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Showing a Vector Field Is Not Conservative
snippet: Showing a Vector Field Is Not Conservative: Show that rotational vector field \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {y,-x} \right\rangle is not conservative. Let P\left( {x,y} \right) = y \text{and} Q\left( {x,y} \right) =...

<example number="6.12" title="Showing a Vector Field Is Not Conservative">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Show that rotational vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {y,-x} \right\rangle$$ is not conservative.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$P\left( {x,y} \right) = y \text{and} Q\left( {x,y} \right) = -x.$$ If F is conservative, then the cross-partials would be equal—that is, $$P_{y}$$ would equal $$Q_{x.}$$ Therefore, to show that F is not conservative, check that $$P_{y} \neq Q_{x}.$$ Since $$P_{y} = 1$$ and $$Q_{x} = -1,$$ the vector field is not conservative.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.13" title="Showing a Vector Field Is Not Conservative">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Is vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {7,-2,x^{3}} \right\rangle$$ conservative?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$P(x,y,z) = 7,$$ $$Q(x,y,z) = -2,$$ and $$R(x,y,z) = x^{3}.$$ If F is conservative, then all three cross-partial equations will be satisfied—that is, if F is conservative, then $$P_{y}$$ would equal $$Q_{x},Q_{z}$$ would equal $$R_{y},$$ and $$R_{x}$$ would equal $$P_{z}.$$ Note that $$P_{y} = Q_{x} = R_{y} = Q_{z} = 0,$$ so the first two necessary equalities hold. However, $$R_{x} = 3x^{2}$$ and $$P_{z} = 0$$ so $$R_{x} \neq P_{z}.$$ Therefore, $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }$$ is not conservative.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a function with a domain that includes the smooth curve $$C$$ that is parameterized by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {x(t),y(t),z(t)} \right\rangle,$$ $$a \leq t \leq b.$$ The scalar line integral of $$f$$ along $$C$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{C}{f(x,y,z)ds = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( P_{i}^{*} \right) \text{Δ} s_{i}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>if this limit exists $$(t_{i}^{*}$$ and $$\text{Δ} s_{i}$$ are defined as in the previous paragraphs). If C is a planar curve, then C can be represented by the parametric equations $$x = x(t),y = y(t),$$ and $$a \leq t \leq b.$$ If C is smooth and $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is a function of two variables, then the scalar line integral of $$f$$ along C is defined similarly as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{C}{f(x,y)ds = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( P_{i}^{*} \right) \text{Δ} s_{i}}},$$</paragraph>

title: Finding the Value of a Line Integral
snippet: Finding the Value of a Line Integral: Find the value of integral \int_{C}{2ds,} where C is the upper half of the unit circle. The integrand is f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2. Figure 6.14 shows the graph of f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2, curve C,...
body_xml: Find the value of integral $$\int_{C}{2ds,}$$ where $$C$$ is the upper half of the unit circle. The integrand is $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2.$$ Figure 6.14 shows the graph of $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2,$$ curve C, and the sheet formed by them. Notice that this sheet has the same area as a rectangle with width $$\pi$$ and length 2. Therefore, $$\int_{C}{2ds = 2\pi.}$$ To see that $$\int_{C}{2ds = 2\pi}$$ using the definition of line integral, we let $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)$$ be a parameterization of C. Then, $$f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( t_{i} \right)} \right) = 2$$ for any number $$t_{i}$$ in the domain of r. Therefore, $$\begin{matrix} {\int_{C}fds} & {= \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}f\left( \textbf{r}\left( t_{i}^{*} \right) \right) \text{Δ} s_{i}} \\ & {= \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}2 \text{Δ} s_{i}} \\ & {= 2\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n} \text{Δ} s_{i}} \\ & {= 2\left( \text{length of C} \right)} \\ & {= 2\pi.} \end{matrix}$$

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="6.4" title="Scalar Line Integral Calculation">
    <heading level="4">Scalar Line Integral Calculation</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a continuous function with a domain that includes the smooth curve C with parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {x(t),y(t),z(t)} \right\rangle,a \leq t \leq b.$$ Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)ds = {\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} \right)\sqrt{\left( {x^{\prime}(t)} \right)^{2} + \left( {y^{\prime}(t)} \right)^{2} + \left( {z^{\prime}(t)} \right)^{2}}}}dt.}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Similarly,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y} \right)ds = {\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} \right)\sqrt{\left( {x^{\prime}(t)} \right)^{2} + \left( {y^{\prime}(t)} \right)^{2}}}}dt}$$</paragraph>

title: Evaluating a Line Integral
snippet: Evaluating a Line Integral: Find the value of integral \int_{C}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z} \right)ds,} where C is part of the helix parameterized by \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {\cos t,\sin t,t} \right\rangle, 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi....
body_xml:
<example number="6.15" title="Evaluating a Line Integral">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the value of integral $$\int_{C}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z} \right)ds,}$$ where $$C$$ is part of the helix parameterized by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {\cos t,\sin t,t} \right\rangle,$$ $$0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To compute a scalar line integral, we start by converting the variable of integration from arc length s to t. Then, we can use Equation 6.8 to compute the integral with respect to t. Note that $$f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} \right) = \cos^{2}t + \sin^{2}t + t = 1 + t$$ and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \sqrt{\left( {x^{\prime}(t)} \right)^{2} + \left( {y^{\prime}(t)} \right)^{2} + \left( {z^{\prime}(t)} \right)^{2}} & {= \sqrt{\left( {-\sin (t)} \right)^{2} + \cos^{2}(t) + 1}} \\ & {= \sqrt{2}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{C}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z} \right)ds = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left( {1 + t} \right)\sqrt{2}dt.}}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that Equation 6.8 translated the original difficult line integral into a manageable single-variable integral. Since</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left( {1 + t} \right)}\sqrt{2}dt} & {= \left\lbrack {\sqrt{2}t + \frac{\sqrt{2}t^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}} \\ & {= 2\sqrt{2}\pi + 2\sqrt{2}\pi^{2},} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{C}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z} \right)ds = 2\sqrt{2}\pi + 2\sqrt{2}\pi^{2}}}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>
