title: Independence of Parameterization
snippet: Independence of Parameterization: Find the value of integral \int_{C}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z} \right)ds,} where C is part of the helix parameterized by \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {\cos \left( {2t} \right),\sin \left( {2t}...
body_xml:
<example number="6.16" title="Independence of Parameterization">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the value of integral $$\int_{C}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z} \right)ds,}$$ where $$C$$ is part of the helix parameterized by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {\cos \left( {2t} \right),\sin \left( {2t} \right),2t} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq \pi.$$ Notice that this function and curve are the same as in the previous example; the only difference is that the curve has been reparameterized so that time runs twice as fast.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>As with the previous example, we use Equation 6.8 to compute the integral with respect to t. Note that $$f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} \right) = \cos^{2}\left( {2t} \right) + \sin^{2}\left( {2t} \right) + 2t = 2t + 1$$ and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} \sqrt{\left( x^{'}(t) \right)^{2} + \left( y^{'}(t) \right)^{2} + \left( z'(t) \right)^{2}} & {= \sqrt{\left( { \text{−2sin} \left( { \text{2} t} \right)} \right)^{2} + \left( {2\cos \left( { \text{2} t} \right)} \right)^{2} + 2^{2}}} \\ & \sqrt{4\sin^{2}\left( {2t} \right) + 4\cos^{2}\left( {2t} \right) + 4} \\ & {= 2\sqrt{2}} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>so we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z} \right)ds}} & {= 2\sqrt{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\left( {1 + 2t} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= 2\sqrt{2}\left\lbrack {t + t^{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi}} \\ & {= 2\sqrt{2}\left( {\pi + \pi^{2}} \right).} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that this agrees with the answer in the previous example. Changing the parameterization did not change the value of the line integral. Scalar line integrals are independent of parameterization, as long as the curve is traversed exactly once by the parameterization.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.17" title="Calculating Arc Length">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A wire has a shape that can be modeled with the parameterization $$\textbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \cos t,\sin t,\frac{2}{3}t^{3/2} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 4\pi.$$ Find the length of the wire.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The length of the wire is given by $${\int_{C}{1ds}},$$ where C is the curve with parameterization r. Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \text{The length of the wire} & {= {\int_{C}{1ds}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4\pi}{\left\| {\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t)} \right\| dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4\pi}{\sqrt{\left( {-\sin t} \right)^{2} + \cos^{2}t + t}dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4\pi}{\sqrt{1 + t}dt}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack \frac{2\left( {1 + t} \right)^{3/2}}{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{4\pi}} \\ & {= \frac{2}{3}\left( {\left( {1 + 4\pi} \right)^{3/2} - 1} \right).} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

We then have $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }(\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)) = \left\langle {-\sin t,\cos t} \right\rangle \text{and} \mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = \left\langle {-\sin t,\cos t} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{C}\mathbf{ \text{F} }} \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }} & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\left\langle {-\sin t,\cos t} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {-\sin t,\cos t} \right\rangle dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin^{2}t}} + \cos^{2}tdt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi}{1dt}} = \pi.} \end{array}$$ See Figure 6.18.

<example number="6.19" title="Reversing Orientation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the value of integral $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} },}$$ where $$C$$ is the semicircle parameterized by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {\cos (t + \pi),\sin t} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq \pi$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {-y,x} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Notice that this is the same problem as Example 6.18, except the orientation of the curve has been traversed. In this example, the parameterization starts at $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(0) = \left\langle {-1,0} \right\rangle$$ and ends at $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(\pi) = \left\langle {1,0} \right\rangle.$$ By Equation 6.9,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{C}\mathbf{ \text{F} }} \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }} & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\left\langle {-\sin t,\cos (t + \pi)} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {-\sin (t + \pi),\cos t} \right\rangle dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\left\langle {-\sin t,-\cos t} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {\sin t,\cos t} \right\rangle dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\left( {-\sin^{2}t - \cos^{2}t} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi}{-1dt}}} \\ & {= -\pi.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that this is the negative of the answer in Example 6.18. It makes sense that this answer is negative because the orientation of the curve goes against the “flow” of the vector field.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Properties of Vector Line Integrals
snippet: Properties of Vector Line Integrals: Properties of Vector Line Integrals Let F and G be continuous vector fields with domains that include the oriented smooth curve C. Then {\int_{C}{(\mathbf{ \text{F} } + \mathbf{ \text{G} }) \cdot...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="6.5" title="Properties of Vector Line Integrals">
    <heading level="4">Properties of Vector Line Integrals</heading>
    <paragraph>Let F and G be continuous vector fields with domains that include the oriented smooth curve C. Then</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$${\int_{C}{(\mathbf{ \text{F} } + \mathbf{ \text{G} }) \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} = {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} + {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{G} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}$$</item>
      <item>$${\int_{C}{k\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} = k{\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} },}}$$ where k is a constant</item>
      <item>$${\int_{-C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} } =}}{-\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}$$</item>
      <item>Suppose instead that C is a piecewise smooth curve in the domains of F and G, where $$C = C_{1} + C_{2} + \cdots + C_{n}$$ and $$C_{1},C_{2} \text{,…} ,C_{n}$$ are smooth curves such that the endpoint of $$C_{i}$$ is the starting point of $$C_{i + 1}.$$ Then $$\int_{C}\textbf{F} \cdot d\textbf{r} = \int_{C_{1}}\textbf{F} \cdot d\textbf{r} + \int_{C_{2}}\textbf{F} \cdot d\textbf{r} + \cdots + \int_{C_{n}}\textbf{F} \cdot d\textbf{r}.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Using Properties to Compute a Vector Line Integral
snippet: Using Properties to Compute a Vector Line Integral: Find the value of integral {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }}}ds, where C is the rectangle (oriented counterclockwise) in a plane with vertices \left( {0,0}...
body_xml: Find the value of integral $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }}}ds,$$ where C is the rectangle (oriented counterclockwise) in a plane with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right),\left( {2,0} \right),\left( {2,1} \right), \text{and} \left( {0,1} \right),$$ and where $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {x - 2y,y - x} \right\rangle$$ (Figure 6.20). Note that curve C is the union of its four sides, and each side is smooth. Therefore C is piecewise smooth. Let $$C_{1}$$ represent the side from $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {2,0} \right),$$ let $$C_{2}$$ represent the side from $$\left( {2,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {2,1} \right),$$ let $$C_{3}$$ represent the side from $$\left( {2,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,1} \right),$$ and let $$C_{4}$$ represent the side from $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ (Figure 6.20). Then, $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} = {\int_{C_{1}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} + {\int_{C_{2}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} + {\int_{C_{3}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} + {\int_{C_{4}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}.$$ We want to compute each of the four integrals on the right-hand side using Equation 6.8. Before doing this, we need a parameterization of each side of the rectangle. Here are four parameterizations (note that they traverse C counterclockwise): $$\begin{array}{l} {C_{1}:\left\langle {t,0} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 2} \\ {C_{2}:\left\langle {2,t} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 1} \\ {C_{3}:\left\langle {2 - t,1} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 2} \\ {C_{4}:\left\langle {0,1 - t} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 1.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, $$\begin{matrix} {\int_{C_{1}}\textbf{F} \cdot \textbf{T}d\textbf{r}} & {= \int_{0}^{2}\textbf{F}\left( \textbf{r}(t) \right) \cdot \mathbf{r}^{'}(t)dt} \\ & {= \int_{0}^{2}\left\langle t - 2(0),0 - t \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle 1,0 \right\rangle dt = \int_{0}^{2}tdt} \\ & {= \left\lbrack \frac{t^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = 2.} \end{matrix}$$ Notice that the value of this integral is positive, which should not be surprising. As we move along curve C1 from left to right, our movement flows in the general direction of the vector field itself. At any point along C1, the tangent vector to the curve and the corresponding vector in the field form an angle that is less than 90°. Therefore, the tangent vector and the force vector have a positive dot product all along C1, and the line integral will have positive value. The calculations for the three other line integrals are done similarly: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C_{2}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} & {= {\int_{0}^{1}\left\langle {2 - 2t,t - 2} \right\rangle} \cdot \left\langle {0,1} \right\rangle dt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {t - 2} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{t^{2}}{2} - 2t} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = - \frac{3}{2},} \end{array}$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C_{3}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }ds}} & {= {\int_{0}^{2}\left\langle {(2 - t) - 2,1 - (2 - t)} \right\rangle} \cdot \left\langle {-1,0} \right\rangle dt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2}{tdt}} = 2,} \end{array}$$ and $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C_{4}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} & {= {\int_{0}^{1}\left\langle {-2(1 - t),1 - t} \right\rangle} \cdot \left\langle {0,-1} \right\rangle dt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {t - 1} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{t^{2}}{2} - t} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = - \frac{1}{2}.} \end{array}$$ Thus, we have $${\int_{C}\mathbf{ \text{F} }} \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} } = 2.$$

snippet: Calculating the Mass of a Wire: Calculate the mass of a spring in the shape of a curve parameterized by \left\langle {t,2 \cos t,2 \sin t} \right\rangle, 0 \leq t \leq \frac{\pi}{2}, with a density function given by \rho(x,y,z) = e^{x} +...
body_xml: Calculate the mass of a spring in the shape of a curve parameterized by $$\left\langle {t,2 \cos t,2 \sin t} \right\rangle,$$ $$0 \leq t \leq \frac{\pi}{2},$$ with a density function given by $$\rho(x,y,z) = e^{x} + yz$$ kg/m (Figure 6.21). To calculate the mass of the spring, we must find the value of the scalar line integral $${\int_{C}{\left( {e^{x} + yz} \right)ds}},$$ where C is the given helix. To calculate this integral, we write it in terms of t using Equation 6.8: $$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{C}e^{x}} + yzds} & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\left( {\left( {e^{t} + 4 \cos t \sin t} \right)\sqrt{1 + \left( {-2 \cos t} \right)^{2} + \left( {2 \sin t} \right)^{2}}} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\left( {\left( {e^{t} + 4 \cos t \sin t} \right)\sqrt{5}} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{5}\left\lbrack {e^{t} + 2 \sin^{2}t} \right\rbrack_{t = 0}^{t = \pi/2}} \\ & {= \sqrt{5}\left( {e^{\pi/2} + 1} \right).} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the mass is $$\sqrt{5}\left( {e^{\pi/2} + 1} \right)$$ kg.

Let C denote the given path. We need to find the value of $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}.$$ To do this, we use Equation 6.9: $$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{C}\mathbf{ \text{F} }} \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }} & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {\left\langle {t^{5},t^{3},t^{6}} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {2t,1,4t^{3}} \right\rangle} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {2t^{6} + t^{3} + 4t^{9}} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{2t^{7}}{7} + \frac{t^{4}}{4} + \frac{2t^{10}}{5}} \right\rbrack_{t = 0}^{t = 1} = \frac{131}{140}.} \end{array}$$

snippet: Flux across a Curve: Calculate the flux of \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {2x,2y} \right\rangle across a unit circle oriented counterclockwise (Figure 6.24). To compute the flux, we first need a parameterization of the unit circle. We...
body_xml: Calculate the flux of $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {2x,2y} \right\rangle$$ across a unit circle oriented counterclockwise (Figure 6.24). To compute the flux, we first need a parameterization of the unit circle. We can use the standard parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {\cos t,\sin t} \right\rangle,$$ $$0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.$$ The normal vector to a unit circle is $$\left\langle {\cos t,\sin t} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore, the flux is $$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }}}ds} & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left\langle {2 \cos t,2 \sin t} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {\cos t,\sin t} \right\rangle}} dt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left( {2 \cos^{2}t + 2 \sin^{2}t} \right)} dt = 2{\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left( {\cos^{2}t + \sin^{2}t} \right)} dt} \\ & {= 2{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{dt}} = 4\pi.} \end{array}$$

snippet: Calculating Circulation: Let \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle - y,x \right\rangle be the vector field from Example 6.16 and let C represent the unit circle oriented counterclockwise. Calculate the circulation of F along C. We use the...

<example number="6.25" title="Calculating Circulation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle - y,x \right\rangle$$ be the vector field from Example 6.16 and let C represent the unit circle oriented counterclockwise. Calculate the circulation of F along C.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We use the standard parameterization of the unit circle: $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {\cos t,\sin t} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.$$ Then, $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} \right) = \left\langle {-\sin t,\cos t} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = \left\langle {-\sin t,\cos t} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore, the circulation of F along C is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{C}\mathbf{ \text{F} }} \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }ds} & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left\langle {-\sin t,\cos t} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {-\sin t,\cos t} \right\rangle dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left( {\sin^{2}t + \cos^{2}t} \right)} dt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{dt}} = 2\pi.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that the circulation is positive. The reason for this is that the orientation of C “flows” with the direction of F. At any point along the circle, the tangent vector and the vector from F form an angle of less than 90°, and therefore the corresponding dot product is positive.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The work done by F on the particle is the circulation of F along C: $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }ds}}.$$ We use the parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {2 \cos t,2 \sin t} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 2\pi$$ for C. Then, $$\mathbf{r^{\prime}}(t) = \left\langle {-2 \sin t,2 \cos t} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} \right) = \left\langle {-2,2 \sin t} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore, the circulation of F along C is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{T} }ds} & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left\langle {-2,2 \sin t} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {-2 \sin t,2 \cos t} \right\rangle dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left( {4 \sin t + 4 \sin t \cos t} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {-4 \cos t + 4 \sin^{2}t} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}} \\ & {= \left( {-4 \cos (2\pi) + 2 \sin^{2}(2\pi)} \right) - \left( {-4 \cos (0) + 4 \sin^{2}(0)} \right)} \\ & {= -4 + 4 = 0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The force field does zero work on the particle.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that the circulation of F along C is zero. Furthermore, notice that since F is the gradient of $$f(x,y) = -2x + \frac{y^{2}}{2},$$ F is conservative. We prove in a later section that under certain broad conditions, the circulation of a conservative vector field along a closed curve is zero.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Curve C is a closed curve if there is a parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t),a \leq t \leq b$$ of C such that the parameterization traverses the curve exactly once and $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(a) = \mathbf{ \text{r} }(b).$$ Curve C is a simple curve if C does not cross itself. That is, C is simple if there exists a parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t),a \leq t \leq b$$ of C such that r is one-to-one over $$\left( {a,b} \right).$$ It is possible for $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(a) = \mathbf{ \text{r} }(b),$$ meaning that the simple curve is also closed.</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Determining Whether a Curve Is Simple and Closed: Is the curve with parameterization \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {\cos t,\frac{\sin (2t)}{2}} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 2\pi a simple closed curve? Note that \mathbf{ \text{r}...
body_xml: Is the curve with parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {\cos t,\frac{\sin (2t)}{2}} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 2\pi$$ a simple closed curve? Note that $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(0) = \left\langle {1,0} \right\rangle = \mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {2\pi} \right);$$ therefore, the curve is closed. The curve is not simple, however. To see this, note that $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = \left\langle {0,0} \right\rangle = \mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( \frac{3\pi}{2} \right),$$ and therefore the curve crosses itself at the origin (Figure 6.26).

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>A region D is a connected region if, for any two points $$P_{1}$$ and $$P_{2},$$ there is a path from $$P_{1}$$ to $$P_{2}$$ with a trace contained entirely inside D. A region D is a simply connected region if D is connected for any simple closed curve C that lies inside D, and curve C can be shrunk continuously to a point while staying entirely inside D. In two dimensions, a region is simply connected if it is connected and has no holes.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Evaluating a Line Integral and the Antiderivatives of the Endpoints
snippet: Evaluating a Line Integral and the Antiderivatives of the Endpoints: Let \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {2x,4y} \right\rangle. Calculate \int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} },} where C is the line...
body_xml: Let $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {2x,4y} \right\rangle.$$ Calculate $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} },}$$ where C is the line segment from (0,0) to (2,2)(Figure 6.28). We use Equation 6.9 to calculate $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }.}$$ Curve C can be parameterized by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {2t,2t} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 1.$$ Then, $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)} \right) = \left\langle {4t,8t} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }^{\prime}(t) = \left\langle {2,2} \right\rangle,$$ which implies that $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} & {= {\int_{0}^{1}\left\langle {4t,8t} \right\rangle} \cdot \left\langle {2,2} \right\rangle dt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{(8t + 16t)}}dt = {\int_{0}^{1}{24t dt}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {12t^{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = 12.} \end{array}$$ Notice that $$F = \text{∇} f,$$ where $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} + 2y^{2}.$$ If we think of the gradient as a derivative, then $$f$$ is an “antiderivative” of F. In the case of single-variable integrals, the integral of derivative $$g^{\prime}(x)$$ is $$g(b) - g(a),$$ where a is the start point of the interval of integration and b is the endpoint. If vector line integrals work like single-variable integrals, then we would expect integral F to be $$f\left( P_{1} \right) - f\left( P_{0} \right),$$ where $$P_{1}$$ is the endpoint of the curve of integration and $$P_{0}$$ is the start point. Notice that this is the case for this example: $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} } = {\int_{C}{ \text{∇} f.d\mathbf{ \text{r} } = 12}}}$$ and $$f\left( {2,2} \right) - f\left( {0,0} \right) = 4 + 8 - 0 = 12.$$ In other words, the integral of a “derivative” can be calculated by evaluating an “antiderivative” at the endpoints of the curve and subtracting, just as for single-variable integrals.

title: The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals
snippet: The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals: The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals Let C be a piecewise smooth curve with parameterization \mathbf{ \text{r} }(t),a \leq t \leq b. Let f be a function of two or three variables with...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="6.7" title="The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals">
    <heading level="4">The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals</heading>
    <paragraph>Let C be a piecewise smooth curve with parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t),a \leq t \leq b.$$ Let $$f$$ be a function of two or three variables with first-order partial derivatives that exist and are continuous on C. Then,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{C}{ \text{∇} f.d\mathbf{ \text{r} } = f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(b)} \right) - f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(a)} \right).}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Applying the Fundamental Theorem
snippet: Applying the Fundamental Theorem: Calculate integral \int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} },} where \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {2x \ln y,\frac{x^{2}}{y} + z^{2},2yz} \right\rangle and C is a...
body_xml:
<example number="6.29" title="Applying the Fundamental Theorem">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate integral $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} },}$$ where $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {2x \ln y,\frac{x^{2}}{y} + z^{2},2yz} \right\rangle$$ and C is a curve with parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {t^{2},t,t} \right\rangle,1 \leq t \leq e$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>without using the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals and</item>
        <item>using the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>First, let’s calculate the integral without the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals and instead use Equation 6.9: $$\begin{matrix} {\int_{C}\textbf{F} \cdot d\textbf{r}} & {= \int_{1}^{e}\textbf{F}\left( \textbf{r}(t) \right).\textbf{r}^{'}(t)dt} \\ & {= \int_{1}^{e}\left\langle 2t^{2}\ln t,\frac{t^{4}}{t} + t^{2},2t^{2} \right\rangle.\left\langle 2t,1,1 \right\rangle dt} \\ & {= \int_{1}^{e}\left( 4t^{3}\ln t + t^{3} + 3t^{2} \right)dt} \\ & {= \int_{1}^{e}4t^{3}\ln tdt + \int_{1}^{e}\left( t^{3} + 3t^{2} \right)dt} \\ & {= \int_{1}^{e}4t^{3}\ln tdt + \left\lbrack \frac{t^{4}}{4} + t^{3} \right\rbrack_{1}^{e}} \\ & {= 2\int_{1}^{e}t^{3}\ln tdt + \frac{e^{4}}{4} + e^{3} - \frac{5}{4}.} \end{matrix}$$ Integral $$\int_{1}^{e}{t^{3}\ln tdt}$$ requires integration by parts. Let $$u = \ln t$$ and $$dv = t^{3}.$$ Then $$u = \ln t,dv = t^{3}$$ and $$du = \frac{1}{t}dt,v = \frac{t^{4}}{4}.$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{1}^{e}{t^{3}\ln tdt}} & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{t^{4}}{4}\ln t} \right\rbrack_{1}^{e} - \frac{1}{4}{\int_{1}^{e}{t^{3}dt}}} \\ & {= \frac{e^{4}}{4} - \frac{1}{4}\left( {\frac{e^{4}}{4} - \frac{1}{4}} \right).} \end{array}$$ Thus, $$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{C}\mathbf{ \text{F} }} \cdot dr} & {= 4{\int_{1}^{e}{t^{3}\ln tdt + \frac{e^{4}}{4} + e^{3} - \frac{5}{4}}}} \\ & {= 4\left( {\frac{e^{4}}{4} - \frac{1}{4}\left( {\frac{e^{4}}{4} - \frac{1}{4}} \right)} \right) + \frac{e^{4}}{4} + e^{3} - \frac{5}{4}} \\ & {= e^{4} - \frac{e^{4}}{4} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{e^{4}}{4} + e^{3} - \frac{5}{4}} \\ & {= e^{4} + e^{3} - 1.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>Given that $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}\ln y + yz^{2}$$ is a potential function for F, let’s use the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals to calculate the integral. Note that $$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{C}\mathbf{ \text{F} }} \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }} & {= {\int_{C}{ \text{∇} f.d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}} \\ & {= f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(e)} \right) - f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(1)} \right)} \\ & {= f\left( {e^{2},e,e} \right) - f\left( {1,1,1} \right)} \\ & {= e^{4} + e^{3} - 1.} \end{array}$$ This calculation is much more straightforward than the calculation we did in (a). As long as we have a potential function, calculating a line integral using the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals is much easier than calculating without the theorem.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Showing That a Vector Field Is Not Conservative
snippet: Showing That a Vector Field Is Not Conservative: Use path independence to show that vector field \mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {x^{2}y,y + 5} \right\rangle is not conservative. We can indicate that F is not conservative by...
body_xml: Use path independence to show that vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {x^{2}y,y + 5} \right\rangle$$ is not conservative. We can indicate that F is not conservative by showing that F is not path independent. We do so by giving two different paths, $$C_{1}$$ and $$C_{2},$$ that both start at $$(0,0)$$ and end at $$(1,1),$$ and yet $${\int_{C_{1}}\mathbf{ \text{F} }} \cdot dr \neq {\int_{C_{2}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }.}}$$ Let $$C_{1}$$ be the curve with parameterization $$\textbf{r}_{1}(t) = \left\langle {t,t} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 1$$ and let $$C_{2}$$ be the curve with parameterization $$\textbf{r}_{2}(t) = \left\langle {t,t^{2}} \right\rangle,0 \leq t \leq 1$$ (Figure 6.31). Then $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C_{1}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\textbf{r}}} & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {\textbf{r}_{1}(t)} \right) \cdot \textbf{r}_{1}{}^{\prime}(t)dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\left\langle {t^{3},t + 5} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {1,1} \right\rangle dt}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {t^{3} + t + 5} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{t^{4}}{4} + \frac{t^{2}}{2} + 5t} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{23}{4}} \end{array}$$ and $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C_{2}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\textbf{r}}} & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {\textbf{r}_{2}(t)} \right) \cdot \textbf{r}_{2}\prime(t)dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\left\langle {t^{4},t^{2} + 5} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {1,2t} \right\rangle dt}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {t^{4} + 2t^{3} + 10t} \right)dt}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{t^{5}}{5} + \frac{t^{4}}{2} + 5t^{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{57}{10}.} \end{array}$$ Since $${\int_{C_{1}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} \neq {\int_{C_{2}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} },}}$$ the value of a line integral of F depends on the path between two given points. Therefore, F is not independent of path, and F is not conservative.

title: Finding a Potential Function
snippet: Finding a Potential Function: Find a potential function for \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {2xy^{3},3x^{2}y^{2} + \cos (y)} \right\rangle, thereby showing that F is conservative. Suppose that f(x,y) is a potential...
body_xml:
<example number="6.31" title="Finding a Potential Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find a potential function for $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {2xy^{3},3x^{2}y^{2} + \cos (y)} \right\rangle,$$ thereby showing that F is conservative.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Suppose that $$f(x,y)$$ is a potential function for F. Then, $$\text{∇} f = \mathbf{ \text{F} },$$ and therefore</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f_{x} = 2xy^{3} \text{and} f_{y} = 3x^{2}y^{2} + \cos y.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Integrating the equation $$f_{x} = 2xy^{3}$$ with respect to x yields the equation</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f(x,y) = x^{2}y^{3} + h(y).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that since we are integrating a two-variable function with respect to x, we must add a constant of integration that is a constant with respect to x, but may still be a function of y. The equation $$f(x,y) = x^{2}y^{3} + h(y)$$ can be confirmed by taking the partial derivative with respect to x:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {x^{2}y^{3}} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {h(y)} \right) = 2xy^{3} + 0 = 2xy^{3}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$f$$ is a potential function for F,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f_{y} = 3x^{2}y^{2} + \cos (y),$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and therefore</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$3x^{2}y^{2} + h^{\prime}(y) = 3x^{2}y^{2} + \cos (y).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This implies that $$h\prime(y) = \cos y,$$ so $$h(y) = \sin y + C.$$ Therefore, any function of the form $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2}y^{3} + \sin (y) + C$$ is a potential function. Taking, in particular, $$C = 0$$ gives the potential function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2}y^{3} + \sin (y).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To verify that $$f$$ is a potential function, note that $$\text{∇} f = \left\langle {2xy^{3},3x^{2}y^{2} + \cos y} \right\rangle = \mathbf{ \text{F} }.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="procedure" source_type="Problem-Solving Strategy" title="Problem-Solving Strategy">
    <heading level="4">Problem-Solving Strategy: Finding a Potential Function for a Conservative Vector Field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {P\left( {x,y} \right),Q\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\rangle$$</heading>
    <list type="ordered">

      <item>Take the partial derivative of $$g\left( {x,y} \right) + h(y)$$ with respect to y, which results in the function $$g_{y}\left( {x,y} \right) + h^{\prime}(y).$$</item>
      <item>Use the equation $$g_{y}\left( {x,y} \right) + h^{\prime}(y) = Q\left( {x,y} \right)$$ to find $$h^{\prime}(y).$$</item>
      <item>Integrate $$h^{\prime}(y)$$ to find $$h(y).$$</item>
      <item>Any function of the form $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = g\left( {x,y} \right) + h(y) + C,$$ where C is a constant, is a potential function for F.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

<example number="6.32" title="Finding a Potential Function in ℝ3ℝ3">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find a potential function for $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {2xy,x^{2} + 2yz^{3},3y^{2}z^{2} + 2z} \right\rangle,$$ thereby showing that $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }$$ is conservative.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Suppose that $$f$$ is a potential function. Then, $$\text{∇} f = \mathbf{ \text{F} }$$ and therefore $$f_{x} = 2xy.$$ Integrating this equation with respect to x yields the equation $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}y + g\left( {y,z} \right)$$ for some function g. Notice that, in this case, the constant of integration with respect to x is a function of y and z.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$f$$ is a potential function,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x^{2} + 2yz^{3} = f_{y} = x^{2} + g_{y}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$g_{y} = 2yz^{3}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Integrating this function with respect to y yields</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$g\left( {y,z} \right) = y^{2}z^{3} + h(z)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>for some function $$h(z)$$ of z alone. (Notice that, because we know that g is a function of only y and z, we do not need to write $$g\left( {y,z} \right) = y^{2}z^{3} + h\left( {x,z} \right).)$$ Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}y + g\left( {y,z} \right) = x^{2}y + y^{2}z^{3} + h(z).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To find $$f$$ , we now must only find h. Since $$f$$ is a potential function,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$3y^{2}z^{2} + 2z = g_{z} = 3y^{2}z^{2} + h^{\prime}(z).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This implies that $$h^{\prime}(z) = 2z,$$ so $$h(z) = z^{2} + C.$$ Letting $$C = 0$$ gives the potential function</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}y + y^{2}z^{3} + z^{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To verify that $$f$$ is a potential function, note that $$\text{∇} f = \left\langle {2xy,x^{2} + 2yz^{3},3y^{2}z^{2} + 2z} \right\rangle = \mathbf{ \text{F} }.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.33" title="Finding a Potential Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find a potential function $$f$$ for $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = -G\left\langle {\frac{x}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}},\frac{y}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Suppose that $$f$$ is a potential function. Then, $$\text{∇} f = \mathbf{ \text{F} }$$ and therefore</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f_{x} = \frac{-Gx}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To integrate this function with respect to x, we can use u-substitution. If $$u = x^{2} + y^{2},$$ then $$\frac{du}{2} = xdx,$$ so</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int\frac{-Gx}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}}dx} & {= {\int\frac{-G}{2u^{3/2}}}du} \\ & {= \frac{G}{\sqrt{u}} + h(y)} \\ & {= \frac{G}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}} + h(y)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>for some function $$h(y).$$ Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f(x,y) = \frac{G}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}} + h(y).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$f$$ is a potential function for F,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f_{y} = \frac{-Gy}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$f(x,y) = \frac{G}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}} + h(y),$$ $$f_{y}$$ also equals $$\frac{-Gy}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}} + h^{\prime}(y).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{-Gy}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}} + h\prime(y) = \frac{-Gy}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}},$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>which implies that $$h^{\prime}(y) = 0.$$ Thus, we can take $$h(y)$$ to be any constant; in particular, we can let $$h(y) = 0.$$ The function</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{G}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>is a potential function for the gravitational field F. To confirm that $$f$$ is a potential function, note that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} { \text{∇} f} & {= \left\langle {- \frac{1}{2} \frac{G}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}\left( {2x} \right), - \frac{1}{2} \frac{G}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}\left( {2y} \right)} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \left\langle {\frac{-Gx}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}},\frac{-Gy}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \mathbf{ \text{F} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.34" title="Determining Whether a Vector Field Is Conservative">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {xy^{2}z,x^{2}yz,z^{2}} \right\rangle$$ is conservative.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Note that the domain of F is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ and $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ is simply connected. Therefore, we can use Cross-Partial Property of Conservative Fields to determine whether F is conservative. Let</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xy^{2}z,Q\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz, \text{and} R\left( {x,y,z} \right) = z^{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$Q_{z} = x^{2}y$$ and $$R_{y} = 0,$$ the vector field is not conservative.</paragraph>
    </solution>

<example number="6.35" title="Determining Whether a Vector Field Is Conservative">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {x \ln (y),\frac{x^{2}}{2y}} \right\rangle$$ is conservative.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Note that the domain of F is the part of $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ in which $$y > 0.$$ Thus, the domain of F is part of a plane above the x-axis, and this domain is simply connected (there are no holes in this region and this region is connected). Therefore, we can use Cross-Partial Property of Conservative Fields to determine whether F is conservative. Let</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P\left( {x,y} \right) = x \ln (y) \text{and} Q\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{x^{2}}{2y}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then $$P_{y} = \frac{x}{y} = Q_{x}$$ and thus F is conservative.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals
snippet: Using the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals: Calculate line integral {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\textbf{r}}}, where \mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y,z) = \left\langle {2xe^{y}z + e^{x}z,x^{2}e^{y}z,x^{2}e^{y} + e^{x}} \right\rangle...
body_xml:
<example number="6.36" title="Using the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate line integral $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\textbf{r}}},$$ where $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y,z) = \left\langle {2xe^{y}z + e^{x}z,x^{2}e^{y}z,x^{2}e^{y} + e^{x}} \right\rangle$$ and C is any smooth curve that goes from the origin to $$(1,1,1).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Before trying to compute the integral, we need to determine whether F is conservative and whether the domain of F is simply connected. The domain of F is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{3},$$ which is connected and has no holes. Therefore, the domain of F is simply connected. Let</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P(x,y,z) = 2xe^{y}z + e^{x}z,Q(x,y,z) = x^{2}e^{y}z, \text{and} R(x,y,z) = x^{2}e^{y} + e^{x}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>so that $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q,R} \right\rangle.$$ Since the domain of F is simply connected, we can check the cross partials to determine whether F is conservative. Note that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} P_{y} & = & {2xe^{y}z = Q_{x}} \\ P_{z} & = & {2xe^{y} + e^{x} = R_{x}} \\ Q_{z} & = & {x^{2}e^{y} = R_{y}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, F is conservative.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To evaluate $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\textbf{r}}$$ using the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals, we need to find a potential function $$f$$ for F. Let $$f$$ be a potential function for F. Then, $$\text{∇} f = \mathbf{ \text{F} },$$ and therefore $$f_{x} = 2xe^{y}z + e^{x}z.$$ Integrating this equation with respect to x gives $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}e^{y}z + e^{x}z + h\left( {y,z} \right)$$ for some function h. Differentiating this equation with respect to y gives $$x^{2}e^{y}z + h_{y} = Q = x^{2}e^{y}z,$$ which implies that $$h_{y} = 0.$$ Therefore, h is a function of z only, and $$f(x,y,z) = x^{2}e^{y}z + e^{x}z + h(z).$$ To find h, note that $$f_{z} = x^{2}e^{y} + e^{x} + h\prime(z) = R = x^{2}e^{y} + e^{x}.$$ Therefore, $$h\prime(z) = 0$$ and we can take $$h(z) = 0.$$ A potential function for F is $$f(x,y,z) = x^{2}e^{y}z + e^{x}z.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now that we have a potential function, we can use the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals to evaluate the integral. By the theorem,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} & {= {\int_{C}{ \text{∇} f \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}} \\ & {= f(1,1,1) - f(0,0,0)} \\ & {= 2e.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Notice that if we hadn’t recognized that F is conservative, we would have had to parameterize C and use Equation 6.9. Since curve C is unknown, using the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals is much simpler.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Work Done on a Particle
snippet: Work Done on a Particle: Let \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {2xy^{2},2x^{2}y} \right\rangle be a force field. Suppose that a particle begins its motion at the origin and ends its movement at any point in a plane...
body_xml:
<example number="6.37" title="Work Done on a Particle">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {2xy^{2},2x^{2}y} \right\rangle$$ be a force field. Suppose that a particle begins its motion at the origin and ends its movement at any point in a plane that is not on the x-axis or the y-axis. Furthermore, the particle’s motion can be modeled with a smooth parameterization. Show that F does positive work on the particle.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We show that F does positive work on the particle by showing that F is conservative and then by using the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To show that F is conservative, suppose $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ were a potential function for F. Then, $$\text{∇} f = \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {2xy^{2},2x^{2}y} \right\rangle$$ and therefore $$f_{x} = 2xy^{2}$$ and $$f_{y} = 2x^{2}y.$$ Equation $$f_{x} = 2xy^{2}$$ implies that $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2}y^{2} + h(y).$$ Deriving both sides with respect to y yields $$f_{y} = 2x^{2}y + h^{\prime}(y).$$ Therefore, $$h^{\prime}(y) = 0$$ and we can take $$h(y) = 0.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>If $$f(x,y) = x^{2}y^{2},$$ then note that $$\text{∇} f = \left\langle {2xy^{2},2x^{2}y} \right\rangle = \mathbf{ \text{F} },$$ and therefore $$f$$ is a potential function for F.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let $$(a,b)$$ be the point at which the particle stops is motion, and let C denote the curve that models the particle’s motion. The work done by F on the particle is $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}.$$ By the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} & {= {\int_{C}{ \text{∇} f \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}} \\ & {= f(a,b) - f(0,0)} \\ & {= a^{2}b^{2}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$a \neq 0$$ and $$b \neq 0,$$ by assumption, $$a^{2}b^{2} > 0.$$ Therefore, $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} > 0,$$ and F does positive work on the particle.</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Notice that this problem would be much more difficult without using the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals. To apply the tools we have learned, we would need to give a curve parameterization and use Equation 6.9. Since the path of motion C can be as exotic as we wish (as long as it is smooth), it can be very difficult to parameterize the motion of the particle.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Applying Green’s Theorem over a Rectangle
snippet: Applying Green’s Theorem over a Rectangle: Calculate the line integral {\int_{C}{x^{2}ydx + (y - 3)dy}}, where C is a rectangle with vertices (1,1), (4,1), (4,5), and (1,5) oriented counterclockwise. Let \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y}...
body_xml: Calculate the line integral $${\int_{C}{x^{2}ydx + (y - 3)dy}},$$ where C is a rectangle with vertices $$(1,1),$$ $$(4,1),$$ $$(4,5),$$ and $$(1,5)$$ oriented counterclockwise. Let $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {P\left( {x,y} \right),Q\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\rangle = \left\langle {x^{2}y,y - 3} \right\rangle.$$ Then, $$Q_{x} = 0$$ and $$P_{y} = x^{2}.$$ Therefore, $$Q_{x} - P_{y} = -x^{2}.$$ Let D be the rectangular region enclosed by C (Figure 6.35). By Green’s theorem, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}{x^{2}ydx + (y - 3)dy}} & {= {\iint_{D}{\left( {Q_{x} - P_{y}} \right)dA}}} \\ & {= {\int{\int_{D}{-x^{2}dA}}} = {\int_{1}^{5}{\int_{1}^{4}{-x^{2}dxdy}}}} \\ & {= {\int_{1}^{5}{-21dy}} = -84.} \end{array}$$ If we were to evaluate this line integral without using Green’s theorem, we would need to parameterize each side of the rectangle, break the line integral into four separate line integrals, and use the methods from Line Integrals to evaluate each integral. Furthermore, since the vector field here is not conservative, we cannot apply the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals. Green’s theorem makes the calculation much simpler.

title: Applying Green’s Theorem to Calculate Work
snippet: Applying Green’s Theorem to Calculate Work: Calculate the work done on a particle by force field \mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {y + \sin x,e^{y} - x} \right\rangle as the particle traverses circle x^{2} + y^{2} = 4 exactly once...
body_xml: Calculate the work done on a particle by force field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {y + \sin x,e^{y} - x} \right\rangle$$ as the particle traverses circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ exactly once in the counterclockwise direction, starting and ending at point $$(2,0).$$ Let C denote the circle and let D be the disk enclosed by C. The work done on the particle is $$W = {\int_{C}{\left( {y + \sin x} \right)dx + (e^{y} - x)dy}}.$$ As with Example 6.38, this integral can be calculated using tools we have learned, but it is easier to use the double integral given by Green’s theorem (Figure 6.36). Let $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {P\left( {x,y} \right),Q\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\rangle = \left\langle {y + \sin x,e^{y} - x} \right\rangle.$$ Then, $$Q_{x} = -1$$ and $$P_{y} = 1.$$ Therefore, $$Q_{x} - P_{y} = -2.$$ By Green’s theorem, $$\begin{array}{cl} W & {= {\int_{C}{(y + \sin (x))dx + (e^{y} - x)dy}}} \\ & {= {\iint_{D}{\left( {Q_{x} - P_{y}} \right)dA}} = {\iint_{D}{-2dA}}} \\ & {= -2\left( { \text{area} (D)} \right) = -2\pi\left( 2^{2} \right) = -8\pi.} \end{array}$$

title: Applying Green’s Theorem over an Ellipse
snippet: Applying Green’s Theorem over an Ellipse: Calculate the area enclosed by ellipse \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1 (Figure 6.37). Let C denote the ellipse and let D be the region enclosed by C. Recall that ellipse C can be...
body_xml: Calculate the area enclosed by ellipse $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$ (Figure 6.37). Let C denote the ellipse and let D be the region enclosed by C. Recall that ellipse C can be parameterized by $$x = a \cos t,y = b \sin t,0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.$$ Calculating the area of D is equivalent to computing double integral $${\iint_{D}{dA}}.$$ To calculate this integral without Green’s theorem, we would need to divide D into two regions: the region above the x-axis and the region below. The area of the ellipse is $$\int_{-a}^{a}{\int_{0}^{\sqrt{b^{2} - {({{bx}/a})}^{2}}}{dydx + {\int_{-a}^{a}{\int_{-\sqrt{b^{2} - {({{bx}/a})}^{2}}}^{0}{dydx.}}}}}$$ These two integrals are not straightforward to calculate (although when we know the value of the first integral, we know the value of the second by symmetry). Instead of trying to calculate them, we use Green’s theorem to transform $$\iint_{D}{dA}$$ into a line integral around the boundary C. Consider vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {P,Q} \right\rangle = \left\langle {- \frac{y}{2},\frac{x}{2}} \right\rangle.$$ Then, $$Q_{x} = \frac{1}{2}$$ and $$P_{y} = - \frac{1}{2},$$ and therefore $$Q_{x} - P_{y} = 1.$$ Notice that F was chosen to have the property that $$Q_{x} - P_{y} = 1.$$ Since this is the case, Green’s theorem transforms the line integral of F over C into the double integral of 1 over D. By Green’s theorem, $$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ & \\ {\iint_{D}{dA}} & {= {\iint_{D}{\left( {Q_{x} - P_{y}} \right)dA}}} \\ & {= {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{C}{-ydx + xdy}}} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{-b \sin t(-a \sin t) + a\left( {\cos t} \right)b \cos tdt}}} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{ab \cos^{2}t + ab \sin^{2}tdt}} = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{abdt}} = \pi ab.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the area of the ellipse is $$\pi ab.$$

snippet: Green’s Theorem, Flux Form: Green’s Theorem, Flux Form Let D be an open, simply connected region with a boundary curve C that is a piecewise smooth, simple closed curve that is oriented counterclockwise (Figure 6.38). Let \mathbf{ \text{F}...

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="6.13" title="Green’s Theorem, Flux Form">
    <heading level="4">Green’s Theorem, Flux Form</heading>
    <paragraph>Let D be an open, simply connected region with a boundary curve C that is a piecewise smooth, simple closed curve that is oriented counterclockwise (Figure 6.38). Let $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q} \right\rangle$$ be a vector field with component functions that have continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing D. Then,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }ds = {\iint_{D}{P_{x} + Q_{y}dA}}}}.$$</paragraph>

title: Applying Green’s Theorem for Flux across a Circle
snippet: Applying Green’s Theorem for Flux across a Circle: Let C be a circle of radius r centered at the origin (Figure 6.39) and let \mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {x,y} \right\rangle. Calculate the flux across C. Let D be the disk...
body_xml: Let C be a circle of radius r centered at the origin (Figure 6.39) and let $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {x,y} \right\rangle.$$ Calculate the flux across C. Let D be the disk enclosed by C. The flux across C is $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }ds}}.$$ We could evaluate this integral using tools we have learned, but Green’s theorem makes the calculation much more simple. Let $$P\left( {x,y} \right) = x$$ and $$Q\left( {x,y} \right) = y$$ so that $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q} \right\rangle.$$ Note that $$P_{x} = 1 = Q_{y},$$ and therefore $$P_{x} + Q_{y} = 2.$$ By Green’s theorem, $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }ds = {\int{\int_{D}{2dA =}}}}}2{\int{\int_{D}{dA.}}}$$ Since $$\int{\int_{D}{dA}}$$ is the area of the circle, $${\int{\int_{D}{dA}}} = \pi r^{2}.$$ Therefore, the flux across C is $$2\pi r^{2}.$$

title: Applying Green’s Theorem for Flux across a Triangle
snippet: Applying Green’s Theorem for Flux across a Triangle: Let S be the triangle with vertices (0,0), (1,0), and (0,3) oriented clockwise (Figure 6.40). Calculate the flux of \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {P\left( {x,y}...
body_xml: Let S be the triangle with vertices $$(0,0),$$ $$(1,0),$$ and $$(0,3)$$ oriented clockwise (Figure 6.40). Calculate the flux of $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {P\left( {x,y} \right),Q\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\rangle = \left\langle {x^{2} + e^{y},x + y} \right\rangle$$ across S. To calculate the flux without Green’s theorem, we would need to break the flux integral into three line integrals, one integral for each side of the triangle. Using Green’s theorem to translate the flux line integral into a single double integral is much more simple. Let D be the region enclosed by S. Note that $$P_{x} = 2x$$ and $$Q_{y} = 1;$$ therefore, $$P_{x} + Q_{y} = 2x + 1.$$ Green’s theorem applies only to simple closed curves oriented counterclockwise, but we can still apply the theorem because $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }ds = -}}{\int_{-S}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }ds}}$$ and $$-S$$ is oriented counterclockwise. By Green’s theorem, the flux is $$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ & \\ {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }ds}} & {= {\int_{-S}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }ds}}} \\ & {= -{\iint_{D}{\left( {P_{x} + Q_{y}} \right)dA}}} \\ & {= -{\iint_{D}{\left( {2x + 1} \right)dA}}.} \end{array}$$ Notice that the top edge of the triangle is the line $$y = -3x + 3.$$ Therefore, in the iterated double integral, the y-values run from $$y = 0$$ to $$y = -3x + 3,$$ and we have $$\begin{array}{cl} {-{\iint_{D}{\left( {2x + 1} \right)dA}}} & {= -{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{-3x + 3}{\left( {2x + 1} \right)dydx}}}} \\ & {= -{\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {2x + 1} \right)\left( {-3x + 3} \right)dx}} = -{\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {-6x^{2} + 3x + 3} \right)dx}}} \\ & {= -\left\lbrack {-2x^{3} + \frac{3x^{2}}{2} + 3x} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = - \frac{5}{2}.} \end{array}$$

title: Applying Green’s Theorem for Water Flow across a Rectangle
snippet: Applying Green’s Theorem for Water Flow across a Rectangle: Water flows from a spring located at the origin. The velocity of the water is modeled by vector field \mathbf{ \text{v} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {5x + y,x + 3y}...
body_xml: Water flows from a spring located at the origin. The velocity of the water is modeled by vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {5x + y,x + 3y} \right\rangle$$ m/sec. Find the amount of water per second that flows across the rectangle with vertices $$\left( {-1,-2} \right),\left( {1,-2} \right),\left( {1,3} \right), \text{and} \left( {-1,3} \right),$$ oriented counterclockwise (Figure 6.41). Let C represent the given rectangle and let D be the rectangular region enclosed by C. To find the amount of water flowing across C, we calculate flux $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} {ds}}.}$$ Let $$P\left( {x,y} \right) = 5x + y$$ and $$Q\left( {x,y} \right) = x + 3y$$ so that $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left( {P,Q} \right).$$ Then, $$P_{x} = 5$$ and $$Q_{y} = 3.$$ By Green’s theorem, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} {ds}}}} & {= {\iint_{D}{\left( {P_{x} + Q_{y}} \right)dA}}} \\ & {= {\iint_{D}{8dA}}} \\ & {= 8\left( { \text{area of} D} \right) = 80.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the water flux is 80 m2/sec.

title: Finding a Stream Function
snippet: Finding a Stream Function: Verify that rotation vector field \mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {y,-x} \right\rangle is source free, and find a stream function for F. Note that the domain of F is all of \mathbb{R}^{2}, which is simply...
body_xml: Verify that rotation vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {y,-x} \right\rangle$$ is source free, and find a stream function for F. Note that the domain of F is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{2},$$ which is simply connected. Therefore, to show that F is source free, we can show any of items 1 through 4 from the previous list to be true. In this example, we show that item 4 is true. Let $$P\left( {x,y} \right) = y$$ and $$Q\left( {x,y} \right) = -x.$$ Then $$P_{x} + 0 = Q_{y},$$ and therefore $$P_{x} + Q_{y} = 0.$$ Thus, F is source free. To find a stream function for F, proceed in the same manner as finding a potential function for a conservative field. Let g be a stream function for F. Then $$g_{y} = y,$$ which implies that $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{y^{2}}{2} + h(x).$$ Since $$-g_{x} = Q = -x,$$ we have $$h \text{'} (x) = x.$$ Therefore, $$h(x) = \frac{x^{2}}{2} + C.$$ Letting $$C = 0$$ gives stream function $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{y^{2}}{2}.$$ To confirm that g is a stream function for F, note that $$g_{y} = y = P$$ and $$-g_{x} = -x = Q.$$ Notice that source-free rotation vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }(x,y) = \left\langle {y,-x} \right\rangle$$ is perpendicular to conservative radial vector field $$\text{∇} g = \left\langle {x,y} \right\rangle$$ (Figure 6.42).

title: Satisfying Laplace’s Equation
snippet: Satisfying Laplace’s Equation: For vector field \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {e^{x}\sin y,e^{x}\cos y} \right\rangle, verify that the field is both conservative and source free, find a potential function for F,...
body_xml:
<example number="6.45" title="Satisfying Laplace’s Equation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {e^{x}\sin y,e^{x}\cos y} \right\rangle,$$ verify that the field is both conservative and source free, find a potential function for F, and verify that the potential function is harmonic.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$P\left( {x,y} \right) = e^{x}\sin y$$ and $$Q\left( {x,y} \right) = e^{x}\cos y.$$ Notice that the domain of F is all of two-space, which is simply connected. Therefore, we can check the cross-partials of F to determine whether F is conservative. Note that $$P_{y} = e^{x}\cos y = Q_{x},$$ so F is conservative. Since $$P_{x} = e^{x}\sin y$$ and $$Q_{y} = - e^{x}\sin y,P_{x} + Q_{y} = 0$$ and the field is source free.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To find a potential function for F, let $$f$$ be a potential function. Then, $$\text{∇} f = \mathbf{ \text{F} },$$ so $$f_{x} = e^{x}\sin y.$$ Integrating this equation with respect to x gives $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = e^{x}\sin y + h(y).$$ Since $$f_{y} = e^{x}\cos y,$$ differentiating $$f$$ with respect to y gives $$e^{x}\cos y = e^{x}\cos y + h \text{'} (y).$$ Therefore, we can take $$h(y) = 0,$$ and $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = e^{x}\sin y$$ is a potential function for $$f.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To verify that $$f$$ is a harmonic function, note that $$f_{xx} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {e^{x}\sin y} \right) = e^{x}\sin y$$ and</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$f_{yy} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {e^{x}\cos y} \right) = -e^{x}\sin y.$$ Therefore, $$f_{xx} + f_{yy} = 0,$$ and $$f$$ satisfies Laplace’s equation.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Green’s Theorem on a Region with Holes
snippet: Using Green’s Theorem on a Region with Holes: Calculate integral \oint_{\partial D}\left( \sin \text{x} - \frac{y^{3}}{3} \right)dx + \left( \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \sin \text{y} \right)dy, where D is the annulus given by the polar inequalities...
body_xml:
<example number="6.46" title="Using Green’s Theorem on a Region with Holes">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate integral</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\oint_{\partial D}\left( \sin \text{x} - \frac{y^{3}}{3} \right)dx + \left( \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \sin \text{y} \right)dy,$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>where D is the annulus given by the polar inequalities $$1 \leq \mathbf{ \text{r} } \leq 2,$$ $$0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Although D is not simply connected, we can use the extended form of Green’s theorem to calculate the integral. Since the integration occurs over an annulus, we convert to polar coordinates:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{\partial D}{\left( {\sin x - \frac{y^{3}}{3}} \right)dx + \left( {\frac{x^{3}}{3} + \sin y} \right)dy}} & {= {\iint_{D}{\left( {Q_{x} - P_{y}} \right)dA}}} \\ & {= {\iint_{D}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)dA}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{1}^{2}{r^{3}drd\theta}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\frac{15}{4}d\theta}}} \\ & {= \frac{15\pi}{2}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using the Extended Form of Green’s Theorem
snippet: Using the Extended Form of Green’s Theorem: Let \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q} \right\rangle = \left\langle {\frac{y}{x^{2} + y^{2}}, - \frac{x}{x^{2} + y^{2}}} \right\rangle and let C be any simple closed curve in a plane...
body_xml: Let $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q} \right\rangle = \left\langle {\frac{y}{x^{2} + y^{2}}, - \frac{x}{x^{2} + y^{2}}} \right\rangle$$ and let C be any simple closed curve in a plane oriented counterclockwise. What are the possible values of $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }?}$$ We use the extended form of Green’s theorem to show that $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}$$ is either 0 or $$-2\pi$$ —that is, no matter how crazy curve C is, the line integral of F along C can have only one of two possible values. We consider two cases: the case when C encompasses the origin and the case when C does not encompass the origin. Case 1: C Does Not Encompass the Origin In this case, the region enclosed by C is simply connected because the only hole in the domain of F is at the origin. We showed in our discussion of cross-partials that F satisfies the cross-partial condition. If we restrict the domain of F just to C and the region it encloses, then F with this restricted domain is now defined on a simply connected domain. Since F satisfies the cross-partial property on its restricted domain, the field F is conservative on this simply connected region and hence the circulation $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}$$ is zero. Case 2: C Does Encompass the Origin In this case, the region enclosed by C is not simply connected because this region contains a hole at the origin. Let $$C_{1}$$ be a circle of radius a centered at the origin so that $$C_{1}$$ is entirely inside the region enclosed by C (Figure 6.46). Give $$C_{1}$$ a clockwise orientation. Let D be the region between $$C_{1}$$ and C, and C is orientated counterclockwise. By the extended version of Green’s theorem, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} } + {\int_{C_{1}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}}} & {= \left. \iint{}_{D}{Q_{x} - P_{y}dA} \right.} \\ & {= {\iint_{D}{- \frac{y^{2} - x^{2}}{{(x^{2} + y^{2})}^{2}} +}}\frac{y^{2} - x^{2}}{{(x^{2} + y^{2})}^{2}}dA} \\ & {= 0,} \end{array}$$ and therefore $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} } =}} - {\int_{C_{1}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }.}}$$ Since $$C_{1}$$ is a specific curve, we can evaluate $${\int_{C_{1}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}}.$$ Let $$x = a \cos t,y = {-a} \sin t,0 \leq t \leq 2\pi$$ be a parameterization of $$C_{1}.$$ Then, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C_{1}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\mathbf{ \text{F} }(\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t)) \cdot \mathbf{ \text{r} } \text{'} (t)dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left\langle {- \frac{\sin (t)}{a}, - \frac{\cos (t)}{a}} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {-a \sin (t),-a \cos (t)} \right\rangle dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sin^{2}(t) + \cos^{2}(t)dt}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{dt}} = 2\pi.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} } =}} - 2\pi.$$

title: Calculating Divergence at a Point
snippet: Calculating Divergence at a Point: If \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = e^{x}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + yz\mathbf{ \text{j} } - yz^{2}\mathbf{ \text{k} }, then find the divergence of F at \left( {0,2,-1} \right). The divergence of F...
body_xml:
<example number="6.48" title="Calculating Divergence at a Point">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>If $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = e^{x}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + yz\mathbf{ \text{j} } - yz^{2}\mathbf{ \text{k} },$$ then find the divergence of F at $$\left( {0,2,-1} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The divergence of F is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( e^{x} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {yz} \right) - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left( {yz^{2}} \right) = e^{x} + z - 2yz.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the divergence at $$\left( {0,2,-1} \right)$$ is $$e^{0} - 1 + 4 = 4.$$ If F represents the velocity of a fluid, then more fluid is flowing out than flowing in at point $$\left( {0,2,-1} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determining Whether a Field Is Magnetic
snippet: Determining Whether a Field Is Magnetic: Is it possible for \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {x^{2}y,y - xy^{2}} \right\rangle to be a magnetic field? If F were magnetic, then its divergence would be zero. The...
body_xml: Is it possible for $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {x^{2}y,y - xy^{2}} \right\rangle$$ to be a magnetic field? If F were magnetic, then its divergence would be zero. The divergence of F is $$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {x^{2}y} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {y - xy^{2}} \right) = 2xy + 1 - 2xy = 1$$ and therefore F cannot model a magnetic field (Figure 6.52).

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="6.15" title="Divergence Test for Source-Free Vector Fields">
    <heading level="4">Divergence Test for Source-Free Vector Fields</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q} \right\rangle$$ be a continuous vector field with differentiable component functions with a domain that is simply connected. Then, $$\text{div} \mathbf{ \text{F} } = 0$$ if and only if F is source free.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Determining Whether a Field Is Source Free
snippet: Determining Whether a Field Is Source Free: Is field \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {x^{2}y,5 - xy^{2}} \right\rangle source free? Note the domain of F is \mathbb{R}^{2}, which is simply connected. Furthermore, F is...
body_xml:
<example number="6.50" title="Determining Whether a Field Is Source Free">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Is field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {x^{2}y,5 - xy^{2}} \right\rangle$$ source free?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Note the domain of F is $$\mathbb{R}^{2},$$ which is simply connected. Furthermore, F is continuous with differentiable component functions. Therefore, we can use Divergence Test for Source-Free Vector Fields to analyze F. The divergence of F is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {x^{2}y} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {5 - xy^{2}} \right) = 2xy - 2xy = 0.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, F is source free by Divergence Test for Source-Free Vector Fields.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Determining Flow of a Fluid
snippet: Determining Flow of a Fluid: Suppose \mathbf{ \text{v} }(x,y) = \left\langle {-xy,y} \right\rangle,y > 0 models the flow of a fluid. Is more fluid flowing into point (1,4) than flowing out? To determine whether more fluid is flowing into...
body_xml: Suppose $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }(x,y) = \left\langle {-xy,y} \right\rangle,y > 0$$ models the flow of a fluid. Is more fluid flowing into point $$(1,4)$$ than flowing out? To determine whether more fluid is flowing into $$(1,4)$$ than is flowing out, we calculate the divergence of v at $${(1,4)}:$$ $$\text{div} \left( \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {-xy} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y) = -y + 1.$$ To find the divergence at $$(1,4),$$ substitute the point into the divergence: $$-4 + 1 = -3.$$ Since the divergence of v at $$(1,4)$$ is negative, more fluid is flowing in than flowing out (Figure 6.53).

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: If \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q,R} \right\rangle is a vector field in \mathbb{R}^{3}, and P_{x}, P_{y}, P_{z}, Q_{y}, Q_{x}, Q_{z}, R_{z}, R_{x}, {and} R_{y} all exist, then the curl of F is defined by...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>If $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q,R} \right\rangle$$ is a vector field in $$\mathbb{R}^{3},$$ and $$P_{x}, P_{y}, P_{z}, Q_{y}, Q_{x}, Q_{z}, R_{z}, R_{x}, {and} R_{y}$$ all exist, then the curl of F is defined by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} { \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} }} & {= \left( {R_{y} - Q_{z}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {P_{z} - R_{x}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {Q_{x} - P_{y}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= \left( {\frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial R}{\partial x}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note that the curl of a vector field is a vector field, in contrast to divergence.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding the Curl of a Three-Dimensional Vector Field
snippet: Finding the Curl of a Three-Dimensional Vector Field: Find the curl of \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {P,Q,R} \right) = \left\langle {x^{2}z,e^{y} + xz,xyz} \right\rangle. The curl is \begin{array}{cl} { \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} }} & {=...
body_xml:
<example number="6.52" title="Finding the Curl of a Three-Dimensional Vector Field">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the curl of $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {P,Q,R} \right) = \left\langle {x^{2}z,e^{y} + xz,xyz} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The curl is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} { \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} }} & {= \nabla \times \mathbf{ \text{F} }} \\ & {= \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ {\partial/{\partial x}} & {\partial/{\partial y}} & {\partial/{\partial z}} \\ P & Q & R \end{matrix} \right|} \\ & {= \left( {R_{y} - Q_{z}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {P_{z} - R_{x}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {Q_{x} - P_{y}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= \left( {xz - x} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {x^{2} - yz} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + z\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Curl of a Two-Dimensional Vector Field
snippet: Finding the Curl of a Two-Dimensional Vector Field: Find the curl of \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q} \right\rangle = \left\langle {y,0} \right\rangle. Notice that this vector field consists of vectors that are all parallel. In...
body_xml: Find the curl of $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {P,Q} \right\rangle = \left\langle {y,0} \right\rangle.$$ Notice that this vector field consists of vectors that are all parallel. In fact, each vector in the field is parallel to the x-axis. This fact might lead us to the conclusion that the field has no spin and that the curl is zero. To test this theory, note that $$\text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left( {Q_{x} - P_{y}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} } = -\mathbf{ \text{k} } \neq 0.$$ Therefore, this vector field does have spin. To see why, imagine placing a paddlewheel at any point in the first quadrant (Figure 6.55). The larger magnitudes of the vectors at the top of the wheel cause the wheel to rotate. The wheel rotates in the clockwise (negative) direction, causing the coefficient of the curl to be negative.

title: Determining the Spin of a Gravitational Field
snippet: Determining the Spin of a Gravitational Field: Show that a gravitational field has no spin. To show that F has no spin, we calculate its curl. Let P(x,y,z) = \frac{x}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}, Q(x,y,z) =...
body_xml:
<example number="6.54" title="Determining the Spin of a Gravitational Field">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Show that a gravitational field has no spin.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To show that F has no spin, we calculate its curl. Let $$P(x,y,z) = \frac{x}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{3/2}},$$ $$Q(x,y,z) = \frac{y}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{3/2}},$$ and $$R(x,y,z) = \frac{z}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}.$$ Then,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} { \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} }} & {= -Gm_{1}m_{2}\left\lbrack {\left( {R_{y} - Q_{z}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {P_{z} - R_{x}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {Q_{x} - P_{y}} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= -Gm_{1}m_{2}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {\left( {\frac{-3yz}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{5/2}} - \left( \frac{-3yz}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{5/2}} \right)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} }} \\ {+ \left( {\frac{-3xz}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{5/2}} - \left( \frac{-3xz}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{5/2}} \right)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ {+ \left( {\frac{-3xy}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{5/2}} - \left( \frac{-3xy}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{5/2}} \right)} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \end{array} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= 0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since the curl of the gravitational field is zero, the field has no spin.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

Then, $$\text{div} \text{curl} \left( \mathbf{ \text{F} } \right) = \nabla \cdot \left( {\nabla \times \mathbf{ \text{F} }} \right) = 0.$$</paragraph>

title: Showing That a Vector Field Is Not the Curl of Another
snippet: Showing That a Vector Field Is Not the Curl of Another: Show that \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = e^{x}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + yz\mathbf{ \text{j} } + xz^{2}\mathbf{ \text{k} } is not the curl of another vector field. That is,...
body_xml:
<example number="6.55" title="Showing That a Vector Field Is Not the Curl of Another">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Show that $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = e^{x}\mathbf{ \text{i} } + yz\mathbf{ \text{j} } + xz^{2}\mathbf{ \text{k} }$$ is not the curl of another vector field. That is, show that there is no other vector G with $$\text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{G} } = \mathbf{ \text{F} }.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Notice that the domain of F is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ and the second-order partials of F are all continuous. Therefore, we can apply the previous theorem to F.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The divergence of F is $$e^{x} + z + 2xz.$$ If F were the curl of vector field G, then $$\text{div} \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \text{div curl} \mathbf{ \text{G} } = 0.$$ But, the divergence of F is not zero, and therefore F is not the curl of any other vector field.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Testing Whether a Vector Field Is Conservative
snippet: Testing Whether a Vector Field Is Conservative: Use the curl to determine whether \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {yz,xz,xy} \right\rangle is conservative. Note that the domain of F is all of \mathbb{R}^{3}, which...
body_xml: Use the curl to determine whether $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {yz,xz,xy} \right\rangle$$ is conservative. Note that the domain of F is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{3},$$ which is simply connected (Figure 6.56). Therefore, we can test whether F is conservative by calculating its curl. The curl of F is $$\left( {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}xy - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}xz} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}yz - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}xy} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}xz - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}yz} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} } = \left( {x - x} \right)\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left( {y - y} \right)\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left( {z - z} \right)\mathbf{ \text{k} } = 0.$$ Thus, F is conservative.

    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>If $$f$$ were such a potential function, then $$f$$ would be harmonic. Note that $$f_{xx} = 2$$ and $$f_{yy} = 0,$$ and so $$f_{xx} + f_{yy} \neq 0.$$ Therefore, $$f$$ is not harmonic and $$f$$ cannot represent an electrostatic potential.</paragraph>
    </solution>

title: Parameterizing a Cylinder
snippet: Parameterizing a Cylinder: Describe surface S parameterized by \mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {u,v} \right) = \left\langle {\cos u,\sin u,v} \right\rangle,-\infty < u < \infty,-\infty < v < \infty. To get an idea of the shape of the surface, we...
body_xml: Describe surface S parameterized by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {u,v} \right) = \left\langle {\cos u,\sin u,v} \right\rangle,-\infty < u < \infty,-\infty < v < \infty.$$ To get an idea of the shape of the surface, we first plot some points. Since the parameter domain is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{2},$$ we can choose any value for u and v and plot the corresponding point. If $$u = v = 0,$$ then $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {0,0} \right) = \left\langle {1,0,0} \right\rangle,$$ so point (1, 0, 0) is on S. Similarly, points $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {\pi,2} \right) = \left( {-1,0,2} \right)$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {\frac{\pi}{2},4} \right) = \left( {0,1,4} \right)$$ are on S. Although plotting points may give us an idea of the shape of the surface, we usually need quite a few points to see the shape. Since it is time-consuming to plot dozens or hundreds of points, we use another strategy. To visualize S, we visualize two families of curves that lie on S. In the first family of curves we hold u constant; in the second family of curves we hold v constant. This allows us to build a “skeleton” of the surface, thereby getting an idea of its shape. First, suppose that u is a constant K. Then the curve traced out by the parameterization is $$\left\langle {\cos K,\sin K,v} \right\rangle,$$ which gives a vertical line that goes through point $$\left( {\cos K,\sin K,v} \right)$$ in the xy-plane. Now suppose that v is a constant K. Then the curve traced out by the parameterization is $$\left\langle {\cos u,\sin u,K} \right\rangle,$$ which gives a circle in plane $$z = K$$ with radius 1 and center (0, 0, K). If u is held constant, then we get vertical lines; if v is held constant, then we get circles of radius 1 centered around the vertical line that goes through the origin. Therefore the surface traced out by the parameterization is cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ (Figure 6.57). Notice that if $$x = \cos u$$ and $$y = \sin u,$$ then $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1,$$ so points from S do indeed lie on the cylinder. Conversely, each point on the cylinder is contained in some circle $$\left\langle {\cos u,\sin u,k} \right\rangle$$ for some k, and therefore each point on the cylinder is contained in the parameterized surface (Figure 6.58). Notice that if we change the parameter domain, we could get a different surface. For example, if we restricted the domain to $$0 \leq u \leq \pi,0 < v < 6,$$ then the surface would be a half-cylinder of height 6.
