title: Describing a Surface
snippet: Describing a Surface: Describe surface S parameterized by \mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {u \cos v,u \sin v,u^{2}} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < \infty,0 \leq v < 2\pi. Notice that if u is held constant, then the resulting curve is a...
body_xml: Describe surface S parameterized by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {u \cos v,u \sin v,u^{2}} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < \infty,0 \leq v < 2\pi.$$ Notice that if u is held constant, then the resulting curve is a circle of radius u in plane $$z = u^{2}.$$ Therefore, as u increases, the radius of the resulting circle increases. If v is held constant, then the resulting curve is a vertical parabola. Therefore, we expect the surface to be an elliptic paraboloid. To confirm this, notice that $$\begin{array}{cl} {x^{2} + y^{2}} & {= \left( {u \cos v} \right)^{2} + \left( {u \sin v} \right)^{2}} \\ & {= u^{2}\cos^{2}v + u^{2}\sin^{2}v} \\ & {= u^{2}} \\ & {= z.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the surface is elliptic paraboloid $$x^{2} + y^{2} = z$$ (Figure 6.59).

title: Finding a Parameterization
snippet: Finding a Parameterization: Give a parameterization of the cone x^{2} + y^{2} = z^{2} lying on or above the plane z = -2. The horizontal cross-section of the cone at height z = u is circle x^{2} + y^{2} = u^{2}. Therefore, a point on the...
body_xml: Give a parameterization of the cone $$x^{2} + y^{2} = z^{2}$$ lying on or above the plane $$z = -2.$$ The horizontal cross-section of the cone at height $$z = u$$ is circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = u^{2}.$$ Therefore, a point on the cone at height u has coordinates $$\left( {u \cos v,u \sin v,u} \right)$$ for angle v. Hence, a parameterization of the cone is $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {u \cos v,u \sin v,u} \right\rangle.$$ Since we are not interested in the entire cone, only the portion on or above plane $$z = -2,$$ the parameter domain is given by $$-2 \leq u < \infty,0 \leq v < 2\pi$$ (Figure 6.60).

title: Identifying Smooth and Nonsmooth Surfaces
snippet: Identifying Smooth and Nonsmooth Surfaces: Which of the figures in Figure 6.64 is smooth? The surface in Figure 6.64(a) can be parameterized by \mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {(2 + \cos v)\cos u,(2 + \cos v)\sin u,\sin v}...
body_xml: Which of the figures in Figure 6.64 is smooth? The surface in Figure 6.64(a) can be parameterized by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {(2 + \cos v)\cos u,(2 + \cos v)\sin u,\sin v} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < 2\pi,0 \leq v < 2\pi$$ (we can use technology to verify). Notice that vectors $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }_{u} = \left\langle {-(2 + \cos v)\sin u,(2 + \cos v)\cos u,0} \right\rangle \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{r} }_{v} = \left\langle {-\sin v \cos u,-\sin v \sin u,\cos v} \right\rangle$$ exist for any choice of u and v in the parameter domain, and $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{r} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{r} }_{v}} & {= \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ {-(2 + \cos v)\sin u} & {(2 + \cos v)\cos u} & 0 \\ {-\sin v \cos u} & {-\sin v \sin u} & {\cos v} \end{matrix} \right|} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {(2 + \cos v)\cos u \cos v} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {(2 + \cos v)\sin u \cos v} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} }} \\ & { + \left\lbrack {(2 + \cos v)\sin v \sin^{2}u + (2 + \cos v)\sin v \cos^{2}u} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{k} }} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {(2 + \cos v)\cos u \cos v} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{i} } + \left\lbrack {(2 + \cos v)\sin u \cos v} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{j} } + \left\lbrack {(2 + \cos v)\sin v} \right\rbrack\mathbf{ \text{k} }.} \end{array}$$ The k component of this vector is zero only if $$v = 0$$ or $$v = \pi.$$ If $$v = 0$$ or $$v = \pi,$$ then the only choices for u that make the j component zero are $$u = 0$$ or $$u = \pi.$$ But, these choices of u do not make the i component zero. Therefore, $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{r} }_{v}$$ is not zero for any choice of u and v in the parameter domain, and the parameterization is smooth. Notice that the corresponding surface has no sharp corners. In the pyramid in Figure 6.64(b), the sharpness of the corners ensures that directional derivatives do not exist at those locations. Therefore, the pyramid has no smooth parameterization. However, the pyramid consists of five smooth faces, and thus this surface is piecewise smooth.

title: Calculating Surface Area
snippet: Calculating Surface Area: Calculate the lateral surface area (the area of the “side,” not including the base) of the right circular cone with height h and radius r. Before calculating the surface area of this cone using Equation 6.18, we...
body_xml: Calculate the lateral surface area (the area of the “side,” not including the base) of the right circular cone with height h and radius r. Before calculating the surface area of this cone using Equation 6.18, we need a parameterization. We assume this cone is in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ with its vertex at the origin (Figure 6.68). To obtain a parameterization, let $$\alpha$$ be the angle that is swept out by starting at the positive z-axis and ending at the cone, and let $$k = \tan \alpha.$$ For a height value v with $$0 \leq v \leq h,$$ the radius of the circle formed by intersecting the cone with plane $$z = v$$ is $$kv.$$ Therefore, a parameterization of this cone is $$\mathbf{ \text{s} }(u,v) = \left\langle {kv \cos u,kv \sin u,v} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < 2\pi,0 \leq v \leq h.$$ The idea behind this parameterization is that for a fixed v value, the circle swept out by letting u vary is the circle at height v and radius kv. As v increases, the parameterization sweeps out a “stack” of circles, resulting in the desired cone. With a parameterization in hand, we can calculate the surface area of the cone using Equation 6.18. The tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {-kv \sin u,kv \cos u,0} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {k \cos u,k \sin u,1} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} & {= \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ {-kv \sin u} & {kv \cos u} & 0 \\ {k \cos u} & {k \sin u} & 1 \end{matrix} \right|} \\ & {= \left\langle {kv \cos u,kv \sin u,-k^{2}v \sin^{2}u - k^{2}v \cos^{2}u} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \left\langle {kv \cos u,kv \sin u,-k^{2}v} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$ The magnitude of this vector is $$\begin{array}{cl} \left\| \left\langle {kv \cos u,kv \sin u,-k^{2}v} \right\rangle \right\| & {= \sqrt{k^{2}v^{2}\cos^{2}u + k^{2}v^{2}\sin^{2}u + k^{4}v^{2}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{k^{2}v^{2} + k^{4}v^{2}}} \\ & {= kv\sqrt{1 + k^{2}}.} \end{array}$$ By Equation 6.18, the surface area of the cone is $$\begin{array}{cl} {\iint_{D}{\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} \right\| dA}} & {= {\int_{0}^{h}{{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{kv\sqrt{1 + k^{2}}}}dudv}}} \\ & {= 2\pi k\sqrt{1 + k^{2}}{\int_{0}^{h}{vdv}}} \\ & {= 2\pi k\sqrt{1 + k^{2}}\left\lbrack \frac{v^{2}}{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{h}} \\ & {= \pi kh^{2}\sqrt{1 + k^{2}}.} \end{array}$$ Since $$k = \tan \alpha = r/h,$$ $$\begin{array}{cl} {\pi kh^{2}\sqrt{1 + k^{2}}} & {= \pi\frac{r}{h}h^{2}\sqrt{1 + \frac{r^{2}}{h^{2}}}} \\ & {= \pi rh\sqrt{1 + \frac{r^{2}}{h^{2}}}} \\ & {= \pi r\sqrt{h^{2} + h^{2}\left( \frac{r^{2}}{h^{2}} \right)}} \\ & {= \pi r\sqrt{h^{2} + r^{2}}.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the lateral surface area of the cone is $$\pi r\sqrt{h^{2} + r^{2}}.$$ The surface area of a right circular cone with radius r and height h is usually given as $$\pi r^{2} + \pi r\sqrt{h^{2} + r^{2}}.$$ The reason for this is that the circular base is included as part of the cone, and therefore the area of the base $$\pi r^{2}$$ is added to the lateral surface area $$\pi r\sqrt{h^{2} + r^{2}}$$ that we found.

snippet: Calculating Surface Area: Show that the surface area of the sphere x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = r^{2} is 4\pi r^{2}. The sphere has parameterization \left\langle {r \cos \theta \sin \phi,r \sin \theta \sin \phi,r \cos \phi} \right\rangle,0 \leq...
body_xml:
<example number="6.63" title="Calculating Surface Area">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Show that the surface area of the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = r^{2}$$ is $$4\pi r^{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The sphere has parameterization</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\langle {r \cos \theta \sin \phi,r \sin \theta \sin \phi,r \cos \phi} \right\rangle,0 \leq \theta < 2\pi,0 \leq \phi \leq \pi.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The tangent vectors are</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta} = \left\langle {-r \sin \theta \sin \phi,r \cos \theta \sin \phi,0} \right\rangle \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi} = \left\langle {r \cos \theta \cos \phi,r \sin \theta \cos \phi,-r \sin \phi} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta}} & {= \left\langle {r^{2}\cos \theta \sin^{2}\phi,r^{2}\sin \theta \sin^{2}\phi,r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta \sin \phi \cos \phi + r^{2}\cos^{2}\theta \sin \phi \cos \phi} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \left\langle {r^{2}\cos \theta \sin^{2}\phi,r^{2}\sin \theta \sin^{2}\phi,r^{2}\sin \phi \cos \phi} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \left. \left\| {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta}} \right. \right\| & {= \sqrt{r^{4}\sin^{4}\phi \cos^{2}\theta + r^{4}\sin^{4}\phi \sin^{2}\theta + r^{4}\sin^{2}\phi \cos^{2}\phi}} \\ & {= \sqrt{r^{4}\sin^{4}\phi + r^{4}\sin^{2}\phi \cos^{2}\phi}} \\ & {= r^{2}\sqrt{\sin^{2}\phi}} \\ & {= r^{2} \sin \phi.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that $$\sin \phi \geq 0$$ on the parameter domain because $$0 \leq \phi < \pi,$$ and this justifies equation $$\sqrt{\sin^{2}\phi} = \sin \phi.$$ The surface area of the sphere is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{r^{2}\sin \phi d\phi d\theta}}} = r^{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{2d\theta}} = 4\pi r^{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We have derived the familiar formula for the surface area of a sphere using surface integrals.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Calculating Surface Area: Find the area of the surface of revolution obtained by rotating y = x^{2},0 \leq x \leq b about the x-axis (Figure 6.70). This surface has parameterization \mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {x,\theta} \right) =...
body_xml: Find the area of the surface of revolution obtained by rotating $$y = x^{2},0 \leq x \leq b$$ about the x-axis (Figure 6.70). This surface has parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {x,\theta} \right) = \left\langle {x,x^{2}\cos \theta,x^{2}\sin \theta} \right\rangle,0 \leq x \leq b,0 \leq \theta < 2\pi.$$ The tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{x} = \left\langle {1,2x \cos \theta,2x \sin \theta} \right\rangle \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta} = \left\langle {0,-x^{2}\sin \theta,x^{2}\cos \theta} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{x} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta}} & {= \left\langle {2x^{3}\cos^{2}\theta + 2x^{3}\sin^{2}\theta,-x^{2}\cos \theta,-x^{2}\sin \theta} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \left\langle {2x^{3},-x^{2}\cos \theta,-x^{2}\sin \theta} \right\rangle} \end{array}$$ and $$\begin{matrix} \mathbf{\left. ||{ \text{t} _{x} \times \text{t} _{\theta}} \right.||} & {= \sqrt{4x^{6} + x^{4}\cos^{2}\theta + x^{4}\sin^{2}\theta}} \\ & {= \sqrt{4x^{6} + x^{4}}} \\ & {= x^{2}\sqrt{4x^{2} + 1}.} \end{matrix}$$ The area of the surface of revolution is $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{0}^{b}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{x^{2}\sqrt{4x^{2} + 1}d\theta dx}}} & {= 2\pi{\int_{0}^{b}{x^{2}\sqrt{4x^{2} + 1}}}dx} \\ & {= 2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{64}\left( {2\sqrt{4x^{2} + 1}\left( {8x^{3} + x} \right){- \sinh }^{-1}\left( {2x} \right)} \right)} \right\rbrack_{0}^{b}} \\ & {= 2\pi\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{64}\left( {2\sqrt{4b^{2} + 1}\left( {8b^{3} + b} \right){- \sinh }^{-1}\left( {2b} \right)} \right)} \right\rbrack.} \end{array}$$

snippet: Calculating a Surface Integral: Calculate surface integral {\iint_{S}5}dS, where S is the surface with parameterization \mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {u,v} \right) = \left\langle {u,u^{2},v} \right\rangle for 0 \leq u \leq 2 and 0 \leq v \leq...
body_xml:
<example number="6.65" title="Calculating a Surface Integral">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate surface integral $${\iint_{S}5}dS,$$ where $$S$$ is the surface with parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {u,v} \right) = \left\langle {u,u^{2},v} \right\rangle$$ for $$0 \leq u \leq 2$$ and $$0 \leq v \leq u.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Notice that this parameter domain D is a triangle, and therefore the parameter domain is not rectangular. This is not an issue though, because Equation 6.19 does not place any restrictions on the shape of the parameter domain.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To use Equation 6.19 to calculate the surface integral, we first find vector $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}.$$ Note that $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {1,2u,0} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {0,0,1} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ 1 & {2u} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right| = \left\langle {2u,-1,0} \right\rangle$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} \right\| = \sqrt{1 + 4u^{2}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>By Equation 6.19,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {{\iint_{S}5}dS} & {= 5{\iint_{D}\sqrt{1 + 4u^{2}}}dA} \\ & {= 5{\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{0}^{u}\sqrt{1 + 4u^{2}}}}dvdu = 5{\int_{0}^{2}{u\sqrt{1 + 4u^{2}}}}du} \\ & {= 5\left\lbrack \frac{\left( {1 + 4u^{2}} \right)^{3/2}}{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2} = \frac{5\left( {17^{3/2} - 1} \right)}{12} \approx 28.79.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Calculating the Surface Integral of a Cylinder
snippet: Calculating the Surface Integral of a Cylinder: Calculate surface integral {\iint_{S}{\left( {x + y^{2}} \right)dS}}, where S is cylinder x^{2} + y^{2} = 4,0 \leq z \leq 3 (Figure 6.71). To calculate the surface integral, we first need a...
body_xml: Calculate surface integral $${\iint_{S}{\left( {x + y^{2}} \right)dS}},$$ where S is cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4,0 \leq z \leq 3$$ (Figure 6.71). To calculate the surface integral, we first need a parameterization of the cylinder. Following Example 6.58, a parameterization is $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {u,v} \right) = \left\langle {2\cos u,2\sin u,v} \right\rangle,0 \leq u \leq 2\pi,0 \leq v \leq 3.$$ The tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {-2\sin u,2\cos u,0} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {0,0,1} \right\rangle.$$ Then, $$\textbf{t}_{u} \times \textbf{t}_{v} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ {- 2\sin u} & {2\cos u} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right| = \left\langle 2\cos u,2\sin u,0 \right\rangle$$ and $$\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} \right\| = \sqrt{{4\cos }^{2}u + {4\sin }^{2}u} = 2.$$ By Equation 6.19, $$\begin{matrix} \\ \\ \\ {\iint_{S}{f(x,y,z)dS = \iint_{D}f\left( {\textbf{r}(u,v)} \right)\left\| \textbf{t}_{u} \times \textbf{t}_{v} \right\|} dA} \\ {= \int_{0}^{3}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left( 2\cos u + 4\sin^{2}u \right)2dudv} \\ {= 2\int_{0}^{3}\left\lbrack 2\sin u + 2u - \sin(2u) \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}dv = 2\int_{0}^{3}4\pi dv = 24\pi.} \end{matrix}$$

snippet: Calculating the Surface Integral of a Piece of a Sphere: Calculate surface integral {\iint_{S}{f(x,y,z)dS}}, where f(x,y,z) = z^{2} and S is the surface that consists of the piece of sphere x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4 that lies on or above...
body_xml: Calculate surface integral $${\iint_{S}{f(x,y,z)dS}},$$ where $$f(x,y,z) = z^{2}$$ and S is the surface that consists of the piece of sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ that lies on or above plane $$z = 1$$ and the disk that is enclosed by intersection plane $$z = 1$$ and the given sphere (Figure 6.72). Notice that S is not smooth but is piecewise smooth; S can be written as the union of its base $$S_{1}$$ and its spherical top $$S_{2},$$ and both $$S_{1}$$ and $$S_{2}$$ are smooth. Therefore, to calculate $${\iint_{S}{z^{2}dS}},$$ we write this integral as $${\iint_{S_{1}}{z^{2}dS}} + {\iint_{S_{2}}{z^{2}dS}}$$ and we calculate integrals $$\iint_{S_{1}}{z^{2}dS}$$ and $${\iint_{S_{2}}{z^{2}dS}}.$$ First, we calculate $${\iint_{S_{1}}{z^{2}dS}}.$$ To calculate this integral we need a parameterization of $$S_{1}.$$ This surface is a disk in plane $$z = 1$$ centered at $$(0,0,1).$$ To parameterize this disk, we need to know its radius. Since the disk is formed where plane $$z = 1$$ intersects sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4,$$ we can substitute $$z = 1$$ into equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4:$$ $$x^{2} + y^{2} + 1 = 4\Rightarrow x^{2} + y^{2} = 3.$$ Therefore, the radius of the disk is $$\sqrt{3}$$ and a parameterization of $$S_{1}$$ is $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {u \cos v,u \sin v,1} \right\rangle,0 \leq u \leq \sqrt{3},0 \leq v \leq 2\pi.$$ The tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {\cos v,\sin v,0} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {-u \sin v,u{co}sv,0} \right\rangle,$$ and thus $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ {\cos v} & {\sin v} & 0 \\ {-u \sin v} & {u \cos v} & 0 \end{matrix} \right| = \left\langle {0,0,u \cos^{2}v + u \sin^{2}v} \right\rangle = \left\langle {0,0,u} \right\rangle.$$ The magnitude of this vector is u. Therefore, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\iint_{S_{1}}{z^{2}dS}} & {= {\int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{f\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v)} \right)}}}\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} \right\| dv du} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}u}} dv du} \\ & {= 2\pi{\int_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{udu}}} \\ & {= 3\pi.} \end{array}$$ Now we calculate $${\iint_{S_{2}}{dS}}.$$ To calculate this integral, we need a parameterization of $$S_{2}.$$ The parameterization of full sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ is $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {\phi,\theta} \right) = \left\langle {2 \cos \theta \sin \phi,2 \sin \theta \sin \phi,2 \cos \phi} \right\rangle,0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi,0 \leq \phi \leq \pi.$$ Since we are only taking the piece of the sphere on or above plane $$z = 1,$$ we have to restrict the domain of $$\phi.$$ To see how far this angle sweeps, notice that the angle can be located in a right triangle, as shown in Figure 6.73 (the $$\sqrt{3}$$ comes from the fact that the base of S is a disk with radius $$\sqrt{3}).$$ Therefore, the tangent of $$\phi$$ is $$\sqrt{3},$$ which implies that $$\phi$$ is $$\pi/3.$$ We now have a parameterization of $$S_{2}:$$ $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {\phi,\theta} \right) = \left\langle {2 \cos \theta \sin \phi,2 \sin \theta \sin \phi,2 \cos \phi} \right\rangle,0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi,0 \leq \phi \leq \pi/3.$$ The tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi} = \left\langle {2 \cos \theta \cos \phi,2 \sin \theta \cos \phi,-2 \sin \phi} \right\rangle \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta} = \left\langle {-2 \sin \theta \sin \phi,u \cos \theta \sin \phi,0} \right\rangle,$$ and thus $$\begin{array}{cl} {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta}} & {= \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ {2 \cos \theta \cos \phi} & {2 \sin \theta \cos \phi} & {-2 \sin \phi} \\ {-2 \sin \theta \sin \phi} & {2 \cos \theta \sin \phi} & 0 \end{matrix} \right|} \\ & {= \left\langle {4 \cos \theta \sin^{2}\phi,4 \sin \theta \sin^{2}\phi,4 \cos^{2}\theta \cos \phi \sin \phi + 4 \sin^{2}\theta \cos \phi \sin \phi} \right\rangle} \\ & {= \left\langle {4 \cos \theta \sin^{2}\phi,4 \sin \theta \sin^{2}\phi,4 \cos \phi \sin \phi} \right\rangle.} \end{array}$$ The magnitude of this vector is $$\begin{array}{cl} \left\| {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta}} \right\| & {= \sqrt{16 \cos^{2}\theta \sin^{4}\phi + 16 \sin^{2}\theta \sin^{4}\phi + 16 \cos^{2}\phi \sin^{2}\phi}} \\ & {= 4\sqrt{\sin^{4}\phi + \cos^{2}\phi \sin^{2}\phi}.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, $$\begin{matrix} {\iint_{S_{2}}zdS} & {= \int_{0}^{\pi \text{/3} }\int_{0}^{2\pi}f\left( {\textbf{r}(\phi,\theta)} \right)\left\| \textbf{t}_{\phi} \times \textbf{t}_{\theta} \right\| d\theta d\phi} \\ & {= \int_{0}^{\pi \text{/3} }\int_{0}^{2\pi}16 \cos^{2}\phi\sqrt{\sin^{4}\phi + \cos^{2}\phi \sin^{2}\phi}d\theta d\phi} \\ & {= 32\pi\int_{0}^{\pi \text{/3} }\cos^{2}\phi\sqrt{\sin^{4}\phi + \cos^{2}\phi \sin^{2}\phi} d\phi} \\ & {= 32\pi\int_{0}^{\pi \text{/3} }\cos^{2}\phi \sin \phi\sqrt{\sin^{2}\phi + \cos^{2}\phi} d\phi} \\ & {= 32\pi\int_{0}^{\pi \text{/3} }\cos^{2}\phi \sin \phi d\phi} \\ & {= 32\pi\left\lbrack - \frac{\cos^{3}\phi}{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi/3} = 32\pi\left\lbrack \frac{1}{3} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{8} \right\rbrack = \frac{28\pi}{3}.} \end{matrix}$$ Since $$\iint_{S}z^{2}dS = \iint_{S_{1}}z^{2}dS + \iint_{S_{2}}z^{2}dS = 3\pi + \frac{28\pi}{3} = \frac{37\pi}{3}$$ In this example we broke a surface integral over a piecewise surface into the addition of surface integrals over smooth subsurfaces. There were only two smooth subsurfaces in this example, but this technique extends to finitely many smooth subsurfaces.

title: Calculating the Mass of a Sheet
snippet: Calculating the Mass of a Sheet: A flat sheet of metal has the shape of surface z = 1 + x + 2y that lies above rectangle 0 \leq x \leq 4 and 0 \leq y \leq 2. If the density of the sheet is given by \rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz,...
body_xml:
<example number="6.68" title="Calculating the Mass of a Sheet">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A flat sheet of metal has the shape of surface $$z = 1 + x + 2y$$ that lies above rectangle $$0 \leq x \leq 4$$ and $$0 \leq y \leq 2.$$ If the density of the sheet is given by $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x^{2}yz,$$ what is the mass of the sheet?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let S be the surface that describes the sheet. Then, the mass of the sheet is given by $$m = {\iint_{S}{x^{2}yzdS}}.$$ To compute this surface integral, we first need a parameterization of S. Since S is given by the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 1 + x + 2y,$$ a parameterization of S is $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {x,y} \right) = \left\langle {x,y,1 + x + 2y} \right\rangle,0 \leq x \leq 4,0 \leq y \leq 2.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{x} = \left\langle {1,0,1} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{y} = \left\langle {1,0,2} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore, $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{x} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{y} = \left\langle {-1,-2,1} \right\rangle$$ and $$\left\| \left. \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{x} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{y} \right\| \right. = \sqrt{6}.$$ By Equation 6.5,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} m & {= {\iint_{S}{x^{2}yz^{}dS}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{6}{\int_{0}^{4}{\int_{0}^{2}{x^{2}y\left( {1 + x + 2y} \right)dydx}}}} \\ & {= \sqrt{6}{\int_{0}^{4}\frac{22x^{2}}{3}} + 2x^{3}dx} \\ & {= \frac{2560\sqrt{6}}{9}} \\ & {\approx 696.74.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Choosing an Orientation
snippet: Choosing an Orientation: Give an orientation of cylinder x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2},0 \leq z \leq h. This surface has parameterization \mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {r \cos u,r \sin u,v} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < 2\pi,0 \leq v \leq h....
body_xml: Give an orientation of cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2},0 \leq z \leq h.$$ This surface has parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {r \cos u,r \sin u,v} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < 2\pi,0 \leq v \leq h.$$ The tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {-r \sin u,r \cos u,0} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {0,0,1} \right\rangle.$$ To get an orientation of the surface, we compute the unit normal vector $$\mathbf{ \text{N} } = \frac{\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}}{\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} \right\|}.$$ In this case, $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {r \cos u,r \sin u,0} \right\rangle$$ and therefore $$\left\| {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} \right\| = \sqrt{r^{2}\cos^{2}u + r^{2}\sin^{2}u} = r.$$ An orientation of the cylinder is $$\mathbf{ \text{N} }(u,v) = \frac{\left\langle {r \cos u,r \sin u,0} \right\rangle}{r} = \left\langle {\cos u,\sin u,0} \right\rangle.$$ Notice that all vectors are parallel to the xy-plane, which should be the case with vectors that are normal to the cylinder. Furthermore, all the vectors point outward, and therefore this is an outward orientation of the cylinder (Figure 6.75).

title: Calculating a Surface Integral

body_xml:
<example number="6.70" title="Calculating a Surface Integral">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate the surface integral $${\iint_{S}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot \mathbf{ \text{N} }d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}},$$ where $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {-y,x,0} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{S} }$$ is the surface with parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {u,v^{2} - u,u + v} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < 3,0 \leq v \leq 4.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {1,-1,1} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {0,2v,1} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {-1 - 2v,-1,2v} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>By Equation 6.21,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {{\iint_{S}\mathbf{ \text{F} }} \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }} & {= {\int_{0}^{4}{\int_{0}^{3}{\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v)} \right)}}} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} \right)dudv} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4}{\int_{0}^{3}{\left\langle {u - v^{2},u,0} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {-1 - 2v,-1,2v} \right\rangle}}} dudv} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4}{\int_{0}^{3}\left\lbrack {\left( {u - v^{2}} \right)\left( {-1 - 2v} \right) - u} \right\rbrack}}dudv} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4}{\int_{0}^{3}\left( {2v^{3} + v^{2} - 2uv - 2u} \right)}}dudv} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4}\left\lbrack {2v^{3}u + v^{2}u - vu^{2} - u^{2}} \right\rbrack}_{0}^{3}dv} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{4}{\left( {6v^{3} + 3v^{2} - 9v - 9} \right)dv}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{3v^{4}}{2} + v^{3} - \frac{9v^{2}}{2} - 9v} \right\rbrack_{0}^{4}} \\ & {= 340.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the flux of F across S is 340.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Calculating Mass Flow Rate
snippet: Calculating Mass Flow Rate: Let \mathbf{ \text{v} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {2x,2y,z} \right\rangle represent a velocity field (with units of meters per second) of a fluid with constant density 80 kg/m3. Let S be hemisphere...
body_xml:
<example number="6.71" title="Calculating Mass Flow Rate">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$\mathbf{ \text{v} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {2x,2y,z} \right\rangle$$ represent a velocity field (with units of meters per second) of a fluid with constant density 80 kg/m3. Let S be hemisphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 9$$ with $$z \geq 0$$ such that S is oriented outward. Find the mass flow rate of the fluid across S.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>A parameterization of the surface is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {\phi,\theta} \right) = \left\langle {3 \cos \theta \sin \phi,3 \sin \theta \sin \phi,3 \cos \phi} \right\rangle,0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi,0 \leq \phi \leq {\pi/2.}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>As in Example 6.64, the tangent vectors are</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta}{= \left\langle {-3 \sin \theta \sin \phi,3 \cos \theta \sin \phi,0} \right\rangle} \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi}{= \left\langle {3 \cos \theta \cos \phi,3 \sin \theta \cos \phi,-3 \sin \phi} \right\rangle},$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and their cross product is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta} = \left\langle {9 \cos \theta \sin^{2}\phi,9 \sin \theta \sin^{2}\phi,9 \sin \phi \cos \phi} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that each component of the cross product is positive, and therefore this vector gives the outward orientation. Therefore we use the orientation $$\mathbf{ \text{N} } = \left\langle {9 \cos \theta \sin^{2}\phi,9 \sin \theta \sin^{2}\phi,9 \sin \phi \cos \phi} \right\rangle$$ for the sphere.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>By [link],</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\iint_{S}{\rho\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} & {= 80{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\mathbf{ \text{v} }\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {\phi,\theta} \right)} \right)}}} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta}} \right)d\phi d\theta} \\ & {= 80{\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}}} \\ & {= 80{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\begin{array}{l} \left\langle {6 \cos \theta \sin \phi,6 \sin \theta \sin \phi,3 \cos \phi} \right\rangle \\ {\cdot \left\langle {9 \cos \theta \sin^{2}\phi,9 \sin \theta \sin^{2}\phi,9 \sin \phi \cos \phi} \right\rangle d\phi d\theta} \end{array}}}} \\ & {= 80{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{54 \sin^{3}\phi + 27 \cos^{2}\phi \sin \phi d\phi d\theta}}}} \\ & {= 80{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{54\left( {1 - \cos^{2}\phi} \right)\sin \phi + 27 \cos^{2}\phi \sin \phi d\phi d\theta}}}} \\ & {= 80{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{54 \sin \phi - 27 \cos^{2}\phi \sin \phi d\phi d\theta}}}} \\ & {= 80{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left\lbrack {-54 \cos \phi + 9 \cos^{3}\phi} \right\rbrack_{\phi = 0}^{\phi = 2\pi}d\theta}}} \\ & {= 80{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{45d\theta}} = 7200\pi.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the mass flow rate is $$7200\pi \text{kg} /\sec / \text{m} ^{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Calculating Heat Flow
snippet: Calculating Heat Flow: A cast-iron solid cylinder is given by inequalities x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 1, 1 \leq z \leq 4. The temperature at point (x,y,z) in a region containing the cylinder is T(x,y,z) = \left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)z. Given...
body_xml:
<example number="6.72" title="Calculating Heat Flow">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A cast-iron solid cylinder is given by inequalities $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 1,$$ $$1 \leq z \leq 4.$$ The temperature at point $$(x,y,z)$$ in a region containing the cylinder is $$T(x,y,z) = \left( {x^{2} + y^{2}} \right)z.$$ Given that the thermal conductivity of cast iron is 55, find the heat flow across the boundary of the solid if this boundary is oriented outward.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let S denote the boundary of the object. To find the heat flow, we need to calculate flux integral $${\iint_{S}{-k\nabla T \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}}.$$ Notice that S is not a smooth surface but is piecewise smooth, since S is the union of three smooth surfaces (the circular top and bottom, and the cylindrical side). Therefore, we calculate three separate integrals, one for each smooth piece of S. Before calculating any integrals, note that the gradient of the temperature is $$\nabla T = \left\langle {2xz,2yz,x^{2} + y^{2}} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>First we consider the circular bottom of the object, which we denote $$S_{1}.$$ We can see that $$S_{1}$$ is a circle of radius 1 centered at point $$(0,0,1),$$ sitting in plane $$z = 1.$$ This surface has parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {v \cos u,v \sin u,1} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < 2\pi,0 \leq v \leq 1.$$ Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {-v \sin u,v \cos u,0} \right\rangle \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {\cos u,v \sin u,0} \right\rangle,$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {0,0,-v \sin^{2}u - v \cos^{2}u} \right\rangle = \left\langle {0,0,-v} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since the surface is oriented outward and $$S_{1}$$ is the bottom of the object, it makes sense that this vector points downward. By Equation 6.21, the heat flow across $$S_{1}$$ is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\iint_{S_{1}}{-k\nabla T \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\nabla T(u,v) \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} \right)dvdu}}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left\langle {2v \cos u,2v \sin u,v^{2}\cos^{2}u + v^{2}\sin^{2}u} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {0,0,-v} \right\rangle dvdu}}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left\langle {2v \cos u,2v \sin u,v^{2}} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {0,0,-v} \right\rangle dvdu}}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{{\int_{0}^{1}{-v^{3}}}dvdu}} = -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{- \frac{1}{4}du}} = \frac{55\pi}{2}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now let’s consider the circular top of the object, which we denote $$S_{2}.$$ We see that $$S_{2}$$ is a circle of radius 1 centered at point $$(0,0,4),$$ sitting in plane $$z = 4.$$ This surface has parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {v \cos u,v \sin u,4} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < 2\pi,0 \leq v \leq 1.$$ Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {-v \sin u,v \cos u,0} \right\rangle \text{and} \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {\cos u,v \sin u,0} \right\rangle,$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {0,0,-v \sin^{2}u - v \cos^{2}u} \right\rangle = \left\langle {0,0,-v} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since the surface is oriented outward and $$S_{1}$$ is the top of the object, we instead take vector $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {0,0,v} \right\rangle.$$ By Equation 6.21, the heat flow across $$S_{1}$$ is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int{\int_{S_{2}}{-k}}}\nabla T \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }} & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\nabla T\left( {u,v} \right) \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u}} \right)dvdu}}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left\langle {8v \cos u,8v \sin u,v^{2}\cos^{2}u + v^{2}\sin^{2}u} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {0,0,v} \right\rangle dvdu}}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left\langle {8v \cos u,8v \sin u,v^{2}} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {0,0,v} \right\rangle dvdu}}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{v^{3}dvdu}}} = - \frac{55\pi}{2}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Last, let’s consider the cylindrical side of the object. This surface has parameterization $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(u,v) = \left\langle {\cos u,\sin u,v} \right\rangle,0 \leq u < 2\pi,1 \leq v \leq 4.$$ By Example 6.66, we know that $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {\cos u,\sin u,0} \right\rangle.$$ By Equation 6.21,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\iint_{S_{3}}{-k\nabla T \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{1}^{4}{\nabla T(u,v) \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u}} \right)dvdu}}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{{\int_{1}^{4}{\left\langle {2v \cos u,2v \sin u,\cos^{2}u + \sin^{2}u} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {\cos u,\sin u,0} \right\rangle}}dvdu}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{{\int_{0}^{1}{\left\langle {2v \cos u,2v \sin u,1} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {\cos u,\sin u,0} \right\rangle}}dvdu}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{{\int_{0}^{1}\left( {2v \cos^{2}u + 2v \sin^{2}u} \right)}dvdu}}} \\ & {= -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{{\int_{0}^{1}{2v}}dvdu}} = -55{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{du}} = -110\pi.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, the rate of heat flow across S is $$\frac{55\pi}{2} - \frac{55\pi}{2} - 110\pi = -110\pi.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="6.19" title="Stokes’ Theorem">
    <heading level="4">Stokes’ Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>Let S be a piecewise smooth oriented surface with a boundary that is a simple closed curve C with positive orientation (Figure 6.79). If F is a vector field with component functions that have continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing S, then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} = {\iint_{S}{ \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Verifying Stokes’ Theorem for a Specific Case
snippet: Verifying Stokes’ Theorem for a Specific Case: Verify that Stokes’ theorem is true for vector field \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {y,2z,x^{2}} \right\rangle and surface S, where S is the paraboloid z = 4 - x^{2}...
body_xml: Verify that Stokes’ theorem is true for vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y,z} \right) = \left\langle {y,2z,x^{2}} \right\rangle$$ and surface S, where S is the paraboloid $$z = 4 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ . Assume the surface is outward oriented and $$z \geq 0$$ . As a surface integral, you have $$g(x,y) = 4 - x^{2} - y^{2},g_{x} = -2x$$ and $$g_{y} = -2y$$ $$\begin{aligned} { \text{curl} \mathbf{F} } & {= \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{ \text{i} } & \mathbf{ \text{j} } & \mathbf{ \text{k} } \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ y & {2z} & x^{2} \end{matrix} \right|} \end{aligned} = \left\langle -2,-2x,-1 \right\rangle.$$ By Equation 6.19, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\iint_{S}{ \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} & {= {\iint_{D}{ \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {\phi,\theta} \right)} \right)}} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\phi} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{\theta}} \right)dA} \\ & {= {\iint_{D}{\left\langle {-2,-2x,-1} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle 2x,2y,1 \right\rangle dA}}} \\ & {= {\int_{-2}^{2}{\int_{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}^{\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}}\left( {-4x-4xy-1} \right)}}dydx} \\ & {= \int_{-2}^{2}{\left( -8x\sqrt{4 - x^{2}}-2\sqrt{4 - x^{2}} \right)dx}} \\ & {{= -4}\pi} \end{array}$$ As a line integral, you can parameterize C by $$\mathbf{ \text{r} }(t) = \left\langle {2 \cos t,2 \sin t,0} \right\rangle 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi$$ . By Equation 6.19, $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left\langle \left. 2\sin t,0,4\cos^{2}t \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle -2\sin t,2\cos t,0 \right\rangle dt \right.}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{-4\sin^{2}tdt = -4\pi}}} \end{array}$$ Therefore, we have verified Stokes' theorem for this example.

title: Calculating a Surface Integral
snippet: Calculating a Surface Integral: Calculate surface integral {\iint_{S}{ \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}}, where S is the surface, oriented outward, in Figure 6.84 and \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {z,2xy,x +...
body_xml: Calculate surface integral $${\iint_{S}{ \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}},$$ where S is the surface, oriented outward, in Figure 6.84 and $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {z,2xy,x + y} \right\rangle.$$ Note that to calculate $$\iint_{S}{ \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}$$ without using Stokes’ theorem, we would need to use Equation 6.19. Use of this equation requires a parameterization of S. Surface S is complicated enough that it would be extremely difficult to find a parameterization. Therefore, the methods we have learned in previous sections are not useful for this problem. Instead, we use Stokes’ theorem, noting that the boundary C of the surface is merely a single circle with radius 1. By Stokes’ theorem, $${\iint_{S}{ \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} = {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} },}}$$ where C has parameterization $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \left. \sin t,0,1 - \cos t \right\rangle \right.,0 \leq t < 2\pi.$$ By Equation 6.9, $$\begin{matrix} {\iint_{S} \text{curl} \textbf{F} \cdot d\textbf{S}} & {= \int_{C}\textbf{F} \cdot d\textbf{r}} \\ & {= \int_{0}^{2\pi}\left\langle {\left. 1 - \cos t ,0, + \sin t \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle - \sin t,0,\cos t \right\rangle dt} \right. } \\ & {= \int_{0}^{2\pi}\left( - \sin t + 2\sin t \cos t \right) dt} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left( - \sin t + \text{sin 2t)} \textit{dt} \right.}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack { \text{+cos} t + \frac{1}{2}\cos 2t} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack { \text{+cos} 2\pi + \frac{1}{2}\cos 4\pi} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack { \text{+cos} 0 + \frac{1}{2}\cos 0} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= 0} \end{matrix}$$

body_xml:
<example number="6.75" title="Calculating a Line Integral">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate the line integral $${\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}},$$ where $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {xy,x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2},yz} \right\rangle$$ and C is the boundary of the parallelogram with vertices $$(0,0,1),(0,1,0),(2,1, - 2),$$ and $$(2,0, - 1).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To calculate the line integral directly, we need to parameterize each side of the parallelogram separately, calculate four separate line integrals, and add the result. This is not overly complicated, but it is time-consuming.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>By contrast, let’s calculate the line integral using Stokes’ theorem. Let S denote the surface of the parallelogram. Note that S is the portion of the graph of $$z = 1 - x - y$$ for $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ varying over the rectangular region with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right),$$ $$\left( {0,1} \right),$$ $$\left( {2,0} \right),$$ and $$\left( {2,1} \right)$$ in the xy-plane. Therefore, a parameterization of S is $$\left\langle {x,y,1 - x - y} \right\rangle,0 \leq x \leq 2,0 \leq y \leq 1.$$ The curl of F is $$\left\langle {{-z},0,x} \right\rangle,$$ and Stokes’ theorem and Equation 6.19 give</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{C}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{r} }}} & {= {\iint_{S}{ \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{ \text{curl} \mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {x,y} \right) \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{x} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{y}} \right)}}}dydx} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left\langle {-\left( {1 - x - y} \right) \text{,0,x} } \right\rangle \cdot \left( {\left\langle {1,0,-1} \right\rangle \times \left\langle {0,1,-1} \right\rangle} \right)}}}dydx} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left\langle {x + y - 1,0,x} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {1,1,1} \right\rangle}}}dydx} \\ & {{\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{2x + y - 1}}}dydx} \\ & {= 3.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the magnetic field does not change with respect to time, $$- \frac{\partial\mathbf{ \text{B} }}{\partial t} = \mathbf{0}.$$ By Faraday’s law, the curl of the electric field is therefore also zero.</paragraph>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="6.20" title="The Divergence Theorem">
    <heading level="4">The Divergence Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>Let S be a piecewise, smooth closed surface that encloses solid E in space. Assume that S is oriented outward, and let F be a vector field with continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing E (Figure 6.87). Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left. \iiint{}_{E}{ \text{div} \mathbf{ \text{F} }dV =} \right.{\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}}.$$</paragraph>

title: Verifying the Divergence Theorem
snippet: Verifying the Divergence Theorem: Verify the divergence theorem for vector field \mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {x - y,x + z,z - y} \right\rangle and surface S that consists of cone x^{2} + y^{2} = z^{2},0 \leq z \leq 1, and the...
body_xml:
<example number="6.77" title="Verifying the Divergence Theorem">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Verify the divergence theorem for vector field $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {x - y,x + z,z - y} \right\rangle$$ and surface S that consists of cone $$x^{2} + y^{2} = z^{2},0 \leq z \leq 1,$$ and the circular top of the cone (see the following figure). Assume this surface is oriented outward.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let E be the solid cone enclosed by S. To verify the theorem for this example, we show that $$\left. \iiint{}_{E}{ \text{div} \mathbf{ \text{F} }dV =} \right.{\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}}$$ by calculating each integral separately.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To compute the triple integral, note that $$\text{div} \mathbf{ \text{F} } = P_{x} + Q_{y} + R_{z} = 2,$$ and therefore the triple integral is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\iiint_{E}{ \text{div} \mathbf{ \text{F} }dV}} & {= 2{\iiint_{E}{dV}}} \\ & {= 2\left( { \text{volume of} E} \right).} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The volume of a right circular cone is given by $$\pi r^{2}\frac{h}{3}.$$ In this case, $$h = r = 1.$$ Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\iiint_{E}{ \text{div} \mathbf{ \text{F} }dV}} = 2\left( { \text{volume of} E} \right) = \frac{2\pi}{3}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To compute the flux integral, first note that S is piecewise smooth; S can be written as a union of smooth surfaces. Therefore, we break the flux integral into two pieces: one flux integral across the circular top of the cone and one flux integral across the remaining portion of the cone. Call the circular top $$S_{1}$$ and the portion under the top $$S_{2}.$$ We start by calculating the flux across the circular top of the cone. Notice that $$S_{1}$$ has parameterization</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {u,v} \right) = \left\langle {u \cos v,u \sin v,1} \right\rangle,0 \leq u \leq 1,0 \leq v \leq 2\pi.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, the tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {\cos v,\sin v,0} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {-u \cos v,u \sin v,0} \right\rangle.$$ Therefore, the flux across $$S_{1}$$ is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\iint_{S_{1}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {u,v} \right)} \right)}}} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v}} \right)dA} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left\langle {u \cos v - u \sin v,u \cos v + 1,1 - u \sin v} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {0,0,u} \right\rangle}}}dvdu} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{u - u^{2}\sin v}}} dvdu = \pi.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We now calculate the flux over $$S_{2}.$$ A parameterization of this surface is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {u,v} \right) = \left\langle {u \cos v,u \sin v,u} \right\rangle,0 \leq u \leq 1,0 \leq v \leq 2\pi.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The tangent vectors are $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {\cos v,\sin v,1} \right\rangle$$ and $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {-u \sin v,u \cos v,0} \right\rangle,$$ so the cross product is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} = \left\langle {-u \cos v,-u \sin v,u} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that the negative signs on the x and y components induce the inward orientation of the cone. Since the surface is oriented outward, we use vector $$\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u} = \left\langle {u \cos v,u \sin v,-u} \right\rangle$$ in the flux integral. The flux across $$S_{2}$$ is then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\iint_{S_{2}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\mathbf{ \text{F} }\left( {\mathbf{ \text{r} }\left( {u,v} \right)} \right)}}} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{ \text{t} }_{v} \times \mathbf{ \text{t} }_{u}} \right)dA} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left\langle {u \cos v - u \sin v,u \cos v + u,u - \sin v} \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle {u \cos v,u \sin v,-u} \right\rangle}}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}u^{2}}}\cos^{2}v + 2u^{2}\sin v - u^{2}dvdu = - \frac{\pi}{3}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The total flux across S is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\iint_{S_{2}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} = {\iint_{S_{1}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} + {\iint_{S_{2}}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} = \frac{2\pi}{3} = \left. \iiint{}_{E} \text{div} \right. \mathbf{ \text{F} }dV,$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and we have verified the divergence theorem for this example.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.78" title="Applying the Divergence Theorem">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Calculate the surface integral $${\iint_{S}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}},$$ where S is cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1,0 \leq z \leq 2,$$ including the circular top and bottom, and $$\mathbf{ \text{F} } = \left\langle {\frac{x^{3}}{3} + yz,\frac{y^{3}}{3} - \sin \left( {xz} \right),z - x - y} \right\rangle.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We could calculate this integral without the divergence theorem, but the calculation is not straightforward because we would have to break the flux integral into three separate integrals: one for the top of the cylinder, one for the bottom, and one for the side. Furthermore, each integral would require parameterizing the corresponding surface, calculating tangent vectors and their cross product, and using Equation 6.19.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>By contrast, the divergence theorem allows us to calculate the single triple integral $$\left. \iiint{}_{E} \text{div} \right. \mathbf{ \text{F} }dV,$$ where E is the solid enclosed by the cylinder. Using the divergence theorem and converting to cylindrical coordinates, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \left. \iint{}_{s}{\mathbf{ \text{F} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }} \right. & {= \left. \iiint{}_{E} \text{div} \right. \mathbf{ \text{F} } dV} \\ & {= \left. \iiint{}_{E}\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + 1} \right) \right.dV} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2}{\left( {r^{2} + 1} \right)r dz}}}} dr d\theta} \\ & {= \frac{3}{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta}} = 3\pi.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Applying the Divergence Theorem
snippet: Applying the Divergence Theorem: Let \mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {- \frac{y}{z},\frac{x}{z},0} \right\rangle be the velocity field of a fluid. Let C be the solid cube given by 1 \leq x \leq 4,2 \leq y \leq 5,1 \leq z \leq 4, and let...
body_xml: Let $$\mathbf{ \text{v} } = \left\langle {- \frac{y}{z},\frac{x}{z},0} \right\rangle$$ be the velocity field of a fluid. Let C be the solid cube given by $$1 \leq x \leq 4,2 \leq y \leq 5,1 \leq z \leq 4,$$ and let S be the boundary of this cube (see the following figure). Find the flow rate of the fluid across S. The flow rate of the fluid across S is $${\iint_{S}{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}}.$$ Before calculating this flux integral, let’s discuss what the value of the integral should be. Based on Figure 6.90, we see that if we place this cube in the fluid (as long as the cube doesn’t encompass the origin), then the rate of fluid entering the cube is the same as the rate of fluid exiting the cube. The field is rotational in nature and, for a given circle parallel to the xy-plane that has a center on the z-axis, the vectors along that circle are all the same magnitude. That is how we can see that the flow rate is the same entering and exiting the cube. The flow into the cube cancels with the flow out of the cube, and therefore the flow rate of the fluid across the cube should be zero. To verify this intuition, we need to calculate the flux integral. Calculating the flux integral directly requires breaking the flux integral into six separate flux integrals, one for each face of the cube. We also need to find tangent vectors, compute their cross product, and use Equation 6.19. However, using the divergence theorem makes this calculation go much more quickly: $$\begin{array}{cl} {\iint_{S}{\mathbf{ \text{v} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} & {= \left. \iiint{}_{C}{ \text{div} \left( \mathbf{ \text{v} } \right)} \right.dV} \\ & {= \left. \iiint{}_{C}0 \right. dV = 0.} \end{array}$$ Therefore the flux is zero, as expected.

title: The Divergence of FrFr Is Zero
snippet: The Divergence of FrFr Is Zero: Verify that the divergence of \mathbf{ \text{F} }_{r} is zero where \mathbf{ \text{F} }_{r} is defined (away from the origin). Since r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}, the quotient rule gives us...
body_xml:
<example number="6.80" title="The Divergence of FrFr Is Zero">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Verify that the divergence of $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }_{r}$$ is zero where $$\mathbf{ \text{F} }_{r}$$ is defined (away from the origin).</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since $$r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}},$$ the quotient rule gives us</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( \frac{x}{r^{3}} \right)} & {= \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( \frac{x}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{3/2}} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{3/2} - x\left\lbrack {\frac{3}{2}\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{1/2}2x} \right\rbrack}{\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)^{3}}} \\ & {= \frac{r^{3} - 3x^{2}r}{r^{6}} = \frac{r^{2} - 3x^{2}}{r^{5}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Similarly,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( \frac{y}{r^{3}} \right) = \frac{r^{2} - 3y^{2}}{r^{5}} \text{and} \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left( \frac{z}{r^{3}} \right) = \frac{r^{2} - 3z^{2}}{r^{5}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} { \text{div} \mathbf{ \text{F} }_{r}} & {= \frac{r^{2} - 3x^{2}}{r^{5}} + \frac{r^{2} - 3y^{2}}{r^{5}} + \frac{r^{2} - 3z^{2}}{r^{5}}} \\ & {= \frac{3r^{2} - 3\left( {x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}} \right)}{r^{5}}} \\ & {= \frac{3r^{2} - 3r^{2}}{r^{5}} = 0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="6.81" title="Using Gauss’ law">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose we have four stationary point charges in space, all with a charge of 0.002 Coulombs (C). The charges are located at $$(0,1,1),(1,1,4),(-1,0,0), \text{and} (-2,-2,2).$$ Let E denote the electrostatic field generated by these point charges. If S is the sphere of radius 2 oriented outward and centered at the origin, then find $${\iint_{S}{\mathbf{ \text{E} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>According to Gauss’ law, the flux of E across S is the total charge inside of S divided by the electric constant. Since S has radius 2, notice that only two of the charges are inside of S: the charge at $$(0,1,1)$$ and the charge at $$(-1,0,0).$$ Therefore, the total charge encompassed by S is 0.004 and, by Gauss’ law,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\iint_{S}{\mathbf{ \text{E} } \cdot d\mathbf{ \text{S} }}} = \frac{0.004}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 4.518 \times 10^{9} \text{V-m} .$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Definition: A second-order differential equation is linear if it can be written in the form a_{2}(x)y^{''} + a_{1}(x)y^{\prime} + a_{0}(x)y = r(x), where a_{2}(x), a_{1}(x), a_{0}(x), and r(x) are real-valued functions and a_{2}(x) is not...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>A second-order differential equation is linear if it can be written in the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$a_{2}(x)y^{''} + a_{1}(x)y^{\prime} + a_{0}(x)y = r(x),$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$a_{2}(x),$$ $$a_{1}(x),$$ $$a_{0}(x),$$ and $$r(x)$$ are real-valued functions and $$a_{2}(x)$$ is not identically zero. If $$r(x) \equiv 0$$ —in other words, if $$r(x) = 0$$ for every value of x—the equation is said to be a homogeneous linear equation. If $$r(x) \neq 0$$ for some value of $$x,$$ the equation is said to be a nonhomogeneous linear equation.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Classifying Second-Order Equations
snippet: Classifying Second-Order Equations: Classify each of the following equations as linear or nonlinear. If the equation is linear, determine further whether it is homogeneous or nonhomogeneous. y^{''} + 3x^{4}y^{\prime} + x^{2}y^{2} = x^{3}...
body_xml:
<example number="7.1" title="Classifying Second-Order Equations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Classify each of the following equations as linear or nonlinear. If the equation is linear, determine further whether it is homogeneous or nonhomogeneous.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$y^{''} + 3x^{4}y^{\prime} + x^{2}y^{2} = x^{3}$$</item>
        <item>$$(\sin x)y^{''} + (\cos x)y^{\prime} + 3y = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$4t^{2}x^{''} + 3txx^{\prime} + 4x = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$5y^{''} + y = 4x^{5}$$</item>
        <item>$$(\cos x)y^{''} - \sin y^{\prime} + (\sin x)y - \cos x = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$8ty^{''} - 6t^{2}y^{\prime} + 4ty - 3t^{2} = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$\sin (x^{2})y^{''} - (\cos x)y^{\prime} + x^{2}y = y^{\prime} - 3$$</item>
        <item>$$y^{''} + 5xy^{\prime} - 3y = \cos y$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>This equation is nonlinear because of the $$y^{2}$$ term.</item>
        <item>This equation is linear. There is no term involving a power or function of $$y,$$ and the coefficients are all functions of $$x.$$ The equation is already written in standard form, and $$r(x)$$ is identically zero, so the equation is homogeneous.</item>
        <item>This equation is nonlinear. Note that, in this case, x is the dependent variable and t is the independent variable. The second term involves the product of $$x$$ and $$x^{\prime},$$ so the equation is nonlinear.</item>
        <item>This equation is linear. Since $$r(x) = 4x^{5},$$ the equation is nonhomogeneous.</item>
        <item>This equation is nonlinear, because of the $$\sin y^{\prime}$$ term.</item>
        <item>This equation is linear. Rewriting it in standard form gives $$8t^{2}y^{''} - 6t^{2}y^{\prime} + 4ty = 3t^{2}.$$ With the equation in standard form, we can see that $$r(t) = 3t^{2},$$ so the equation is nonhomogeneous.</item>
        <item>This equation looks like it’s linear, but we should rewrite it in standard form to be sure. We get $$\sin (x^{2})y^{''} - (\cos x + 1)y^{\prime} + x^{2}y = -3.$$ This equation is, indeed, linear. With $$r(x) = -3,$$ it is nonhomogeneous.</item>
        <item>This equation is nonlinear because of the $$\cos y$$ term.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="7.2" title="Verifying a Solution">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Consider the linear, homogeneous differential equation</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x^{2}y^{''} - xy^{\prime} - 3y = 0.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Looking at this equation, notice that the coefficient functions are polynomials, with higher powers of $$x$$ associated with higher-order derivatives of $$y.$$ Show that $$y = x^{3}$$ is a solution to this differential equation.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$y = x^{3}.$$ Then $$y^{\prime} = 3x^{2}$$ and $$y^{''} = 6x.$$ Substituting into the differential equation, we see that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {x^{2}y^{''} - xy\prime - 3y} & {= x^{2}\left( {6x} \right) - x\left( {3x^{2}} \right) - 3\left( x^{3} \right)} \\ & {= 6x^{3} - 3x^{3} - 3x^{3}} \\ & {= 0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Verifying the Superposition Principle
snippet: Verifying the Superposition Principle: Consider the differential equation y^{''} - 4y^{\prime} - 5y = 0. Given that e^{-x} and e^{5x} are solutions to this differential equation, show that 4e^{-x} + e^{5x} is a solution. We have y(x) =...
body_xml:
<example number="7.3" title="Verifying the Superposition Principle">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Consider the differential equation</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y^{''} - 4y^{\prime} - 5y = 0.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Given that $$e^{-x}$$ and $$e^{5x}$$ are solutions to this differential equation, show that $$4e^{-x} + e^{5x}$$ is a solution.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(x) = 4e^{-x} + e^{5x}, \text{so} y^{\prime}(x) = -4e^{-x} + 5e^{5x} \text{and} y^{''}(x) = 4e^{-x} + 25e^{5x}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {y^{''} - 4y^{\prime} - 5y} & {= \left( {4e^{-x} + 25e^{5x}} \right) - 4\left( {-4e^{-x} + 5e^{5x}} \right) - 5\left( {4e^{-x} + e^{5x}} \right)} \\ & {= 4e^{-x} + 25e^{5x} + 16e^{-x} - 20e^{5x} - 20e^{-x} - 5e^{5x}} \\ & {= 0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, $$y(x) = 4e^{-x} + e^{5x}$$ is a solution.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving Second-Order Equations with Constant Coefficients
snippet: Solving Second-Order Equations with Constant Coefficients: Find the general solution to the following differential equations. Give your answers as functions of x. y^{''} + 3y^{\prime} - 4y = 0 y^{''} + 6y^{\prime} + 13y = 0 y^{''} +...
body_xml:
<example number="7.6" title="Solving Second-Order Equations with Constant Coefficients">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the general solution to the following differential equations. Give your answers as functions of x.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$y^{''} + 3y^{\prime} - 4y = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$y^{''} + 6y^{\prime} + 13y = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$y^{''} + 2y^{\prime} + y = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$y^{''} - 5y^{\prime} = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$y^{''} - 16y = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$y^{''} + 16y = 0$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Note that all these equations are already given in standard form (step 1).</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The characteristic equation is $$\lambda^{2} + 3\lambda - 4 = 0$$ (step 2). This factors into $$\left( {\lambda + 4} \right)\left( {\lambda - 1} \right) = 0,$$ so the roots of the characteristic equation are $$\lambda_{1} = -4$$ and $$\lambda_{2} = 1$$ (step 3). Then the general solution to the differential equation is $$y(x) = c_{1}e^{-4x} + c_{2}e^{x} \text{(step 4)} .$$</item>
        <item>The characteristic equation is $$\lambda^{2} + 6\lambda + 13 = 0$$ (step 2). Applying the quadratic formula, we see this equation has complex conjugate roots $$-3 \pm 2i$$ (step 3). Then the general solution to the differential equation is $$y(t) = e^{-3t}\left( {c_{1}\cos 2t + c_{2}\sin 2t} \right) \text{(step 4)} .$$</item>
        <item>The characteristic equation is $$\lambda^{2} + 2\lambda + 1 = 0$$ (step 2). This factors into $$\left( {\lambda + 1} \right)^{2} = 0,$$ so the characteristic equation has a repeated real root $$\lambda = -1$$ (step 3). Then the general solution to the differential equation is $$y(t) = c_{1}e^{-t} + c_{2}te^{-t} \text{(step 4).}$$</item>
        <item>The characteristic equation is $$\lambda^{2} - 5\lambda$$ (step 2). This factors into $$\lambda\left( {\lambda - 5} \right) = 0,$$ so the roots of the characteristic equation are $$\lambda_{1} = 0$$ and $$\lambda_{2} = 5$$ (step 3). Note that $$e^{0x} = e^{0} = 1,$$ so our first solution is just a constant. Then the general solution to the differential equation is $$y(x) = c_{1} + c_{2}e^{5x} \text{(step 4)} .$$</item>
        <item>The characteristic equation is $$\lambda^{2} - 16 = 0$$ (step 2). This factors into $$(\lambda + 4)(\lambda - 4) = 0,$$ so the roots of the characteristic equation are $$\lambda_{1} = 4$$ and $$\lambda_{2} = -4$$ (step 3). Then the general solution to the differential equation is $$y(x) = c_{1}e^{4x} + c_{2}e^{-4x} \text{(step 4)} .$$</item>
        <item>The characteristic equation is $$\lambda^{2} + 16 = 0$$ (step 2). This has complex conjugate roots $$\pm 4i$$ (step 3). Note that $$e^{0x} = e^{0} = 1,$$ so the exponential term in our solution is just a constant. Then the general solution to the differential equation is $$y(t) = c_{1}\cos 4t + c_{2}\sin 4t \text{(step 4)} .$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Solving an Initial-Value Problem: Solve the following initial-value problem: y^{''} + 3y^{\prime} - 4y = 0, y(0) = 1, y^{\prime}(0) = -9. We already solved this differential equation in Example 7.6a. and found the general solution to be...
body_xml:
<example number="7.7" title="Solving an Initial-Value Problem">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following initial-value problem: $$y^{''} + 3y^{\prime} - 4y = 0,$$ $$y(0) = 1,$$ $$y^{\prime}(0) = -9.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We already solved this differential equation in Example 7.6a. and found the general solution to be</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(x) = c_{1}e^{-4x} + c_{2}e^{x}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime}(x) = -4c_{1}e^{-4x} + c_{2}e^{x}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>When $$x = 0,$$ we have $$y(0) = c_{1} + c_{2}$$ and $$y^{\prime}(0) = -4c_{1} + c_{2}.$$ Applying the initial conditions, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {c_{1} + c_{2}} & = & 1 \\ {-4c_{1} + c_{2}} & = & {-9.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then $$c_{1} = 1 - c_{2}.$$ Substituting this expression into the second equation, we see that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {-4(1 - c_{2}) + c_{2}} & = & -9 \\ {-4 + 4c_{2} + c_{2}} & = & -9 \\ {5c_{2}} & = & -5 \\ c_{2} & = & {-1.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, $$c_{1} = 2$$ and the solution to the initial-value problem is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(x) = 2e^{-4x} - e^{x}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="7.8" title="Solving an Initial-Value Problem and Graphing the Solution">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve the following initial-value problem and graph the solution:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y^{''} + 6y^{\prime} + 13y = 0, y(0) = 0, y^{\prime}(0) = 2$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We already solved this differential equation in Example 7.6b. and found the general solution to be</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(x) = e^{-3x}\left( {c_{1}\cos 2x + c_{2}\sin 2x} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime}(x) = e^{-3x}\left( {-2c_{1}\sin 2x + 2c_{2}\cos 2x} \right) - 3e^{-3x}\left( {c_{1}\cos 2x + c_{2}\sin 2x} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>When $$x = 0,$$ we have $$y(0) = c_{1}$$ and $$y^{\prime}(0) = 2c_{2} - 3c_{1}.$$ Applying the initial conditions, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} c_{1} & = & 0 \\ {-3c_{1} + 2c_{2}} & = & {2.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, $$c_{1} = 0,$$ $$c_{2} = 1,$$ and the solution to the initial value problem is shown in the following graph.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y = e^{-3x}\sin 2x.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Initial-Value Problem Representing a Spring-Mass System
snippet: Initial-Value Problem Representing a Spring-Mass System: The following initial-value problem models the position of an object with mass attached to a spring. Spring-mass systems are examined in detail in Applications. The solution to the...
body_xml:
<example number="7.9" title="Initial-Value Problem Representing a Spring-Mass System">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The following initial-value problem models the position of an object with mass attached to a spring. Spring-mass systems are examined in detail in Applications. The solution to the differential equation gives the position of the mass with respect to a neutral (equilibrium) position (in meters) at any given time. (Note that for spring-mass systems of this type, it is customary to define the downward direction as positive.)</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y^{''} + 2y^{\prime} + y = 0,y(0) = 1,y^{\prime}(0) = 0$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Solve the initial-value problem and graph the solution. What is the position of the mass at time $$t = 2$$ sec? How fast is the mass moving at time $$t = 1$$ sec? In what direction?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>In Example 7.6c. we found the general solution to this differential equation to be</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(t) = c_{1}e^{-t} + c_{2}te^{-t}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime}(t) = -c_{1}e^{-t} + c_{2}\left( {-te^{-t} + e^{-t}} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>When $$t = 0,$$ we have $$y(0) = c_{1}$$ and $$y^{\prime}(0) = -c_{1} + c_{2}.$$ Applying the initial conditions, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} c_{1} & = & 1 \\ {{-c}_{1} + c_{2}} & = & {0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, $$c_{1} = 1,$$ $$c_{2} = 1,$$ and the solution to the initial value problem is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(t) = e^{-t} + te^{-t}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This solution is represented in the following graph. At time $$t = 2,$$ the mass is at position $$y(2) = e^{-2} + 2e^{-2} = 3e^{-2} \approx 0.406$$ m below equilibrium.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To calculate the velocity at time $$t = 1,$$ we need to find the derivative. We have $$y(t) = e^{-t} + te^{-t},$$ so</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime}(t) = -e^{-t} + e^{-t} - te^{-t} = -te^{-t}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then $$y^{\prime}(1) = -e^{-1} \approx - 0.3679.$$ At time $$t = 1,$$ the mass is moving upward at 0.3679 m/sec.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Solving a Boundary-Value Problem
snippet: Solving a Boundary-Value Problem: In Example 7.6f. we solved the differential equation y^{''} + 16y = 0 and found the general solution to be y(t) = c_{1}\cos 4t + c_{2}\sin 4t. If possible, solve the boundary-value problem if the boundary...
body_xml:
<example number="7.10" title="Solving a Boundary-Value Problem">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>In Example 7.6f. we solved the differential equation $$y^{''} + 16y = 0$$ and found the general solution to be $$y(t) = c_{1}\cos 4t + c_{2}\sin 4t.$$ If possible, solve the boundary-value problem if the boundary conditions are the following:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$y(0) = 0,$$ $$y\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$y(0) = 1,$$ $$y\left( \frac{\pi}{8} \right) = 0$$</item>
        <item>$$y\left( \frac{\pi}{8} \right) = 0,$$ $$y\left( \frac{3\pi}{8} \right) = 2$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(t) = c_{1}\cos 4t + c_{2}\sin 4t.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Applying the first boundary condition given here, we get $$y(0) = c_{1} = 0.$$ So the solution is of the form $$y(t) = c_{2}\sin 4t.$$ When we apply the second boundary condition, though, we get $$y\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) = c_{2}\sin \left( {4\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right)} \right) = c_{2}\sin \pi = 0$$ for all values of $$c_{2}.$$ The boundary conditions are not sufficient to determine a value for $$c_{2},$$ so this boundary-value problem has infinitely many solutions. Thus, $$y(t) = c_{2}\sin 4t$$ is a solution for any value of $$c_{2}.$$</item>
        <item>Applying the first boundary condition given here, we get $$y(0) = c_{1} = 1.$$ Applying the second boundary condition gives $$y\left( \frac{\pi}{8} \right) = c_{2} = 0,$$ so $$c_{2} = 0.$$ In this case, we have a unique solution: $$y(t) = \cos 4t.$$</item>
        <item>Applying the first boundary condition given here, we get $$y\left( \frac{\pi}{8} \right) = c_{2} = 0.$$ However, applying the second boundary condition gives $$y\left( \frac{3\pi}{8} \right) = -c_{2} = 2,$$ so $$c_{2} = -2.$$ We cannot have $$c_{2} = 0 = -2,$$ so this boundary value problem has no solution.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <heading level="4">General Solution to a Nonhomogeneous Equation</heading>

    <paragraph math="block">$$a_{2}(x)y^{''} + a_{1}(x)y^{\prime} + a_{0}(x)y = r(x).$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Also, let $$c_{1}y_{1}(x) + c_{2}y_{2}(x)$$ denote the general solution to the complementary equation. Then, the general solution to the nonhomogeneous equation is given by</paragraph>

title: Verifying the General Solution
snippet: Verifying the General Solution: Given that y_{p}(x) = x is a particular solution to the differential equation y^{''} + y = x, write the general solution and check by verifying that the solution satisfies the equation. The complementary...
body_xml:
<example number="7.11" title="Verifying the General Solution">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Given that $$y_{p}(x) = x$$ is a particular solution to the differential equation $$y^{''} + y = x,$$ write the general solution and check by verifying that the solution satisfies the equation.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The complementary equation is $$y^{''} + y = 0,$$ which has the general solution $$c_{1}\cos x + c_{2}\sin x.$$ So, the general solution to the nonhomogeneous equation is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(x) = c_{1}\cos x + c_{2}\sin x + x.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To verify that this is a solution, substitute it into the differential equation. We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime}(x) = -c_{1}\sin x + c_{2}\cos x + 1 \text{and} y^{''}(x) = -c_{1}\cos x - c_{2}\sin x.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {y^{''}(x) + y(x)} & {= -c_{1}\cos x - c_{2}\sin x + c_{1}\cos x + c_{2}\sin x + x} \\ & {= x.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, $$y(x)$$ is a solution to $$y^{''} + y = x.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Undetermined Coefficients When r(x)r(x) Is a Polynomial
snippet: Undetermined Coefficients When r(x)r(x) Is a Polynomial: Find the general solution to y^{''} + 4y^{\prime} + 3y = 3x. The complementary equation is y^{''} + 4y^{\prime} + 3y = 0, with general solution c_{1}e^{-x} + c_{2}e^{-3x}. Since r(x)...
body_xml:
<example number="7.12" title="Undetermined Coefficients When r(x)r(x) Is a Polynomial">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the general solution to $$y^{''} + 4y^{\prime} + 3y = 3x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The complementary equation is $$y^{''} + 4y^{\prime} + 3y = 0,$$ with general solution $$c_{1}e^{-x} + c_{2}e^{-3x}.$$ Since $$r(x) = 3x,$$ the particular solution might have the form $$y_{p}(x) = Ax + B.$$ If this is the case, then we have $$y_{p}{}^{\prime}(x) = A$$ and $$y_{p}{} \text{''} (x) = 0.$$ For $$y_{p}$$ to be a solution to the differential equation, we must find values for $$A$$ and $$B$$ such that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {y^{''} + 4y^{\prime} + 3y} & = & {3x} \\ {0 + 4(A) + 3(Ax + B)} & = & {3x} \\ {3Ax + (4A + 3B)} & = & {3x.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Setting coefficients of like terms equal, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {3A} & = & 3 \\ {4A + 3B} & = & {0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, $$A = 1$$ and $$B = - \frac{4}{3},$$ so $$y_{p}(x) = x - \frac{4}{3}$$ and the general solution is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(x) = c_{1}e^{-x} + c_{2}e^{-3x} + x - \frac{4}{3}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Undetermined Coefficients When r(x)r(x) Is an Exponential: Find the general solution to y^{''} - y^{\prime} - 2y = 2e^{3x}. The complementary equation is y^{''} - y^{\prime} - 2y = 0, with the general solution c_{1}e^{-x} + c_{2}e^{2x}....
body_xml:
<example number="7.13" title="Undetermined Coefficients When r(x)r(x) Is an Exponential">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the general solution to $$y^{''} - y^{\prime} - 2y = 2e^{3x}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The complementary equation is $$y^{''} - y^{\prime} - 2y = 0,$$ with the general solution $$c_{1}e^{-x} + c_{2}e^{2x}.$$ Since $$r(x) = 2e^{3x},$$ the particular solution might have the form $$y_{p}(x) = Ae^{3x}.$$ Then, we have $$y_{p}{}^{\prime}(x) = 3Ae^{3x}$$ and $$y_{p}{} \text{''} (x) = 9Ae^{3x}.$$ For $$y_{p}$$ to be a solution to the differential equation, we must find a value for $$A$$ such that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} {y^{''} - y^{\prime} - 2y} & = & {2e^{3x}} \\ {9Ae^{3x} - 3Ae^{3x} - 2Ae^{3x}} & = & {2e^{3x}} \\ {4Ae^{3x}} & = & {2e^{3x}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, $$4A = 2$$ and $$A = {1/2}.$$ Then, $$y_{p}(x) = \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)e^{3x},$$ and the general solution is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y(x) = c_{1}e^{-x} + c_{2}e^{2x} + \frac{1}{2}e^{3x}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>
